title: A Capability Kernel for Agent Authorization: Design and Threat Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Capability Kernel for Agent Authorization: Design and Threat Model
detail.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly decide what input/output (IO) actions to take-reading files, calling tools, invoking models, spawning subagents-while the authorization of those actions is left implicit in the agent framework or the language model itself. We describe authgate-kernel, a minimal trusted computing base (TCB) that interposes a structural, deterministic authorization check between any decision-maker and any IO target. The contribution is a design and threat model : authority is represented as a chain of signed, scoped, expiring capability proofs, and a small stateless verify function decides Permit/Deny with no heuristics, no model calls, and no global state. We position the design against policy engines (OPA/Rego), OS mandatory access control (SELinux), object-capability systems, and syscall sandboxes (seccomp/gVisor), arguing that the distinguishing property is a small, attenuating, revocable capability chain bound to a cryptographic trust root. We are deliberately precise about verification status. The design's safety invariants are specified in TLA+ and partially proved in Lean 4 and Kani; however, at the time of writing the TLA+ model has not been run through the TLC model checker (no Java toolchain available), two Lean theorems are sorry-admitted, three properties are stated as axioms reducible to cryptographic or undecidability boundaries, and six Lean "theorems" are tautological stubs. We therefore make no blanket "formally verified" claim; we present a verification-status table whose entries are a strict subset of what is actually machine-checkable from the committed artifacts. The Python reference implementation's test suite (1167 tests) passes; the Rust TCB test suite could not be run in our environment and we report no count for it rather than inventing one. We give no end-to-end latency benchmark because we could not run one reproducibly.

detail.abstract:
Autonomous AI agents now hold credentials, interpret goals, and execute multi-step operations inside production systems, including in regulated financial institutions. A capable governance literature has emerged in response: zero trust control frameworks, threat taxonomies, and binding regulation. What has not emerged is a disclosure layer: a standard format in which an organization states which controls it operates, at which maturity tier, supported by what evidence. Every prior trust market of comparable stakes solved this problem with a comparable instrument, financial reporting through IFRS, payments interoperability through ISO 20022, and service organization security through SOC 2. This paper examines how those disclosure and interoperability standards achieved adoption, extracts the conditions that generalize, and applies them to agent governance. It then presents the design rationale for AA-1, the Agent Governance Attestation, an open seven-section disclosure specification built on Anthropic's Zero Trust for AI Agents control taxonomy, with particular attention to the property that distinguishes agentic systems from every prior attestation subject: their behaviour changes
between filings. The paper proposes a continuous attestation model in which validity is bound to architecture state and behavioural baselines rather than to the calendar, defines sector profiles for financial services and for government and high-assurance deployments, and states the standard's limitations plainly, including the gaming risks of self-attestation and the open measurement problem for behavioural conformance

detail.title: From Agent Identity to Agent Economy: Measuring the Operational Readiness of ERC-8004 AI Agents
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether blockchain-registered AI agents demonstrate operational readiness beyond identity registration. Using a dataset of ERC-8004 agents on Ethereum, we construct an agent-level feature table covering identity status, metadata, service declarations, reputation feedback, transfers, and cross-chain registration. We develop an operational readiness framework based on observable evidence layers and complement it with network analysis of owner-agent, feedback-client, wallet-transfer, and combined evidence relationships. The results show that early ERC-8004 adoption is registration-heavy but operationally shallow. While the identity layer is visible at scale, metadata availability, service exposure, reputation formation, and cross-chain evidence remain limited. Ownership and feedback activity are also highly concentrated, suggesting that early participation is shaped by a small number of high-activity wallets and clients. The network analysis further shows that richer operational evidence clusters around a small subset of agents rather than being broadly distributed across the ecosystem. The findings suggest that ERC-8004 provides an important identity layer for decentralized AI agents, but the transition from agent identity to agent economy remains incomplete.

detail.abstract: A single architectural pattern explains two June 2026 supply-chain compromises that on the surface involve different systems and different threat communities. In the first incident, attackers adopted orphan or abandoned packages in the Arch User Repository (AUR), spoofed git commit metadata to inherit the trust of the long-standing maintainer, and delivered a Rust binary infostealer paired with an optional eBPF rootkit through over four hundred confirmed packages, with community trackers reporting up to one thousand five hundred. In the second, Liu and colleagues audited 98,380 agent skills across public marketplaces for their USENIX Security 2026 paper and reported 157 confirmed malicious skills covering a median of three of six kill-chain phases, with 84.2 percent of vulnerabilities hidden in natural-language instructions rather than in code. Both attacks succeeded because runtime enforcement trusted the manifest's declarations without binding those declarations to a verified origin. This paper analyses the two cases through a single architectural lens, names the pattern as trust inheritance without manifest-bound enforcement, and surveys  the closely related agentic-workflow lock-file mitigation introduced by GitHub Agentic Workflows in public preview on the same day as the AUR campaign onset. The paper argues that the manifest-to-runtime binding pattern named in OWASP AISVS C9 (research chapter, merged June 2026) and the  chain-audit schema being drafted in adjacent CSA Non-Human Identity working-group work provide a verification-side architecture for both layers. Open research questions on cross-layer detection, integrity-binding scope, and reversibility-graded gate selection are catalogued.

title: A Unified, Invariant,Geometry Based Measurement Theory for Machine Cognition: NCAP-10

detail.title: A Unified, Invariant,Geometry Based Measurement Theory for Machine Cognition: NCAP-10
detail.abstract:
NCAP-10 is a management accessible measurement framework for evaluating how artificial and machine cognitive systems behave, adapt, and regulate themselves over time, independent of their underlying architecture. Unlike benchmark or human norm based evaluation, NCAP-10 represents a cognitive system as a geometric object on a difficulty manifold equipped with a family of measurement distributions and an induced Fisher information metric. From this object, NCAP-10 derives architecture invariant observables stability, sensitivity, synchrony, plasticity, memory retention, attractor structure, and capability as well as an economic layer that expresses value, risk, return on resources, and control cost as invariant functionals on the same geometric structure. 
     This revision closes the gaps present in the original NCAP-10 draft. Every abstract operator (Φ, Ψ, Ω, E) is given an explicit construction in terms of g I and p(m | d), illustrated by a fully worked example (a two channel difficulty manifold with a logistic measurement model). The admissible transformation group T is defined concretely as reparametrizations of the difficulty manifold together with sufficient statistic recodings of the observable space, and the distortion metric d G on the space of information metrics is given explicitly as the affine invariant metric on symmetric positive definite matrices. The Invariance Theorem is proved directly from these constructions rather than asserted by definitional fiat. The Estimation Procedures section is completed and made operational for at least three concrete system classes (transformer based language models, recurrent/attractor networks, and neuromorphic spiking systems). Each section is accompanied by a diagram illustrating the corresponding structure.

title: Moneyness as Closure Capacity: A Closure-Service Theory of Moneyness

detail.title: Moneyness as Closure Capacity: A Closure-Service Theory of Moneyness
detail.abstract: Money is final settlement authority. This paper argues that moneyness exists as closure capacity and varies as closure service. Closure capacity concerns institutional eligibility to discharge obligations within a settlement domain; closure service concerns the strength, reliability, and scope of discharge. Existing theories explain acceptability, liquidity, monetary hierarchy, legal authority, payment finality, or the unit of account, but they do not fully explain how final settlement authority becomes delegated to concrete instruments that close obligations in specific domains. The paper explains moneyness through a four-part institutional mechanism. Monetary vehicles carry final settlement authority; empowerment mechanisms transmit closure service; monetary proxies perform delegated closure; and settlement domains define where such closure is recognized, tested, and limited. This framework explains why bank deposits, stablecoins, platform balances, central bank reserves, and other money-like instruments possess different degrees of moneyness across domains. Its contribution is conceptual, institutional, and analytical. It distinguishes money from moneyness, identifies the mechanism through which moneyness is generated, and explains the heterogeneity, value, and fragility of money-like instruments without reducing moneyness to liquidity, credit, legal tender status, or denomination. The framework further shows why apparent moneyness can diverge from monetary integrity and why credit expansion can generate obligation-settlement mismatch.

detail.abstract:
Independent barber shops and beauty salons in the United Kingdom continue to rely on fragmented, manual booking processes despite growing consumer demand for digital convenience. This working paper develops and presents an evidence-based business plan and market entry framework for Handsome and Beautiful (HnB), a two-sided digital platform combining AI-powered style try-on with online appointment booking for independent hair, beauty, nail, tattoo and piercing businesses in Belfast, Northern Ireland.

The study is grounded in a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic literature review covering platform business model theory, pricing models for two-sided markets and market entry frameworks for digital ventures, drawing on key contributions from Rochet and Tirole (2003), Armstrong (2006), Parker, Van Alstyne and Choudary (2016), Moore (2014), Mamonov (2023) and Bichler (2025). Original primary data was collected through two surveys conducted in Belfast in early 2026: a business survey of 18 independent salon and barber owner-managers, and a customer survey of 103 Belfast residents and regular visitors, analysed using descriptive statistics and thematic coding in Python and Microsoft Excel.

Key findings confirm that the most acute operational pain points among Belfast providers are empty slots and low-capacity utilisation (77.8%), lack of online visibility and difficulty acquiring new clients (61.1%), and scheduling errors and double bookings (61.1%). On the demand side, 68.0% of customer respondents find the HnB concept attractive, 84.5% express openness to an AI try-on feature, and 73.8% indicate willingness to pay a small deposit to secure appointments, while 74.8% expect the platform itself to be free to use.

These findings support a hybrid freemium revenue model combining a 15% commission on new client bookings, an optional £29/month premium subscription for providers, and a £0.75 deposit processing margin per transaction, with customers accessing the platform at no direct cost. The market entry strategy follows a beachhead approach centred on Belfast, prioritising supply-side onboarding of 20–30 reputable local salons before public customer launch. Three-year financial projections indicate revenues growing from approximately £11,200 in Year 1 to £87,100 in Year 3, approaching operational breakeven in Year 3, with an initial funding requirement of £40,000–£50,000. Burn rate analysis confirms that the upper funding bound provides a critical additional buffer of approximately three months under a pessimistic scenario of 20% slower revenue growth.

The paper contributes to the emerging literature on digital platform adoption by locally focused micro-business serving ventures and provides a replicable analytical framework for practitioners and researchers examining platform entry in geographically bounded local service markets.

title: The $812 Billion Illusion: A Law and Economics Case for Replacing PDF with Block-Semantic Trust Architectures
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The $812 Billion Illusion: A Law and Economics Case for Replacing PDF with Block-Semantic Trust Architectures
detail.abstract:
The dominant digital document standard, the Portable Document Format (PDF), ratified by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) in 2008 but engineered by Adobe Systems in 1993, was designed to replicate the visual layout of physical paper on computer displays. While highly successful for printing, it is structurally opaque: text is encoded as positioned glyphs, semantic relationships are absent at the byte level, and data provenance is decoupled from the file itself. In high-friction sectors like United States healthcare, this opacity enforces a continuous reliance on manual administrative processing and proprietary data extraction tools, contributing to an estimated $812 billion in administrative waste annually. Similarly, tax authorities (e.g., IRS, HMRC), securities regulators (e.g., SEC), and sovereign states struggle with verification costs, document forgery, and systemic reporting inefficiencies stemming from unstructured legacy formats.

This paper presents a legal and economic analysis of digital document architecture, introducing the Universal Document™ Standard (UDS) 1.0 as a first-principles, open-source alternative. UDS restructures the document substrate into a block-semantic, tamper-evident framework utilizing cryptographically sealed payloads (.uds), revisable block structures (.udr), and self-contained asset bundles (.udz). We argue that embedding structured semantics, machine readability, and cryptographic signatures directly into the file schema can reduce transaction friction, prevent administrative compliance failures and audit discrepancies, and protect professional sovereignty in a post-Chevron regulatory environment.

This paper also examines the systemic utility of UDS as an infrastructure for national digital sovereignty and zero-trust public identity networks (modeled after frameworks in Sweden and Estonia). By replacing brittle data-scraping middleware and centralized validation databases with self-validating, offline-first document payloads, UDS offers international health authorities (CMS, NHS), tax administrations, and securities markets a highly efficient, non-repudiable format for automated ledger indexing. The paper establishes a socio-economic justification for the implementation of zero-cost, zero-telemetry document SDKs as a public utility to eliminate systemic administrative waste.

detail.abstract: Modern deep generative models, including Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and Diffusion-based Score Matching architectures, synthesize high-dimensional data by learning continuous mappings from low-dimensional latent spaces. However, these models frequently exhibit structural instability, topological tearing, and semantic discontinuity within their latent representations. This paper introduces a novel, mathematically rigorous framework that unifies Riemannian Differential Geometry and Optimal Transport (OT) theory to analyze, quantify, and enforce structural stability in generative latent spaces. By equipping the latent manifold with a data-dependent pullback metric, we define a localized geometric structure where geodesics accurately reflect semantic trajectories. We formulate a curvature-bounded optimal transport problem under this Riemannian metric, establishing that bounding the sectional curvature minimizes distortion during latent interpolation. Theoretical proofs guarantee the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of the proposed stable transport maps. Experiments conducted across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets validate that bounding latent sectional curvatures within an optimal transport framework guarantees topological preservation, eliminates mode collapse, and significantly reduces Fréchet Inception Distance (FID).

title: Walking a Tightrope: Freemium Design and Marketplace Incentives in Generative AI Services
affiliations: , , Arizona State University (ASU) - Department of Information Systems and Tsinghua University, School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Walking a Tightrope: Freemium Design and Marketplace Incentives in Generative AI Services
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of generative AI (GenAI) has given rise to a new class of digital service economies, in which providers monetize general-purpose GenAI services through freemium business models while increasingly experimenting with marketplaces for user-generated custom services. Although these marketplaces enhance user value by enabling access to specialized custom services and generate strategically valuable data through custom-service usage, they also impose developer compensation costs and reshape providers' incentives for core service design. Consequently, whether marketplace introduction is economically beneficial and how providers should jointly design free-tier quality and developer compensation remain unclear. To address these questions, we develop a game-theoretic model of a GenAI provider that offers free and premium versions of general services and decides whether to introduce a marketplace for custom services. In the marketplace regime, the provider jointly chooses free-tier quality and perusage developer compensation, recognizing that these two levers shape user adoption, marketplace activity, customdata generation, and overall profitability. Our analysis yields four key insights. First, marketplace introduction is not always profit-enhancing; it can reduce provider profit when user adoption costs for general services are sufficiently high. Second, after marketplace introduction, the provider may optimally improve rather than degrade free-tier quality, particularly when developers' production costs are relatively low. Third, the optimal per-usage compensation does not necessarily rise with the value of custom data; it can decrease when developers' production costs are high. Fourth, marketplace adoption does not always improve social welfare; welfare gains arise only when the marginal value of custom data is sufficiently high, and even then, a welfare-improving marketplace may remain unattractive to the provider. These findings highlight how this emerging business model, which combines freemium service provision, a user-generated service marketplace, and custom-data generation, can fundamentally alter stakeholder incentives and the design of GenAI marketplaces, while also suggesting a potential role for policy in aligning private incentives with societal value.

detail.title: Riding AI To Utopia Or Dystopia? Nlp, Llm, And News Informatics Insights For Artificial Intelligence Impacts On Education, Healthcare, Robotics And Workforce, Changing Human Society
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is accelerating societal transformation at an unprecedented pace, generating both utopian aspirations and dystopian anxieties. Human civilization has undergone fundamental changes through every technological revolution starting with the Industrial Age and continuing through the digital era as AI emerges as the next paradigm shift. This paper studies the public discourse on AI by analyzing extensive news headlines on AI using natural language processing (NLP) methods. Our research applies sentiment analysis and topic modeling to a global dataset across education, healthcare, robotics, workforce, and society to identify the dominant narratives shaping public perception. Media coverage presents AI as a dual force that brings human benefits and existential dangers according to our research findings. By moving beyond the utopia-dystopia dichotomy, we show that AI's social effects will emerge from the dynamic relationship between governance systems, ethical protections, and Human-Enhancive AI (HEAI) frameworks. We provide practical insights about AI's future impact and present strategies for maximizing AI benefits while mitigating its risks.

detail.abstract:
AI systems can succeed at the task while weakening the human being responsible for the task. That failure mode is not captured by most current AI evaluation, which primarily measures model behavior, output quality, safety, fairness, and moment-level user experience. This paper argues that the next generation of AI evaluation must also measure what repeated AI use leaves the human able to do across time.

The paper introduces capacity-degradation risk: the risk that repeated interaction with AI weakens the human capacities required for meaningful oversight, judgment, authorship, and responsibility. It defines Heart as an operational design construct composed of seven capacities: agency, discernment, authorship, moral attention, humility, courage, and truthful self-relation. The paper distinguishes model-behavior risk, addressed by model specifications and safety evaluations, from human-capacity effects, which current evaluation practice does not systematically measure.

The argument reframes “human in the loop” as an insufficient design standard unless the human capacity required for meaningful participation in the loop is itself preserved. It proposes seven principles for Heart-preserving AI design, a minimal viable evaluation using baseline and withdrawal testing, and a Capacity-Degradation Risk Report for structured governance, product, and audit contexts.

The paper is conceptual and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim empirical validation of capacity degradation through AI use. It makes the failure mode precise enough to test and proposes the design and evaluation apparatus required to test it.

title: PRISM: A Source-First Enterprise Architecture Standard and Framework Family for the Modern Organization
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: PRISM: A Source-First Enterprise Architecture Standard and Framework Family for the Modern Organization
detail.abstract: The current enterprise architecture landscape, while solid in theory has a gap problem, not a theory problem. The major frameworks such as Zachman, TOGAF, ArchiMate-are rigorous, they are well-maintained, and widely documented. They were also designed for organizations with dedicated EA practitioners, have separate governance processes, and architecture as a separate discipline. However, most engineering teams do not work that way. Much of the architecture work ends up in Visio files, draw.io and shared drives, which gets stale quickly within months, and ends up describing a system that no longer exists. PRISM takes a different starting point: architecture artifacts as plain-text YAML files, which are governed by git, validated by JSON Schemas, and authored by anyone on the team. The framework organizes the enterprise across five interconnected layers which includes, People and Place, Reality, Intent, Signal, and Movement, and additionally extends into six focused disciplines covering infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI architecture, application architecture, data, and product validation. By design, all seven frameworks share the same authoring conventions throughout. This paper introduces the PRISM framework family: its design rationale, the structure of each framework, how they connect, and where the current boundaries are. PRISM is presented as an open standard at version 1.0, and is designed to be refined through practitioner feedback and adoption over time.

detail.abstract:
AI can make human work look better while leaving the human less able to do the work unaided. This paper formalizes that hidden tradeoff.

It introduces capacity-degradation risk: the measurable risk that repeated AI collaboration erodes the human judgment, reasoning, and discernment the collaboration still depends on. The paper’s central result is that observed output quality can decouple from retained human capacity by design. As machine assistance increases, quality can remain high while human capacity declines, making the most obvious performance measure an actively misleading one.

To make the risk measurable, the paper proposes a capacity ledger, a capacity-dynamics model, a realization function, and a retained-responsibility scope limiter that separates harmful erosion from benign specialization. It then specifies a two-leg instrument: an offload-ratio estimator derived from transcript structure, validated against unaided probes.

The paper does not claim field validation. It offers a reference specification and research MVP for a missing layer in human-AI evaluation: not just what the pair produced, but what the human remains able to do.

detail.abstract: Human oversight is not a control merely because it is assigned. It is a control only if it can be performed under the conditions in which the AI system will actually operate. AI deployed in critical infrastructure relies on human supervision as a risk control, but existing governance frameworks do not yet provide a cross-sector measurement architecture for determining whether that supervision is performable under operational conditions. This paper specifies one. It identifies four conditions under which a human supervisory layer fails: alert fatigue, automation bias, authorization by decision class, and override and intervention design under load. Each is defined in measurable terms that hold across sectors, because the conditions are properties of human cognition rather than of any one sector's technology. The conditions are organized into a measurement architecture that separates the crosssector specification from its sector-specific instantiation. The specification is worked through four critical-infrastructure sectors and mapped onto the trustworthiness characteristics and the governance, mapping, and measurement functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

detail.abstract: The European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) subjects conduct long governed by Article 102 TFEU—product integration, most-favored-nation clauses, self-preferencing, data combination, and duty-to-deal obligations—to categorical rules stripped of effects analysis, efficiency defenses, and the consumer-welfare standard. This white paper argues that the DMA marks a decisive move from market oversight to market ordering. Where competition law polices market processes through evidence, effects, defenses, and judicial review, the DMA empowers the European Commission to prescribe market outcomes through open-ended standards of “fairness” and “contestability.” The Commission’s early enforcement record against Meta, Apple, and Google shows how the DMA’s structural-unfairness axiom gives the Commission continuing authority to redesign digital markets from the center. Business-user satisfaction becomes the regime’s proxy for the public interest, while consumer choice is instrumentalized: respected when it moves users away from gatekeeper ecosystems, treated as evidence of insufficient intervention when it does not. The paper situates the DMA within a broader political-economy shift. Its logic reflects ordoliberal confidence in a nobilitas naturalis capable of defining the market order, Karl Polanyi’s account of market re-embedding, and Herman Schwartz’s cycles of state-market reassertion. But under the DMA, re-embedding occurs through the administrative state, not society. The result is economic statecraft: competition policy used to redistribute rents, shape market structure, and advance strategic objectives. Parallel moves in Article 102 guidance, merger control, and industrial policy suggest that digital markets may be the leading edge of a broader turn toward market ordering. The paper ends by arguing that the DMA’s costs are not drafting defects but entailments of the ordering model. By removing effects analysis, efficiency defenses, meaningful merits review, and consumer-welfare constraints, the DMA heightens error costs, aggravates the knowledge problem, weakens resistance to capture, and creates an autopoietic evaluative architecture that reproduces its own assumptions rather than tests them. Whether competition law’s disciplining safeguards can be reconstructed inside a regime designed to dispense with them may determine the legitimacy of the next decade of European market governance.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of the global agro-food sector has led to the generation of massive quantities of agricultural waste, fundamentally composed of recalcitrant lignocellulosic biomass. Traditional disposal methods, such as incineration and landfilling, exacerbate environmental degradation and greenhouse gas emissions. Simultaneously, there is growing toxicological concern regarding the persistent use of synthetic food preservatives (e.g., BHA, BHT, and sulfites), which have been linked to oxidative stress and carcinogenic pathways. This research explores a highly scalable, sustainable "Green Chemistry" approach to address both critical challenges by integrating solid waste management with bioenergy production. The study investigates the kinetic efficacy of a specialized microbial enzyme consortium primarily comprising Cellulases, Pectinases, and Xylanases in catalytically hydrolyzing the complex structural matrices of agricultural residues (specifically citrus peels and wheat straw). The primary objective is to facilitate the enhanced release of bound phenolic compounds and potent antioxidants for use as natural, safe antimicrobial agents in food matrices. Furthermore, to establish a true zero-waste circular bioeconomy, the resulting sugar-rich secondary hydrolysate is redirected as an optimal, highly fermentable carbon substrate for Microbial Fuel Cells (MFCs). By cultivating exoelectrogenic bacterial biofilms on graphite anodes, the system synergistically generates sustainable bioelectricity. This dual biovalorization strategy aims to significantly reduce the environmental footprint of academic institutions while providing high-value bio-additives for the food industry and localized renewable energy for campus infracts.

title: Spectral Shape Residual: A Lightweight Spec-Tral Diagnostic For Attention Weight Matrices

detail.title: Spectral Shape Residual: A Lightweight Spec-Tral Diagnostic For Attention Weight Matrices

detail.abstract:
We introduce the Spectral Shape Residual (SSR), a lightweight metric computed directly from the query and key weight matrices of attention layers-no forward pass, no training data needed. SSR measures how similar the singular value distributions of W Q and W K are: when they match perfectly, SSR is zero. 

We study SSR across four settings organized as a 2×2 analytical framework (toy vs. production LLM; static snapshot vs. training dynamics)-a design that systematically covers the conditions under which spectral weight-space signals can arise. In toy transformers trained on modular arithmetic, SSR drops to near-machine precision after grokking, and this drop happens 200-1,900 steps before the model generalizes-making SSR an early warning signal. In production LLMs (LLaMA-3-8B (hereafter LLaMA), Gemma-4-31B-IT (hereafter Gemma)), SSR decreases systematically with layer depth, and RL-distilled models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B (hereafter R1)) show lower SSR than their base model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (hereafter Qwen)) in 45 out of 48 layers. In OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining, 18.8% of attention heads show persistent monotonic decline in SSR before grokking completes, concentrated in deep layers (L10-L13); the median SSR of these heads falls 40% below its peak 582B tokens before grokking completes. 

SSR requires only one SVD per attention head and no evaluation data, making it deployable as a zero-overhead structural health monitor directly inside training pipelines. For both pre-training (does the model grok?) and post-training (does RL alignment shift spectral structure?), SSR provides a continuous signal without running a single forward pass.

detail.abstract: This paper asks whether the validity of Clausewitzian war theory is bound to a particular social formation, and what follows when the frame is applied to a formation it does not describe. Reading On War as an unfinished, developing work, it reconstructs from the text a formation law: Clausewitz gives the form of war as the historical description of a formation, not as the nature of war, and states this himself (VIII.6.B; VIII.3.B; I.1.23; VIII.2). The boundedness concerns the thick operational apparatus, not the universal element of the primary trinity. From the three conditions of the eighteenth-century cabinet-war formation, a controllable central will, calculability in number and time, and the extinction of the tendency toward the extreme, the paper derives a falsifiable validity domain whose diagnostic sign is closability. It positions the account between two debates: against the new wars and non-trinitarian thesis, the claim is not that Clausewitz is obsolete but that he is formation-bounded, which is his own claim; against the weaponized interdependence and geoeconomics literature, the claim is that flow is a medium, of which weaponization is a derivative operation. A sociology-of-knowledge argument explains why the frame persists outside its domain. The application is illustrative, not predictive.

This article examines the Mathadi Boards in Pune, India, as a pioneering example of
corporatist regulation adapted to the informal economy. These tripartite institutions —
comprising workers, employers, and the state — negotiate legally binding agreements
on wages and working conditions for informal labourers, offering social protections and

title: Pragmatic AGI: The Jagged Frontier as Mirrored Knowledge Silos
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Pragmatic AGI: The Jagged Frontier as Mirrored Knowledge Silos
detail.abstract: Frontier language models are highly capable but unevenly so, strong on one task and weak on an adjacent one, in a pattern known as the jagged frontier. The jaggedness has more than one cause. This paper isolates one that has gone unrecognised. On the mirror thesis, a model trained on human text inherits not only human biases but the siloed structure of human knowledge production. It therefore appears to form cross-domain synthesis chiefly where human authors co-located the knowledge, so that the bridges no one wrote are the bridges it never formed. This is the paper's central conjecture, and it is distinct from substrate failures such as tokenisation and arithmetic that more scale will not fix. The reframe is that, for a large class of these gaps, the missing synthesis is constructible from materials the model already holds: entailed in the deductive case, and in the abductive case producible as a candidate that still needs validation. Closing such gaps requires no new external data, only a formed path. Whether such paths can be built deliberately and at scale is an open problem the paper defines rather than solves. The target it names is the de-siloed union of human knowledge, reached by constructing links rather than by scaling, and bounded by a residue: novelty beyond the human frontier and causal reasoning that a model trained on observational text does not reliably reach on its own. The claim is falsifiable: a model's cross-field synthesis should track whether its training corpus connected two fields, not merely how much it covered each, a contrast open in principle to test on models whose training data is documented.

detail.title: Extraction and Analysis of Microplastics Present in Commercially Available Table Salts in the Philippines
detail.abstract: Microplastics are synthetic polymeric particles (1 μm to 5 mm) that persist in various environments due to their resistance to degradation and continuous anthropogenic inputs, posing ecological and health risks. To address the limited data on dietary microplastic contamination in the Philippines, this study analyzed 21 locally and commercially available table salt brands. The mean microplastic abundance across all brands was 91 ± 95 particles kg-1. Philippine-harvested salts exhibited higher mean microplastic abundance (148 ± 97 particles kg-1) than those imported from Australia (63 ± 29 particles kg-1), suggesting potential geographical influences. Coarse salts contained more microplastics (144 ± 117 particles kg-1) than fine salts (55 ± 44 particles kg-1), and unrefined salts also showed higher mean abundance (124 ± 78 particles kg-1) than refined salts (69 ± 82 particles kg-1), suggesting that salt processing and refinement practices may affect contamination levels. Fibers (50.87%) were the most dominant shape, followed by fragments (46.01%) and sheets (3.13%). In terms of color, the most common were blue (51.22%), black (23.78%), and red (14.93%). Polymer identification of 17 representative samples via attenuated total reflectance-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy identified probable polymer types, such as polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene terephthalate, polyacrylic fiber, polyamide, polypropylene, and low-density polyethylene, likely originating from packaging materials, synthetic textiles, fishing gear, construction materials, and household plastic products. Finally, the estimated annual ingestion by a Filipino adult was 347 ± 361 microplastics from table salts alone, posing potential health risks that warrant further investigation.

title: Environmental Breakdown and Inflation Management: A socio-ecological understanding
affiliations: UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, , UCL Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose and London School of Economics

detail.title: Environmental Breakdown and Inflation Management: A socio-ecological understanding
detail.abstract: This paper develops a socio-ecological theory of inflation that integrates ecological economics, conflict inflation theory and rent theory. Ecologically induced price shocks driven by ongoing climate change and nature loss may become increasingly significant at the macroeconomic level due to: (1) the centrality of nature-reliant sectors in production networks; and (2) the market concentration and power of critical private corporations to influence price dynamics and amplify shocks. In the medium to long run, the ability of firms to adapt to price shocks through trade, input and technological substitution will become increasingly impaired, as ecological and geopolitical shocks increase in severity, breadth and complexity. We extend conflict inflation theory to also account for who owns and controls access to resources made increasingly scarce by ecological degradation, as rent extraction may further amplify price pressures. Finally, financial feedback effects may also exacerbate price pressures, notably via the role of speculative demand in inflating prices in globally traded commodity markets. These dynamics mean that supply-side inflationary pressures may shift from being transitory and idiosyncratic, as they are currently treated by central banks, to persistent and structural. We explore the implications of this new paradigm for macroeconomic policy makers and suggest a greater role for fiscal and industrial policy interventions, as well adjustments to current monetary policy frameworks.

title: Public Sentiment Toward Nuclear Energy in Southeast Asia: Evidence from Online Discourse
affiliations: and

detail.title: Public Sentiment Toward Nuclear Energy in Southeast Asia: Evidence from Online Discourse
detail.abstract: Southeast Asia has recently seen renewed debate over deploying nuclear power plants, yet it remains poorly understood how public opinion evolves over time. This paper examines how Reddit (a large international discussion platform) users discuss acceptance of nuclear energy in this area, with Singapore as the focal case, along with Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines as comparative cases. The analysis uses 2,157 Singapore comments and 4,696 comparison comments in neighboring countries, spanning 2016 to 2025. Across the corpus, most comments are neutral or informational (64.0%). Pro-nuclear comments nevertheless outnumber anti-nuclear comments in all four countries where Singapore is the most pro-leaning case in net terms. The most supportive frames are small modular reactors, energy security, climate and clean energy benefits, and cost comparisons with other energy sources. The most cautionary frames concern safety, waste, siting, regional spillovers, and institutional capability. Our central finding is that public acceptance is conditional. Specifically, support rises when nuclear is presented as a modern, modular, professionally regulated technology, and declines when discussions turn to catastrophicaccident scenarios, corruption, old plant legacies, or unresolved waste and siting problems. Our findings provide timely insights into public opinion dynamics that could inform policy design and communication strategies.

title: Effectiveness and safety of community-based ivermectin interventions for malaria control in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis

detail.title: Effectiveness and safety of community-based ivermectin interventions for malaria control in Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Background: Malaria control progress has stalled in many sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) settings despite widespread deployment of existing prevention and treatment strategies. Ivermectin has emerged as a potential transmission-modifying intervention, but evidence of its effectiveness remains uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate its effects on malaria epidemiological, entomological, and safety outcomes in African settings.

Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Ovid Embase, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), and the Pan African Clinical Trial Registry for eligible African studies evaluating ivermectin alone or combined with antimalarial interventions. Random-effects meta-analysis using Restricted Maximum Likelihood estimation was conducted for outcome-specific pooled analyses. Multilevel meta-analysis, robust variance estimation, and Bayesian sensitivity analyses were additionally performed to account for correlated outcomes and reconstructed variance structures.

Findings: Twelve studies contributed 197 outcome-timepoint estimates, including 175 post-intervention estimates. Malaria incidence or infection outcomes showed modest reduction in malaria burden associated with ivermectin-based interventions (risk ratio, RR 0·93, 95% confidence interval, CI 0·85–1·02), although effects varied across intervention settings and implementation strategies. Entomological outcomes demonstrated the strongest intervention effects, with mosquito mortality substantially reduced following ivermectin exposure (RtR 0·59, 95% CI 0·54–0·64), while entomological inoculation rate outcomes also favoured ivermectin interventions (rate ratio, RtR 0·58, 95% CI 0·35–0·96). Mosquito survival outcomes similarly demonstrated reduced vector survival potential (RtR 0·77, 95% CI 0·58–1·01). Serious adverse events or deaths were not clearly increased (RR 1·05, 95% CI 0·74–1·48), but any adverse events were more frequently reported among ivermectin recipients (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.04–2.10).

Interpretation: Community-based ivermectin interventions consistently reduced entomological transmission indicators, although evidence for direct epidemiological benefit remained modest and context-dependent. These findings support ivermectin as a complementary transmission-modifying intervention rather than a standalone malaria elimination strategy.

title: House Prices, Saving, and the Owner-Renter Wealth Gap: A Two-Period Model with Evidence from Japan

detail.title: House Prices, Saving, and the Owner-Renter Wealth Gap: A Two-Period Model with Evidence from Japan

detail.abstract: We examine how housing market fluctuations affect household saving at a monthly frequency and, in turn, shape the wealth gap between renters and owners. We develop a simple two period life cycle model in which renters face a rent burden constraint and precautionary motives for owners facing price risk. The model yields two testable predictions: higher house prices squeeze renters' cash flow and reduce their saving, with the effect tapering once rent burdens are already high, whereas owners' saving largely follows income. Based on Japan's monthly aggregate data from 2009 to 2025, we estimate both long-term and short-term responses. For every 1% increase in real house prices, the renter saving rate decreases by about 0.20 percentage points in the baseline and about 0.14 percentage points with instruments, with the largest effect around four months after the shock. The rent-to-income ratio has a critical threshold of 27-28%. Beyond this ratio, the marginal benefit gradually diminishes. For owners, a 1% increase in income raises the saving rate by approximately 0.59 percentage points. These effects are economically significant and independent of specific combinations of control variables. Policies that ease rental burdens or expand rental supply can increase renter saving and limit the widening wealth gap.

title: Ordinal Patterns of  Time-Changed Brownian Motion: Exact Blindness and a Detection Formula

detail.title: Ordinal Patterns of  Time-Changed Brownian Motion: Exact Blindness and a Detection Formula

detail.abstract:
We study the ordinal pattern (permutation) statistics of time-changed Brownian motion, the canonical structure of stochastic-volatility and multifractal asset-price models. Our first results are negative and exact: for any independent volatility clock the sign-pattern probabilities equal their Brownian values identically; and if consecutive equal-length clock increments are exchangeable (as they are for every time-reversible clock, including the Multifractal Random Walk (MRW) at arbitrary intermittency and stationary rough-volatility models without leverage), then all order-3 ordinal pattern probabilities at equal lags take exactly their Brownian values (1/4, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 1/4). Gaussianity is not required: the classical universality theorem for random walks with i.i.d. symmetric increments extends verbatim to conditionally independent increments with exchangeable volatilities. These results imply that equal-lag permutation entropy provably cannot detect multifractality or stochastic volatility of any kind, and they explain, from first principles, the empirical "order self-similarity" of financial data reported by Bandt (2020).

Our second contribution is positive: the blindness is broken exactly where the symmetry is, at unequal lags. For the MRW with intermittency λ² and window-length ratio κ we prove the closed-form deviation

p_132^MRW − p_132^BM = λ² · (√κ / (16π)) · [ ((κ − 1)/κ) · log(1 + κ) − log κ ] + O(λ³),

independent of the sampling lag and of the integral scale. The deviation is carried jointly by the fluctuation of the log clock ratio and by the Jensen gap between typical and mean scaling, the defining feature of multifractality, and the latter dominates. All proofs are self-contained and largely elementary, given the exact moment formulas and standard moment bounds for the multifractal measure; in particular, no small-deviation theory for multiplicative chaos is needed. Together, the results give an identifiability theorem: two ordinal statistics separate model classes that moment-scaling estimators provably conflate.

detail.abstract: On January 23, 2025, the United States Executive Order (14178) banning central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) signaled a major shift in the digital financial landscape, increasing the divide between the traditional banking sector’s centralized model and the tech sector’s push for decentralized alternatives. Despite this temporary roadblock, the banking sector maintains significant structural advantages in addressing critical macroeconomic challenges through programmable digital currencies—offering unprecedented precision in monetary policy implementation, targeted economic intervention during crises, and potential resolution to the persistent “savings problem” that necessitates continuous monetary expansion. Given the banking industry’s entrenched control over monetary infrastructure—and its role in financing the very tech companies advocating for alternative systems—the question becomes: will they have the final say in this digital currency war? As the rest of the world moves forward with CBDCs, will the United States ban solidify the dominance of traditional financial institutions, or create a window for decentralized alternatives like Bitcoin and stablecoins to rise in prominence? This Article argues that the international momentum toward CBDCs will likely continue, with central bank support and their capability to address macroeconomic challenges potentially making the U.S. ban a temporary pause rather than a permanent disruption. However, without concrete legislative action to either cement or overturn the executive order, the future of digital currency in the United States remains uncertain. The resolution of this tension between banking and tech visions for digital currency will be a defining focus of financial policy debates over the next four years and beyond, with profound implications for America’s role in the global monetary order.

title: Optimal Allocation with Sequential Screening and Costly Verification

detail.title: Optimal Allocation with Sequential Screening and Costly Verification
detail.abstract: This paper extends the costly verification framework of Ben-Porath, Dekel, and Lipman (2014) to a dynamic setting in which the agent initially has private information only about the distribution of his type and learns the realized type over time. The principal sequentially screens the agent through a menu of contracts specifying verification and allocation rules. We provide a complete characterization of the optimal mechanism in any environment. The optimal mechanism either pools all ex ante types and implements deterministic allocation without verification, or screens ex ante types through a menu of randomized rules. We show that, in many environments, eliciting the agent's initial private information allows the principal to extract strictly more surplus than in the static setting.

detail.title: Inequality, Home Production, and Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: I study the role of home production in determining the labor income channel through which monetary policy affects consumption inequality. To this end, I develop a two-agent New Keynesian model with home production.  In the context of my model, hand-to-mouth households experience a sharper decline in labor income compared to richer households in response to a contractionary monetary policy shock. However, they increase home production to a greater extent than richer households do. The resulting labor income channel is therefore one third the size when accounting for home production. In line with my theoretical results, I show empirically that individuals living hand-to-mouth respond to contractionary monetary policy shocks by increasing home production by more than richer people do.

affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Conglomerate Mergers under Multiplicative Growth
detail.abstract: We examine the effects of conglomerate mergers on firm growth and the competitive landscape using an agent-based model. We provide evidence that resource sharing within conglomerates acts as a risk mitigation strategy in multiplicative growth processes, providing incentives for conglomerate formation. Our model shows that even small levels of resource sharing can significantly alter market dynamics, leading to more balanced measures of market concentration and increased firm mobility. Contrary to concerns about market concentration, our results suggest that conglomerate formation can reduce both static and dynamic measures of market concentration.

title: Workers' Health Recovery as a Productive Input
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Workers' Health Recovery as a Productive Input
detail.abstract: This paper treats workers' health recovery, the maintenance of productive capacity, as a productive input rather than a consumption good. Productive capacity, measured by afunctionality index, depreciates through occupational morbidity and is restored by a health sector combining capital, labor, and biomedical knowledge, with semi-endogenous research and development (R&D), subject to stronger diminishing returns in biomedical research ( Eroom's Law). Combined with income-elastic health demand, this generates an endogenous Baumol cost disease: the rise in the relative price of health follows from the R&D structure, not an exogenous productivity gap. Once health recovery is productive, this rise is the cost of an optimal path, not a drag on output. Calibrated to long-run targets of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the model is applied to emerging economies away from the technological frontier. For Brazil, the optimal labor allocation to health is 6.8% of employment against 4.5% observed, an underinvestment robust to thirteen parameter variants, with a welfare cost of 0.6% in consumption equivalents. Restrictinghealth spending to the observed level raises measured gross domestic product (GDP) per capita by 1-2% while lowering welfare: allocations maximizing output and welfare diverge. An out-of-sample test with Mexico, the lowest health spender in the OECD, reinforces the diagnosis without recalibration: optimal spending, 12.9% of GDP, more than doubles the observed level. The optimal health-output share traces a U over the transition, receding during convergence, rising once the relative-price eect dominates. If health recovery sustains productive capacity, investing in it is growth policy.

title: Administrative burden as a modifiable health-system performance problem: a conceptual framework for access, equity and care continuity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Administrative burden as a modifiable health-system performance problem: a conceptual framework for access, equity and care continuity
detail.abstract: AbstractBackground: Administrative burden is increasingly recognised in health systems, but it is often framed as paperwork, implementation friction or administrative cost rather than as a performance-relevant feature generated by policy rules and service design.Objective: This article develops a conceptual framework for analysing how administrative burden can shape health-system performance through access, equity and care continuity.Methods: A problem-led conceptual synthesis integrated four literatures: administrative burden in public administration; patient administrative burden, treatment burden and minimally disruptive medicine; access, disability and health-system performance; and stress/allostasis and biopsychosocial theory. The aim was framework development, not systematic review or causal validation.Results: The framework treats administrative burden as a modifiable health-system performance problem with three analytic levels: institutional rules, categories and procedures; lived work, agency and care relationships; and service consequences plus plausible stress-related pathways. It identifies level confusions that can naturalise administrative categories, misclassify system-generated burden as non-adherence, treat administrative control as costless stewardship and digitalise procedures without reducing total pathway work.Conclusions: Administrative burden should be evaluated as a distributive and modifiable feature of health-system design. Burden-sensitive policy should test whether procedures are proportionate, accessible, evidence-sensitive and equity-preserving while maintaining legitimate stewardship.

title: VerteNet - A Multi-Context Hybrid CNN Transformer for Accurate Vertebral Landmark Localization in Lateral Spine DXA Images

detail.title: VerteNet - A Multi-Context Hybrid CNN Transformer for Accurate Vertebral Landmark Localization in Lateral Spine DXA Images
detail.abstract: Vertebral Landmarks Localization (VLL) in Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA)-based Lateral Spine Imaging (LSI) plays a critical role in evaluating spinal alignment, Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA), and facilitating intervertebral guide placement for Abdominal Aortic Calcification (AAC) quantification. While DXA LSI offers advantages such as reduced cost and lower radiation exposure, its analysis remains challenging due to a low signal-to-noise ratio and imaging artifacts. Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents a promising avenue for improving the precision and accuracy of VLL. This study introduces a novel architecture that employs dual-resolution attention mechanisms to capture both fine-grained local details and broader contextual information. Our approach enhances feature integration by leveraging skip connections and decoder layers through dual-resolution self- and cross-attentions. This design improves the model’s ability to learn complex patterns, ensuring precise vertebral corner localization while maintaining both local and global contextual awareness. We evaluated our proposed framework on DXA LSIs acquired from various machines and found that it outperformed recent state-of-the-art architectures, trained for VLL, achieving a normalized mean error of 4.92 and a normalized median error of 2.35. The proposed framework, VerteNet, enables highly accurate VLL in DXA LSI images from diverse machines and demonstrates superior robustness to low signal-to-noise ratios, owing to its enhanced ability to capture both fine-grained local details and broader contextual information.

title: The Cost of National Pricing: Side Payments and Efficiency under Self-Dispatch with Redispatch in the GB Electricity Market
affiliations: University of Essex

detail.title: The Cost of National Pricing: Side Payments and Efficiency under Self-Dispatch with Redispatch in the GB Electricity Market
detail.abstract: Liberalised electricity markets resolve the nonconvexities created by generation commitment through out-of-market side payments whose magnitude and opacity concern regulators. Most analyses adopt the centralised, nodal-dispatch institution of US independent system operators (ISOs), in which these appear as make-whole payments on top of locational prices. Great Britain (GB) occupies the opposite institutional corner: a single national uniform price cleared under self-dispatch, with network constraints and locked-in commitment resolved afterwards through redispatch in the Balancing Mechanism, the net cost of which is socialised -- recovered uniformly from demand through balancing charges rather than charged to the parties that cause it. Following the 2025 Review of Electricity Market Arrangements (REMA), which retained national pricing and rejected locational pricing, the policy-relevant question is the cost of that choice. We formalise GB arrangements as a two-stage market -- a network-blind national clearing followed by a cost-minimising redispatch -- and prove two central results. First, in a convex economy national-pricing-with-redispatch is welfare-equivalent to nodal pricing, so every unit of realised welfare loss is attributable to commitment nonconvexity. Second, the visible cost of national pricing decomposes into a congestion-rent component that nodal pricing would internalise as merchandising surplus (the standard term for the network revenue an ISO collects from pricing energy differently on the two sides of a binding constraint), plus a strategic redispatch markup; we show this gap is non-negative under the empirically supported condition that minimised nodal make-whole payments are small. We quantify the gap on the Scotland-England (B6) boundary using public Balancing Mechanism data, exploiting the exact correspondence between the model’s two stages and the settlement objects (final physical notifications and flagged bid-offer acceptances), and validate the figure against the published constraint cost. The cost of national pricing is, to first order, the same congestion rent: under nodal pricing the system operator would collect it as merchandising surplus (and could rebate it to consumers), whereas under national pricing it is instead paid out to generators as redispatch and socialised across demand. Measured directly from settlement records, this realised B6 congestion rent is of order £1.1bn in FY 2024/25 -- about 59% of GB system constraint costs and tracking the independent published daily series almost exactly (correlation 0.97); the underlying 9.55 TWh of Scottish-wind curtailment matches independently reported volumes.

detail.abstract:
Background: Health workforce migration from low- and middle-income countries remains a major global health challenge, with implications for health system resilience. Nigeria, one of the largest contributors to the global medical workforce, faces increasing loss of future physicians. This study examined the determinants of migration intention among Nigerian medical students.

Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 1,299 medical students in Kano State, Nigeria, using a semi-structured, self-administered online questionnaire. Statistical analysis was done using IBM SPSS v27. Binary logistic regression identified independent predictors of migration at p < 0·05.

Findings; 63·9% of respondents intended to practice medicine abroad. The most preferred destinations were the United States (45·2%), Canada (44·5%), and the United Kingdom (43·7%). Interest in international practice was high (mean 3·98 ± 0·74), while awareness of licensure pathways was relatively low (mean 2·35 ± 0·96). Major drivers included better remuneration and improved medical infrastructure. Financial constraints (62·1%) was the leading barrier. Migration intention was significantly associated with motivation for studying medicine (p = 0·004), participation in international programs (p < 0·001), and prior exploration of certification processes (p < 0·001). Independent predictors of migration intention included higher interest in international practice (AOR = 2·59; 95% CI: 2·1–3·1) and greater awareness of licensure pathways (AOR = 2·34; 95% CI: 2·0–2·8).

Interpretation: A substantial proportion of Nigerian medical students intend to migrate, reflecting systemic push factors and global pull dynamics. Early, targeted retention strategies within medical training and broader health system reforms are urgently needed to mitigate future workforce losses.

detail.abstract:
Background: Most clinical explainability methods attribute a fixed model output to observed features but fail to generate a patient-specific alternative clinical state. We aimed to develop a conditional counterfactual diffusion model for generative clinical explanations and evaluate its fidelity and physiological plausibility using sepsis as a clinical proof-of-concept application.

Methods: In this multicentre retrospective study, we analysed 41,452 intensive care unit admissions from three hospitals in China between Jan 1, 2023, and Dec 31, 2025 (5,411 with sepsis and 36,041 without sepsis). The proposed model encoded a factual patient profile into a patient-specific latent state and utilised conditional reverse diffusion to generate paired profiles under a target clinical state. We assessed marginal and multivariable fidelity, downstream utility, and the direction and magnitude of paired feature changes, comparing the model against traditional generative baselines.

Results: The conditional counterfactual diffusion model achieved the highest data fidelity among evaluated generators (mean Wasserstein distance, 10.904) and demonstrated strong downstream utility (AUROC 0.872; F1 score 0.528) in train-on-synthetic, test-on-real evaluation. Patient-specific counterfactual simulations identified severe hypoalbuminaemia, lymphopenia, systemic inflammation, and organ dysfunction as key features of early sepsis transitions. Distinct phenotypic patterns were observed across septic shock, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. In an independent cohort of 451 patients who subsequently developed sepsis, simulated profiles closely matched observed clinical states, supporting the clinical plausibility and validity of the approach.

Conclusions: Patient-specific counterfactual diffusion enables explainable disease state modeling by generating waves of individualized physiological scenarios anchored to real patient profiles. Moving beyond conventional static feature attribution, this generative model offers a novel method to simulate how patient profiles transition toward sepsis and its severe complications, providing a new paradigm for interpretable clinical artificial intelligence and personalized decision support in intensive care settings.

title: Disruptive Unification Theory: How Visible Disruption Catalyses Systemic Alignment

detail.title: Disruptive Unification Theory: How Visible Disruption Catalyses Systemic Alignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract:
Large-scale institutional alignment rarely emerges from foresight. Societies routinely possess the knowledge that action is required yet do not act until visible disruption makes inaction impossible. Disruptive Unification Theory addresses this paradox by proposing that systemic alignment occurs principally when a disruptive event crosses a visibility threshold, converting dispersed awareness into collective moral and institutional action. The event achieves this by generating common knowledge in the technical, recursive sense: it converts awareness that was private and distributed into a shared state in which each party not only knows the relevant fact, but knows that the others know it, knows that they know that they know it, and so on without limit. A public, simultaneously witnessed event satisfies this otherwise infinite hierarchy in a single stroke, because its very publicness leaves no level at which one party could doubt that the others saw the same thing.

The theory models three interacting drivers: moral salience, experiential visibility, and financial consequence. The theory advances a central structural claim: the visibility threshold scales in relation to system size. Grounded in Adam Smith's account of the degradation of sympathetic imagination with distance, this scaling explains why small communities sustain alignment without catastrophe while global institutions have historically required existential shocks. To specify the theory's mechanism and its boundary conditions, this paper considers three positive cases (Hiroshima 1945, 9/11 2001, Grenfell Tower 2017) and two contrast cases (COVID-19 and Fukushima). Five propositions are offered to guide empirical development. The paper closes with the governance question which is unavoidably prompted by Disruptive Unification Theory: whether the alignment that catastrophe produces can be manufactured before the event.

title: Japanese Acquisitions in Southeast Asian Finance and Consumer Markets

detail.title: Japanese Acquisitions in Southeast Asian Finance and Consumer Markets
detail.abstract: We assemble and verify a ledger of forty-four Japanese acquisition transactions, about thirty-seven distinct deal programmes, in Southeast Asian banking, consumer finance, insurance and consumer sectors between 2011 and 2026, with sourced consideration of roughly USD 22.6 billion, and we read it against the macroeconomic record on both sides. Three findings organise the paper. First, the wave is large enough to be visible in international banking statistics: BIS consolidated claims of Japanese banks on six ASEAN economies rose from about USD 89 billion at end-2010 to about USD 285 billion at end-2025, and the two largest single deals, MUFG's purchases of Thailand's Bank of Ayudhya and Indonesia's Bank Danamon, appear as discrete jumps in the country series. Second, the division between control and minority positions is set less by acquirer preference than by host law: Japanese megabanks bought majority control exactly where a legal pathway existed (a Thai tender offer; Indonesia's two-banks-merge exception to its 40 percent cap) and stopped at 15 to 20 percent where caps bind, as in Vietnam, while insurers show the mirror image, taking full control in Vietnam's open insurance market and minorities where states or families anchor the register. Third, the outcomes cut against the intuition that control is the prize. The control cases carry the visible damage, a USD 1.9 billion impairment on Danamon and an 82 percent profit collapse at SMBC Indonesia in 2025, while the patient minorities compound quietly and the failed minority, SMBC's fifteen years in Eximbank, illustrates the alternative risk of capital without governance. We also document a second-order structure the aggregate statistics miss: MUFG's Thai subsidiary Krungsri has itself become the acquirer of record across five ASEAN countries, making Bangkok, not Tokyo, the operating centre of Japan's regional consumer-finance expansion.

title: Health promotion and wellness activities under India's Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres: a mixed-methods assessment in three districts of Haryana
affiliations: All India Institute of Medical Sciences, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, All India Institute of Medical Sciences and Centre  for  Community  Medicine,  All  India  Institute  of  Medical  Sciences

detail.title: Health promotion and wellness activities under India's Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres: a mixed-methods assessment in three districts of Haryana
detail.abstract: Background India's Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) mandate health promotion as a core pillar of comprehensive primary care across 12 service domains. Evidence on actual implementation—particularly at sub-health centre (SHC) level and across diverse geographic contexts—is absent. Methods We conducted a concurrent mixed-methods study in three Haryana districts representing distinct urbanisation strata: urban (Faridabad), semi-urban (Palwal), and rural/aspirational (Nuh). Ten PHC/UPHC-HWCs were randomly selected; one linked SHC-HWC per PHC was included by purposive convenience sampling. We administered 2022 IPHS-aligned facility checklists, conducted 43 in-depth interviews with District Programme Managers, Medical Officers, Community Health Officers, Auxiliary Nurse Midwives, Accredited Social Health Activists, and staff nurses, and completed 100 patient exit interviews. Descriptive statistics and domain-based content analysis within a logic model framework were applied. Findings Health promotion received 0·75–2·0% of district health budgets (₹31–73 lakhs, 2022–23) and 10–33% of training session time, with no dedicated budget head. Frontline staff committed a median of 62 hours per month (IQR 58–67) to promotion activities, directed predominantly toward reproductive, maternal, newborn, and child health rather than the full 12-domain wellness mandate. Patient comprehension was 30–40% for facility IEC materials versus 50–80% for interpersonal communication through community platforms. Rural SHC-HWCs conducted 1500–2000 outreach sessions annually—the highest volume across all settings—yet lacked Community Health Officer deployment. Interpretation Health promotion in AB-HWCs is structurally marginalised despite its policy mandate. Policymakers should prioritise ring-fenced wellness budgets, cadre-specific competency-based training, standardised intersectoral reporting, and outcome-oriented monitoring that captures behaviour change rather than activity counts alone.

detail.abstract: U.S. dependence on China for essential medicines is structural—deeper, broader, and more consequential than conventional market analyses suggest. That dependence began with generic medicines and their ingredient but is now growing in biologics manufacturing, first-in-human trials, and synthetic DNA. That dependence is not simply the result of market conditions but rather decades of Chinese state investment. This report undertakes an original analysis of trade and customs data and US Pharmacopeia ingredient sourcing records, mapping supply chain dependencies for major US essential medicines, tier by tier. It also identifies the pathways through which China could practically leverage that dependence to adversely affect the United States and models how those effects would propagate through US health system. Finally, the report outlines a replicable solution framework for each of the major choke points in the US biopharmaceutical supply chain: (a) reliance on China for upstream supplies of generic drugs; (b) the erosion of US manufacturing and clinical trial capacity to China; and (c) US dependence on China for R&D infrastructure for sensitive biotechnology.

title: Who Governs Cyberspace in the age of AI? A Global Stocktake of Cybersecurity Governance

detail.title: Who Governs Cyberspace in the age of AI? A Global Stocktake of Cybersecurity Governance
detail.abstract:
Cyberspace is not ungoverned-it is systematically misgoverned. International instruments, national strategies, and voluntary frameworks have proliferated while security outcomes deteriorated. This inversion-more governance, less resilience-is the "Proliferation Paradox." The paper introduces "Governance Debt": the institutional deficit that accumulates when AI-driven technological change outpaces governance adaptation. This debt compounds across three dimensions: Capacity Debt (threat velocity exceeds institutional response cycles), Authority Debt (no enforcement jurisdiction over borderless AI infrastructure), and Legitimacy Debt (governance authority migrates to unaccountable private actors). 

This paper examines cybersecurity governance in 29 countries. It identifies three institutional models: Integrated Command, Nodal Hybrid, and Fragmented Sectoral. Key finding: institutional architecture predicts operational resilience more consistently than strategy quality or financial investment. The analysis covers 66 governance instruments and reveals four critical weaknesses in how AI challenges current systems: Scale (velocity), Attribution (identity), Dependence (vulnerability to foreign platforms), and Agency (autonomous systems without accountability). The paper calls cloud providers, AI developers, and standards bodies "private leviathans": they exercise sovereign-scale power over cyberspace without democratic mandate or meaningful accountability. 

Using the OECD Strategic Foresight Toolkit, the paper stress-tests six governance models across four 2030 scenarios. Two extremes fail: total centralization (a Global Cyber Agency) and total market-led governance. The "Adaptive Federated Stack"-a five-layer architecture-distributes authority across existing institutions without creating a new apex body. This model performs across all scenarios and resolves all three Governance Debt dimensions. The central argument: between 2026 and 2030, governance success requires interoperability, not unity.

title: Governance Laundering: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in AI Compliance Architectures

detail.title: Governance Laundering: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in AI Compliance Architectures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is affiliated with FERZ, Inc., which develops deterministic-governance infrastructure. The paper’s susceptibility mapping is architectural and a priori, not an empirical vendor ranking.
