detail.abstract:
Enterprise adoption of AI governance tools has outpaced the development of reliable methods for determining whether those tools deliver the compliance properties they advertise. This paper identifies a class of structural failures in AI compliance architectures, including governance laundering, policy theater, vendor-dependent verification, trace-artifact mimicry, delegated authorization, post-hoc signature injection, custody gaps, and semantic drift. These failures arise when organizations mistake governance artifacts, such as logs, dashboards, attestations, certificates, or blockchain-anchored records, for governance evidence: replay-sufficient artifacts that allow an independent third party to reconstruct the policy verdict for a specific AI decision.

The paper formalizes these failures as seven failure-mode families, each tied to a violated evidence-grade governance requirement. It then introduces the Expanded Anti-Laundering Protocol (EALP), a seven-test diagnostic methodology for evaluating whether a candidate governance architecture produces verifiable evidence, merely supports retrospective monitoring, or only generates replay-insufficient artifacts. The protocol tests exportability, offline replay, state completeness, fail-closed behavior, mutation and drift resistance, pre-execution binding, and custody-chain integrity. The paper also maps susceptibility across common AI governance product categories and explains why many failures arise not from vendor deception, but from architectural mismatch between product design and buyer expectations.

The resulting framework gives procurement teams, auditors, regulators, and standards bodies a reproducible method for distinguishing evidence-grade governance from monitoring-grade systems and artifact-only compliance records. It positions governance laundering as a structural diagnosis rather than a vendor-specific accusation, and provides practical terminology for identifying when AI governance claims obscure the authorization artifact gap.

title: Beyond Net Flows: Managing Gross Capital Flows under Collateral Constraints
affiliations: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and

detail.title: Beyond Net Flows: Managing Gross Capital Flows under Collateral Constraints
detail.abstract: Empirical evidence increasingly documents asymmetric effects of policies targeting capital inflows versus outflows, yet theoretical frameworks typically model only net flows. We fill this gap with a collateral-constraint model in which foreign borrowing and residents' overseas investment are modeled as distinct, pledgeable flow types. Private agents neglect how their joint borrowing and investment decisions affect future asset prices and collateral values, generating pecuniary externalities through both domestic and foreign asset price channels. Relative to net-flow benchmarks, our setup implies higher crisis probabilities and greater overborrowing. A system of Pigouvian taxes restores constrained efficiency, with implied interventions that are substantially tighter than those prescribed by net-flow regulations. These results rationalize the observed heterogeneity in gross-flow policy effects and their interactions with global financial conditions, and provide a useful benchmark for evaluating capital flow management frameworks that separately target different categories of international capital flows.

detail.abstract: I study the dynamics of greenhouse gas emissions following unexpected increases in oil prices from supply disruptions. I find that CO 2-equivalent atmospheric concentrations decrease by 0.10 ppm relative to trend following a 10% increase in crude oil prices. This effect is heterogeneous across gases, reflecting a reshuffling of fossil fuel usage. Natural gas and petroleum products fall sharply across the board, while low-quality coal and bioenergy generation rise. Driven by tighter financial conditions and elevated uncertainty, solar capacity contracts. Hybrid and EV adoption increase markedly, partially substituting for conventional internal combustion engine vehicles. * I am grateful to my advisors, Martin Eichenbaum, Diego Känzig and Giorgio Primiceri. title: Feasibility Study of using Artificial Intelligence in Tourism Agencies and its Impact on Human Resource Performance
affiliations: and Work Research Institute

detail.title: Feasibility Study of using Artificial Intelligence in Tourism Agencies and its Impact on Human Resource Performance
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has now penetrated all aspects of human life and various industries. Technology has always played a key role in tourism and hospitality (T&H). Although various aspects of AI application in the tourism industry have been studied so far, its impact on human resources (HR) and the workforce has not been well explored. The purpose of this research is to investigate the feasibility of using AI in tourism and travel agencies and its effects on HR performance. 

At first, interviews were conducted with people working in three tourism agencies located in two tourist-friendly provinces of Iran. Twelve semi-structured interviews were conducted with directors, managers, and employees. The findings were then qualitatively analyzed and categorized. 

he results showed that all employees had embraced the digitalization of tourism and were aware of its benefits, including 24/7 service and data analysis. There were many different opinions and sometimes concerns about job security and organizational roles. Despite the serious challenges of implementing AI in agencies, such as cost, infrastructure, and workforce training; most people welcomed it. We suggest an AI-human combined system to improve the performance of HR in tourism agencies.

title: Uganda: Coupling Infrastructure Vision 2040, NDP IV and the Budget 2026/27 as a Test of Transformation
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Uganda: Coupling Infrastructure Vision 2040, NDP IV and the Budget 2026/27 as a Test of Transformation
detail.abstract: Uganda's infrastructure challenge is not only to build, but to make what is built change the economy. Vision 2040 sets the horizon of a modern, prosperous country moving towards a USD 500 billion economy. NDP IV turns that horizon into a tenfold growth demand. Budget 2026/27 places the demand inside oil, debt, taxation, public investment and state execution. The central question is whether Uganda treats infrastructure as an asset count or as a system of productive relations. Construction can improve visibility without changing productivity. Infrastructure matters only when it lowers costs, raises productivity and strengthens the links between production, markets and public institutions. Coupling matters because development is not the sum of projects. It is the reinforcement among energy, movement, information, finance, skills, institutions and trust. Without that reinforcement, Uganda may accumulate infrastructure and remain structurally thin. With it, infrastructure becomes an operator of monetisation, productivity, revenue and state capability. This paper reads Vision 2040, NDP IV and Budget 2026/27 as a test of that infrastructure imagination, and argues for Layered Operator Appraisal as the discipline needed to move from projects to transformation.

title: Reinventing Legacy: Governance, Succession, and Adaptive Capacity in Indian Family Businesses in the Age of AI, ESG, and Global Economic Transformation

detail.abstract:
Family businesses remain central to Indian capitalism, yet their long-term relevance increasingly depends on whether they can convert inherited control into institutional capability. Recent evidence suggests that Indian family firms remain highly optimistic on growth and expansion, but also exhibit persistent weaknesses in governance modernization, board diversification, succession readiness, and technology investment. At the same time, the external environment has become structurally more demanding: macroeconomic volatility remains elevated even as India continues to be among the world's fastest-growing major economies, while regulatory expectations on related-party oversight, ESG disclosure, and board-level accountability have tightened. This paper argues that family businesses must continuously reinvent themselves because competitive advantage in the twenty-first century is no longer secured by ownership continuity alone; it depends on the capacity to repeatedly redesign governance, capital allocation, leadership pipelines, technological capabilities, and stakeholder legitimacy.

Building on the Ownership-Management-Governance (OMG) framework, the paper develops an expanded model, OMG+ARL, referring to Ownership, Management, Governance, Adaptive Capacity, Renewal, and Legitimacy to explain why some family firms preserve continuity through reinvention while others become trapped by path dependence. The argument integrates corporate governance scholarship, institutional economics, business history, and strategic management to show that reinvention is not a repudiation of family legacy but the mechanism through which legacy is made durable. The paper relies exclusively on publicly available secondary sources available up to June 2026, including regulatory materials, multilateral reports, consultancy surveys, academic literature, and public company disclosures. It concludes by proposing a governance architecture for Indian family businesses that combines family purpose with independent oversight, disciplined succession, AI and digital governance, ESG-linked accountability, and structured portfolio renewal.

title: Could Tariffs Provide a Stimulus? In Search of Elusive Benefits of Protectionism

detail.title: Could Tariffs Provide a Stimulus? In Search of Elusive Benefits of Protectionism
detail.abstract: Motivated by the classical argument for protectionism as demand management, this paper shows two mechanisms under which temporary tariffs stimulate consumption. I show that in complete-market, small open-economy New Keynesian models with roundabout production, tariffs do not raise consumption under flexible prices or when active monetary policy follows targeting rules. The first mechanism for raising consumption requires an accommodative monetary policy toward producer price inflation under a fiscal-led price determination regime, or at the zero lower bound. It predicts that US tariffs depreciate the dollar, as observed around the "Liberation Day" tariffs. In incomplete markets, the second mechanism requires that input-output linkages amplify the impact of an appreciation of the terms of trade on improving consumption enough to offset countervailing forces from lower wages and employment. Tariffs misallocate inputs used in production, and the optimal monetary policy can be either expansionary or contractionary.

title: Structure-Preserving Randomization Inference for Decision Timing
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Structure-Preserving Randomization Inference for Decision Timing
detail.abstract: A realized return does not identify skill: profit confounds the quality of a decision sequence, the structural exposure, and the path's drift. We develop structure-preserving randomization inference, a conditional randomization test that isolates the contribution of decisions by holding the realized structure and exogenous path fixed and re-randomizing only the decision margin from a chosen conditional law. We treat the choice of conditioning measure as model risk: each verdict is identified only given a measure, so the data return a sensitivity range over a declared menu, with a valid intersection-union test for the measure-invariant claim, its power set by the least-favorable measure. The test is finite-sample valid and, under a stated central-limit condition, consistent in the trade count N against a per-trade location shift, with zero noncentrality against pure exposure. In a controlled structural-exposure world White's Reality Check and Hansen's SPA reject a profitable-but-untimed strategy about two-thirds of the time, while the placement test holds its nominal size of 0.050. On daily gold futures no strategy in an eleven-rule panel rejects under the neutral measure, and across 322 cross-asset tests nothing survives multiplicity control; four volatility-filtered rules reject only under volatility-state-matched measures, so no robust, measure-invariant entry-timing skill survives.

title: Early Signals in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket and Colombia's 2026 Presidential Election
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Early Signals in Decentralized Prediction Markets: Evidence from Polymarket and Colombia's 2026 Presidential Election
detail.abstract: On 21 June 2026 Abelardo de la Espriella won Colombia's presidency by 0.96 points (49.66% to 48.70%), the narrowest runoff in the country's history, after topping a 31 May first round that conventional polling had not foreseen. For months the mainstream houses had pointed the other way: they gave the left's Iván Cepeda a double-digit first-round lead and a five-to-twelve-point runoff lead. Decentralized prediction markets-Polymarket and Kalshi-priced de la Espriella's surge earlier and were directionally correct. We apply the Decentralized Prediction Market Voter Framework (DPMVF) of Córdoba Otálora and Themistocleous (2025), combining a Cross-Correlation Function (CCF) and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), to reconstructed campaign series, and we complement it with the accuracy diagnostics of Cutting et al. (2025). The market led the realized swing by roughly three weeks (peak CCF r ≈ 0.95 at a +21-day lag; DTW normalized distance 0.08); it was better calibrated than the polls at every pre-election horizon (Brier 0.37 versus a frozen-poll 0.61 two weeks before the first round, and falling further as the blackout lengthened); and the polls underestimated de la Espriella's first-round share by about twenty points while missing the runoff's sign. The Colombian case sharpens the U.S. 2024 evidence: an electoral-poll blackout (the "ley mordaza") froze conventional signals after 30 April, so the market did not merely lead the polls-it contradicted them and tracked the result alone. We discuss thin liquidity, manipulation, capital-weighting, and external-validity caveats.

title: Schrödinger's Bank: Quantum Superposition to Explain Self-Fulfilling Financial Panics
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Schrödinger's Bank: Quantum Superposition to Explain Self-Fulfilling Financial Panics
detail.abstract: On the morning of 9 March 2023, Silicon Valley Bank was healthy. By the evening it was finished. Depositors asked to take out $42 billion in a single day-about a quarter of the bank-and $100 billion more was lined up for the next morning, some 81% of all deposits in two days. The bank's loans and bonds had not changed. What changed is that everyone looked at the same time. This paper argues that, before a crowd turns to look, a bank's safety is not a fixed-but-unknown fact: it is a superposition-a mix of "survives" and "fails" that has not yet settled-and that a public shock (a rumor, a tweet, a downgrade) works like a measurement that makes the mix collapse into one outcome. The collapse can be self-fulfilling: looking can cause the failure. Using the mathematics, not the physics, of quantum mechanics, I model confidence as a two-state amplitude in which the chance of collapse to failure, P (fail) = |β| 2 , rises with a bank's fragility and with how synchronized public attention is. The model contains the classic multiple-equilibria account of Diamond and Dybvig (1983) as a special case and yields two results. First, a panic is genuinely undecided until it is observed. Second, the looking itself raises the chance of failure, so a bank that would survive a slow twentieth-century run can be killed by a fast twenty-first-century one with the same balance sheet. The framework explains why modern runs are far faster, why a 94%-uninsured bank was so exposed, and why deposit insurance works by erasing the "fail" option before anyone can choose it.

detail.abstract:
We analyze allocation processes in computationally-mediated markets where inferential capacity, rather than price alone, becomes the primary allocative constraint. The paper formalizes the transition from ranking-based allocation under separable valuations to network-dependent allocation under inferential scarcity, where optimal allocation depends on combinatorial complementarities and representation structure.

A canonical allocation problem is introduced to characterize conditions under which independent ranking mechanisms fail to recover globally optimal allocations. We develop five core primitives—inferential scarcity, representational capital, inferential accessibility, computational trust, and network-dependent allocation—and establish formal results concerning irreducibility, computational hardness, and structural exclusion.

The framework extends institutional economics, mechanism design, and computational governance theory to analyze representation protocols as allocative infrastructure within machine-mediated markets. The paper further proposes operational metrics and empirically testable hypotheses for future research across AI-mediated search, recommendation systems, and computational marketplaces.

title: Foreign Direct Investment in Nigeria: A Critical Analysis of Investor Protection under Nigerian Law
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investment in Nigeria: A Critical Analysis of Investor Protection under Nigerian Law
detail.abstract: Foreign investment, particularly Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), remains a vital catalyst for economic development, industrial growth, technology transfer, employment generation, and integration into the global economy. As one of Africa's largest economies and a major destination for foreign capital, Nigeria has adopted various legal and policy measures aimed at attracting and retaining foreign investors. Despite these efforts, challenges such as regulatory uncertainty, foreign exchange constraints, bureaucratic inefficiencies, insecurity, and weak institutional enforcement continue to undermine investor confidence and affect the investment climate. This article critically examines the legal and institutional framework governing foreign direct investment in Nigeria and evaluates the extent to which Nigerian law protects foreign investors. The article adopts the doctrinal research methodology, relying on the analysis of primary and secondary legal materials, including the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission Act, the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, the Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023, bilateral investment treaties, judicial decisions, and relevant scholarly literature. The study finds that Nigeria possesses a relatively robust legal framework for investor protection, providing safeguards against unlawful expropriation, guaranteeing the repatriation of profits and capital, ensuring access to foreign exchange, promoting equal treatment, and facilitating dispute resolution through domestic and international arbitration mechanisms. However, the practical effectiveness of these protections is weakened by policy inconsistency, bureaucratic delays, judicial inefficiency, foreign exchange volatility, corruption, and security concerns. The article concludes that strong legal provisions alone cannot guarantee investor confidence without effective implementation and institutional accountability. It recommends strengthening statutory protections, enhancing regulatory transparency, improving judicial and arbitral enforcement mechanisms, ensuring policy stability, and reinforcing governance and anti-corruption institutions. These measures are necessary to promote a secure and competitive investment environment capable of attracting sustainable foreign investment.

title: Card Payment Systems: The AIDAS Framework for Real-time Threat Mitigation and Explainable Governance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Card Payment Systems: The AIDAS Framework for Real-time Threat Mitigation and Explainable Governance
detail.abstract: Card payment fraud in the United States reached $15.9 billion in reported consumer losses in 2025, with generative AI expected to drive losses to $40 billion by 2027. Traditional rule-based detection systems cannot adequately protect modern multi-scheme environments operating across Mastercard, Visa, China UnionPay (CUP), and JCB networks, where authorization decisions must occur within 300 milliseconds. This paper makes two primary contributions. First, it provides a systematic, practitioner-grounded analysis of AI fraud detection limitations in ISO 8583-based multi-scheme card systems, including a taxonomy of failure modes unique to scheme-heterogeneous environments. Second, it proposes the Adaptive Integrated Detection and Authorization Security (AIDAS) framework: a five-layer model (transaction ingestion, behavioral profiling, anomaly detection, scheme intelligence fusion, and explainable governance) deployable within legacy card management infrastructure without full system replacement. Based on industry benchmarks and simulated multi-scheme evaluation, AIDAS is expected to reduce false positives by 40–85% and detection latency by >60% relative to rule-based systems, while satisfying OCC SR 11-7 (including 2023 AI guidance), FinCEN SAR obligations, and the U.S. Treasury Financial Services AI Risk Management Framework. The framework advances U.S. payment system security, consumer protection, and financial inclusion.

title: Global Mandates, Local Pathways: When Local Frictions Redirect Circularity
affiliations: Unaffiliated Author,  and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business

detail.title: Global Mandates, Local Pathways: When Local Frictions Redirect Circularity
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Sustainability initiatives increasingly push factories to move toward more circular waste management. Yet factories implement these mandates under unequal local infrastructure, verification systems, partner networks, and material markets. We examine the impacts of a common corporate mandate on waste-management responses for factories that are located in developing and developed countries and how factories adapt operational pathways that are shaped by local frictions. Methodology/results: We study a global manufacturing firm that introduced a corporate waste policy in January 2023. Using monthly data from 293 factories in 69 countries from 2017 to 2024, we estimate difference-indifferences and event-study models. After the policy change, developing-country factories increased reuse and decreased recycling relative to developed-country factories. Mechanism analyses show that they redirected waste from recycling facilities toward third parties for reuse, used more diverse treatment pathways, and that these shifts were especially pronounced for easier-to-separate waste such as paper, transport and industrial packaging, and product waste. Interviews suggest that recycling feasibility and verifiability frictions initiated this shift, while resource scarcity and local partner networks made reuse a more feasible and preferable strategy. Managerial implications: Global sustainability mandates should combine standardized goals with flexibility in local implementation. Headquarters should recognize that, where formal recycling channels are weak or difficult to verify, reuse may be a more feasible and preferred response. Local managers can support this transition by mapping residual material streams, developing documentable reuse arrangements, and building local partner networks.

title: Rare Earth Elements: Geopolitics, Supply Chains, Market Monopolies, Trade Conflicts, and China's Strategic Role

detail.title: Rare Earth Elements: Geopolitics, Supply Chains, Market Monopolies, Trade Conflicts, and China's Strategic Role
detail.abstract: The global transition toward a low-carbon economy and the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) have fundamentally elevated the strategic value of critical minerals, particularly Rare Earth Elements (REEs). This exhaustive academic paper explores the geopolitical, economic, and environmental dynamics underpinning the global REE supply chain. Drawing on a comprehensive corpus of recent empirical studies, life cycle assessments, and trade network analyses, the paper evaluates the structural asymmetry of the REE market, characterized by China’s overwhelming dominance in both upstream extraction and midstream refining capacities. Utilizing theoretical frameworks grounded in Resource Dependence Theory (RDT) and weaponized interdependence, this study analyzes how resource power and state interventions have shaped market monopolies, industrial governance, and trade conflicts, most notably the escalating tensions between the United States and China. Critical findings indicate that while non-Chinese suppliers can provide short-term relief to global supply shocks, long-term resilience requires extensive domestic capacity building, robust environmental, social, and governance (ESG) frameworks, and collaborative “friend-shoring” alliances. The paper highlights the “midstream trap,” where nations with advanced manufacturing capabilities remain strategically vulnerable due to a lack of refining infrastructure. Ultimately, this study synthesizes the implications of these dynamics for national security, industrial policy, and environmental governance, providing a rigorous roadmap for future research in multipolar critical mineral trade networks.

title: Navigating Supply Chain Sustainability under Climate Change and Resource Scarcity: Risks and Strategic Responses
affiliations: Quinnipiac University - Quinnipiac University, Quinnipiac University - Quinnipiac University, Quinnipiac University - Quinnipiac University, Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm and Hitit University

detail.title: Navigating Supply Chain Sustainability under Climate Change and Resource Scarcity: Risks and Strategic Responses
detail.abstract: Sustainability and climate change mitigation have become critical priorities in supply chain management, reshaping how companies design and operate their supply networks. This paper investigates how two interconnected environmental megatrends-climate change and resource scarcity-are reshaping the risk profiles of global supply chains and the strategies companies use to build resilience. The study aims to provide an understanding of the drivers and barriers associated with these strategic responses, including digital transformation efforts. To achieve this, we combine an analysis of current environmental trends and supply chain risks with the outcomes of a structured workshop conducted with industry stakeholders, technology experts, and supply chain managers. This methodological approach allows us to capture both macro-level trends and practitioner perspectives on feasible solution approaches. Our findings show that digital technologies such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, and Internet of Things (IoT) hold significant promise for enabling more adaptive, transparent, and sustainable supply chains, but their effective adoption depends on parallel investments in supplier diversification, workforce adaptation, circular-economy practices, and financial risk-transfer mechanisms. The paper synthesizes these into a risk-solution mapping across digital, operational, organizational, and financial dimensions, and identifies the key strategic levers companies are deploying to overcome barriers and enhance resilience. By mapping the intersection of environmental megatrends and supply chain responses, this paper offers actionable insights for researchers and practitioners aiming to strengthen the adaptive capacity and long-term sustainability of supply chains.

title: Brain-Computer Interfaces Enhanced by Large Language Models: Emerging Architectures for Intelligent Language Learning Systems
affiliations: Ladoke Akintola University of Technology

detail.title: Brain-Computer Interfaces Enhanced by Large Language Models: Emerging Architectures for Intelligent Language Learning Systems
detail.abstract: Brain-computer interface technology has demonstrated considerable promise for adaptive language learning through real-time cognitive state monitoring, enabling platforms to adjust content difficulty and pacing in response to learner engagement, fatigue, and cognitive load. Prior work in this series introduced a BCI-driven French language learning platform using a CNN-LSTM cognitive state classifier that achieved 84.6% vocabulary retention, representing a substantial advance over conventional platforms. A remaining limitation of that system and similar BCI learning platforms is the absence of LLM-driven content generation and pedagogical reasoning, which restricts curriculum flexibility and limits the platform's ability to provide rich explanatory feedback in natural language. This paper presents the Brain-Computer Interface Large Language Model Intelligent Language Learning System (BCI-LLM-ILS), which extends the BCIdriven adaptive learning paradigm by integrating a fine-tuned LLM pedagogy agent that generates content, explanations, cultural context, and learner feedback dynamically in response to real-time BCI cognitive state signals. The system adds functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) prefrontal cortex monitoring alongside EEG to provide a richer cognitive load and working memory estimate, informing more nuanced LLM content adaptation than EEG alone supports. Drawing on the hybrid multimodal architecture principles of Hossain et al. [1] and the custom signal processing design of Ghosh et al. [2], the BCI-LLM-ILS cognitive state estimator combines EEG spectral features with fNIRS oxygenation signals in a dualinput CNN-LSTM architecture. Evaluated across six language pairs and a dyslexic learner cohort with 186 participants over ten weeks, BCI-LLM-ILS achieves average vocabulary retention of 93.7%, grammar accuracy of 91.2%, and fluency score of 8.9/10, with an average improvement of 33.5 percentage points over conventional platform controls. The system performs particularly strongly for dyslexic learners, achieving a 41.3 percentage point improvement over controls, suggesting that BCI-LLM adaptive pacing is especially beneficial for learners with non-standard cognitive processing patterns.

detail.abstract: This curated essay collection reflects on the ethical responsibilities of scholars and institutions amid rising violence, crises, and (geo)political tensions. Bringing together diverse voices from the editorial community of the Journal of Business Ethics, the essays collated here explore how academic freedom, care, dissent, and responsibility are negotiated within increasingly politicised and marketized university environments. The contributions address the lived experience of moral injury and vulnerability in proximity to war, the suppression of dissent in corporatized universities, the fragility of academic freedom under political pressure, and the ethical obligations of business ethics scholars confronting structural violence. This essay collection challenges the idea of institutional neutrality and calls for renewed attention to and engagement with care, courage, and collective responsibility in defending academic freedom and sustaining ethical scholarship in increasingly turbulent times.

title: Asymmetric Consumer Preferences and Platform Pricing

detail.title: Asymmetric Consumer Preferences and Platform Pricing
detail.abstract: This paper studies information design in a differentiated-products duopoly with asymmetric consumer preferences. Consumers choose between two firms after receiving private information about their relative match values, and firms then compete in prices. Unlike symmetric benchmarks, the prior distribution of consumer preferences may favor one firm, allowing asymmetry to arise from the full shape of the preference distribution rather than from a single demand or quality parameter. The paper characterizes how asymmetric priors affect firm-optimal, consumer-optimal, and platform-optimal information policies. Firm-optimal information relaxes competition by amplifying perceived differentiation, while consumer-optimal information disciplines prices by making products appear more substitutable. A fee-charging platform faces a different trade-off: it uses information to shape residual demand and extract seller surplus, subject to Bayes plausibility, pricing incentives, and participation constraints. The analysis shows how asymmetric consumer preferences determine equilibrium price gaps, surplus division, and the limits to competition.

title: Integrated Strategies for Union Legitimacy (Re)Building: A Process Model

detail.title: Integrated Strategies for Union Legitimacy (Re)Building: A Process Model
detail.abstract: This study presents a longitudinal analysis examining the process by which the Transport Workers Union (re)established its legitimacy through an integrated strategy encompassing comprehensive campaigns in road transport, aviation, and the gig economy in Australia. We reveal how unions can gain pragmatic legitimacy through power recomposition, moral legitimacy through moral framing, and cognitive legitimacy through the shaping of assumptions. We reveal the systematic transfer of proven strategies to different parts of the industry, adapting to specific conditions and audiences. Our findings provide a framework for unions to revitalize their influence within a dynamic industrial relations landscape.

title: Bayesian Estimation of the Bivariate Generalized Geometric Distribution: A Comparative Study of Beta and Kumaraswamy Priors
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Garden City University College and Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana

detail.title: Bayesian Estimation of the Bivariate Generalized Geometric Distribution: A Comparative Study of Beta and Kumaraswamy Priors
detail.abstract: Stochastic models for correlated count data are crucial in reliability and safety analysis, especially when systems involve correlated events. The bivariate generalized geometric distribution (BGGD) offers a flexible framework for modeling such data. This study evaluates the influence of Beta and Kumaraswamy priors on Bayesian estimation of BGGD parameters. However, existing Bayesian studies of the BGGD have primarily relied on Beta priors without accounting for the impact of different priors. This study addresses this gap by systematically comparing the Kumaraswamy and Beta priors within a Bayesian framework and providing empirical evidence on their relative performance in estimating the BGGD parameter. Posterior distributions were derived using MCMC with Gibbs sampling, and convergence was assessed via trace and autocorrelation plots. The models were compared using Bayesian model selection criteria metrics. The findings revealed that, under the settings considered, the Kumaraswamy prior produced smaller posterior variance (0.02% to 28.51%) and better convergence diagnostics than the Beta prior (0.06% to 29.17%). The study concluded that under this investigation, the Kumaraswamy prior produced more precise posterior estimates, better convergence, than the Beta prior for correlated count processes under the BGGD. Our findings contribute to the systematic evaluation of prior distributions for the BGGD and emphasizes the practical benefits of the Kumaraswamy prior in Bayesian reliability modeling in the manufacturing industry.

title: Learning the Propagation of Policy Shocks in Global Food Trade: A Graph Neural Network Disciplined by Spatial Equilibrium

detail.title: Learning the Propagation of Policy Shocks in Global Food Trade: A Graph Neural Network Disciplined by Spatial Equilibrium
detail.abstract: Export restrictions in staple food markets raise prices far beyond the countries that impose them, yet the incidence of that transmission across the trade network, and the welfare it shifts between developing and developed economies, is hard to measure. This study couples a structural spatial-equilibrium model of the food-trade network with a graph neural network trained to emulate its shock-propagation operator. The panel spans eighteen agricultural commodities from 2008 to 2022; the structural core, an Anderson and van Wincoop multilateral-resistance system calibrated to six core staples, maps a restriction at any origin to the price response at every destination. A graph attention network reproduces this operator out of sample, with a mean coefficient of determination of 0.6496. From it the study derives Systemic Food-Trade Transmission Centrality, ranking origins by the welfare-weighted price pressure of their restrictions. Without being given trade volumes, it identifies Russia for wheat, India for rice, Ukraine for maize, Brazil for soybean and sugar, and Indonesia for palm oil. Welfare losses fall more heavily on developing importers, which bear 1.9456 times the incidence of developed importers, rising to 3.1265 times in rice. A 2022 validation confirms that the model predicts supply reallocation away from the restricting bloc.

title: Risk Budgeting and Hidden Frictions in Taiwan's Six Most Popular ETFs
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Risk Budgeting and Hidden Frictions in Taiwan's Six Most Popular ETFs
detail.abstract:
Taiwan's retail investors commonly treat six dominant ETFs—0050, 006208, 0056, 00878, 00919, and
00929—as if they were spot-like equity portfolios with cash dividends. This paper argues that they are
better understood as spot-wrapped forwards: economically, they package index delivery schedules,
dividend promises, and rebalance rolls into a daily-traded wrapper. The relevant risk is therefore not
only the risk of the underlying stocks, but also the risk created by holding-period tenors, concentration,
factor exposures, tail dependence, and implementation frictions.
We develop a unified risk-budgeting framework combining Forward Tenor Stack measures,
concentration risk (HHI and marginal risk contributions), factor exposures (FF3/FF5), tail dependence
and CVaR, tracking error / market impact / opportunity cost, and dividend sustainability through
equalization reserves. Using split-adjusted FinMind price data for 2018–2025, we estimate monthly,
quarterly, and annual volatility patterns and document that 0050’s annual volatility is approximately
23.2%, comparable in magnitude to the annual-tenor volatility of the 1912–1921 silver benchmark used
as a historical analogy. We also find evidence of calendar-risk amplification around rebalance and ex
dividend windows, particularly for 0050, 0056, and 00929.
The empirical appendix reports high concentration for 0050 and 006208 (HHI ≈ 0.342; TSMC ≈ 57.2%
weight), moderate stock-level concentration but meaningful factor or industry lock-in for the remaining
products, and a nontrivial role for dividend-forward gaps and equalization reserves in high-yield ETFs.
The results suggest that Taiwan’s six popular ETFs are not interchangeable passive baskets; they are
delegated, path-dependent risk-budgeting contracts with month, quarter, and year tenors that
investors do not control directly.

title: Smart Money, Old Patterns, New Amplifiers: Billionaire Portfolio Reallocation, Historical Analogues, and Systemic Risk in the Age of Agentic AI

detail.title: Smart Money, Old Patterns, New Amplifiers: Billionaire Portfolio Reallocation, Historical Analogues, and Systemic Risk in the Age of Agentic AI

detail.abstract:
Between June 2025 and June 2026, several prominent billionaire investors reallocated capital
away from U.S. public equities and toward cash, gold, private markets, and private artificial-
intelligence (AI) exposure. This paper examines two related questions. First, to what extent do
these allocation patterns resemble portfolio positioning observed before major financial
dislocations such as 1929, 1973–74, 1987, 1997–98, and 2000? Second, given the growing
integration of AI, agentic systems, and interconnected cyber infrastructure into financial markets,
could a future shock propagate differently from previous crises?

Drawing on regulatory filings, insider disclosures, industry surveys, and publications from the
Financial Stability Board (FSB), European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB), International Monetary
Fund (IMF), and World Economic Forum (WEF), the paper finds that several contemporary
signals — including structural equity de-risking, elevated market concentration, and rotation into
hard assets — exhibit meaningful historical parallels. Other features, including the scale of
private-market illiquidity and the concentration of AI infrastructure, appear comparatively novel.

The paper does not argue that a crisis is imminent, nor that billionaire portfolio behaviour is itself
a reliable predictor of future market dislocations. Rather, it argues that if a material shock were to
occur, AI-driven, agentic, and cyber-enabled financial systems could compress the time between
initial disruption and broader systemic impact relative to previous cycles. The paper's principal
contribution is therefore not a forecast of crisis, but an examination of how emerging technological
and operational dependencies may alter the transmission characteristics of future financial shocks. The paper concludes with implications for risk managers, allocators, regulators, and
governance practitioners, while highlighting the limitations and uncertainties inherent in historical-
analogue analysis.

title: Systemic Patterns in Transaction Failures: Investigating the PKR 858M Inventory Crisis in Pakistan's E-commerce Ecosystem

detail.abstract:
Pakistan's e-commerce sector has expanded rapidly over the past
decade, but growth has obscured a structural inefficiency: a
substantial fraction of confirmed orders never reach the customer—
locking up an estimated PKR 858 million in inventory that sits
reserved but unsold. This paper works through 584,314 real
transactions from Pakistan's largest marketplace (March 2016 –
August 2018) to figure out why. Three things keep showing up as
culprits: late-night orders placed between 1–5 AM failing at
unusually high rates due to bank batch processing windows; digital
payment gateways—Easypay in particular—canceling at rates well
above cash-on-delivery; and certain product categories, especially
Mobiles & Tablets, carrying structural cancellation rates above
46%. A stacking ensemble (LightGBM + XGBoost + Random
Forest) tuned with Bayesian optimisation is trained, reaching ROC-
AUC of 0.8842—nearly 20 percentage points above a simple three-
feature baseline. SHAP and LIME decompose the drivers of each
prediction. A Loyalty Risk Index is computed for all 115,304 unique
customers; the Watch and At-Risk tiers together account for 78.9%
of total platform revenue, making retention the more urgent
business priority over new-customer acquisition.

detail.abstract: Amazon deforestation determines long-distance ecological impacts as the so-called flying river flowing from the Atlantic captures less Amazonian moisture, which negatively affects precipitation in distant regions westward. The magnitude of the externality depends critically on the strength of the linkage between two distant areas and on the robustness of the recipient downstream system. This paper experimentally studies stylized land-use decisions by landowners, whose activities cascade on water users downstream. After deriving a theoretical benchmark of the underlying continuous dynamic forestmanagement problem, we find that participants partly adjust their behavior to these interdependencies when early-warning signals are in place: deforestation is lower when spillovers are stronger and the downstream system is more fragile, leading to higher forest stocks and less frequent overshooting of critical thresholds.

title: Experience of Food Insecurity and Hunger among Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahido church Traditional school Students in Injibara Town, Awi zone, Amhara, Ethiopia

detail.title: Experience of Food Insecurity and Hunger among Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahido church Traditional school Students in Injibara Town, Awi zone, Amhara, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: Back ground: Food insecurity and Hunger are two distinct concepts. Hunger is a subjective, emotional, and internalized experience. On the other hand, food insecurity is inability to obtain food in a manner that is acceptable in society. This research was aimed to explore the experiences of food insecurity and hunger among Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahido Church (EOTC) traditional schools’ students in Injibara town, Awi zone, Amhara, Ethiopia.Methods: The study employed a mixed method approach including survey (questionnaire), and semi-structured interviews. The two experiential scales validated in Ethiopia, the food insecurity experience scale (FIES) and hunger experience scale (HES), used to collect data from 205 EOTC’s traditional school students in three EOTCs. While descriptive analysis was used to analyze quantitative data, thematic analysis was employed to analyze qualitative data.Result: The result showed that traditional school students were found to be food insecure. Eighty percent of the students reported to have some level of food insecurity which was measured at a Likert scale ranging from rarely, sometimes, and often. The overall FIES score among these students was 6.88, and the overall HHS score was 2.47, suggesting experiences of very-high food insecurity and severe hunger among EOTC traditional students living the Injibara town.Conclusion: This can conclude as, experience food insecurity and hunger among EOTC traditional school students causes for different serious health problems.

title: Relationship Nonbankers
affiliations: and Frankfurt School of Finance and Management

detail.title: Relationship Nonbankers
detail.abstract: Failure to successfully syndicate a leveraged loan can impose substantial costs on the underwriter’s capital. We show that banks’ personal relationships with investors play an important role in mitigating this underwriting risk. Using novel data on the credit committees of the largest leveraged loan investors, collateralized loan obligations, we document that nearly three-quarters of committee members previously worked at investment banks. A committee member's prior bank affiliation increases loan purchases from that bank. We find that banks disproportionately rely on relationship-driven demand for loans that pose significant underwriting risk, but not for loans with higher default risk. Our results highlight the importance of relationships between financial institutions for loan origination.

title: Dollars to Years: Exploring the Link Between National Wealth and Lifespan

detail.title: Dollars to Years: Exploring the Link Between National Wealth and Lifespan
detail.abstract: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita and life expectancy at birth are two of the best-known indicators employed to assess the general level of development of a country. GDP per capita is the average revenue earned per person in a nation, calculated as the whole economic production (GDP) divided by the total population. It is a general measure of the economic power of a nation and the material standard of living of its people. Life expectancy, however, is the average number of years a new born baby can be expected to live if current health and mortality conditions persist (Aburto et al.). Life​‍​‌‍​‍‌ expectancy at birth is the ultimate benchmark that takes into account a mixture of healthcare, diet, sanitation, and other social determinants, hence, it is an essential indicator of public health and standard of living. Studying the relation between these two factors is central to understanding how economic well-being influences human well-being. Quantitative​‍​‌‍​‍‌​‍​‌‍​‍‌ methods like correlation coefficients and regression lines may be used to a more precise and clear way of revealing the connection. Consequently, it not only makes the study process easier but also allows understanding the complex global interrelations of the developmental components at a greater ​‍​‌‍​‍‌​‍​‌‍​‍‌depth.

detail.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) have emerged as an effective treatment for obesity and may reduce other addictive behaviors. We estimate the impact of Medicaid coverage of GLP-1s for weight management on prescription drug use and healthcare utilization related to behavioral health treatments, using variation in the timing of state Medicaid coverage. Coverage led to large increases in GLP-1 prescriptions and spending, but we find no evidence of changes in medications or treatment utilization for nicotine, alcohol, or opioid use disorders. We find declines in prescriptions for mental health medications. At the aggregate level, however, we find no evidence of increases in total Medicaid pharmaceutical spending, but suggestive evidence that coverage increased total Medicaid expenditures. These findings suggest that expanded GLP-1 coverage substantially increased access to obesity treatment, with limited evidence of broader spillover effects on behavioral health care.

title: Salvaging Innovation From Extinction

detail.title: Salvaging Innovation From Extinction

detail.abstract:
Environmental decline has widespread and devastating consequences. Its effect on scientific research remains an underexplored negative externality and provides an additional reason to take protective action. The natural world has already inspired life-saving therapeutics, such as Taxol and GLP-1 drugs, but mass extinction threatens to eliminate countless potential candidates for new therapeutics before scientists can even identify them. While mitigating environmental harm ex ante is an ideal approach, collective action problems have hindered its implementation. Innovation policy should therefore advance existing efforts by prioritizing research, conservation, and information preservation related to these natural resources. 

This Article sets forth a framework focused on three goals: simplification, safeguarding, and scrutiny. To promote simplification, it proposes that the patent office establish an expedited examination program for applications that build upon natural products or support their conservation. With regard to safeguarding, it considers how the patent office could also help preserve valuable information related to such inventions by requiring applicants to make a good faith disclosure of traditional knowledge upon which they substantially rely as a condition of participating in the expedited examination program. For the last goal of scrutiny, it recommends that regulators continually evaluate the effects of these incentives on both innovation and environmental loss. While accelerating natural products research may have adverse environmental effects, such as by encouraging greater use of energy-intensive AI, the potential benefits may outweigh these risks given the possibility that future life-enhancing treatments could be lost forever. A practical approach to innovation policy will complement global efforts to address environmental decline by preserving opportunities for discovery and information before they disappear.

title: National Report on Early-Stage Entrepreneurship in the United States: 2025
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: National Report on Early-Stage Entrepreneurship in the United States: 2025
detail.abstract: This paper tracks four indicators that capture early-stage entrepreneurship activity in the United States: Rate of new entrepreneurs, Opportunity share of new entrepreneurs, Startup early job creation, and Startup early survival rate. These indicators collectively inform the Kauffman Early-Stage Entrepreneurship (KESE) Index, a summary index of entrepreneurial activity. The rate of new entrepreneurs in 2025 was 0.36 percent (i.e. 360 out of 100,000 adults created a new business each month). The rate of new entrepreneurs increased in 2025 and remained higher than pre-pandemic levels. The opportunity share of new entrepreneurs increased to 83.3 percent in 2025 from its low of 69.8 percent in 2020, but remained lower than its prepandemic level of 86.9 percent in 2019. Startup early job creation in 2025 was 5.3 jobs per 1,000 people remaining at the same level as the previous year. Startup job creation dropped in the pandemic but is now above pre-pandemic levels. The startup early survival rate was 77.9 percent in 2025, which is slightly lower than the previous year and lower than pre-pandemic levels. The KESE Index increased in 2025 from the previous year and returned to levels found just prior to the pandemic.

title: Publikacja / Publication Digital Transformation -the "Design for All" Approach: European Accessibility for the Disabled
affiliations: University of Silesia in Katowice

detail.title: Publikacja / Publication Digital Transformation -the "Design for All" Approach: European Accessibility for the Disabled
detail.abstract: Both the UN and the European Commission have been strengthening their regulations concerning the accessibility of products and services by persons with disabilities. Although this is not a new topic, the new regulations are designed to be more binding and to reduce remaining inequity between persons with and without disabilities. Although the topic of accessibility is increasingly better understood and discussed in terms of online systems, it applies just as much to more established technologies such as ATMs or the telephone and even to live human interactions. rat said, the new regulations do robustly address the online space. In addition, the COVID 19 pandemic has, (because so many societal interactions have moved online), drawn even greater attention to existing barriers. The purpose of this study was to outline the framework of legal regulations referring to this problem and to show and analyse the broader context of the changes that are expected once the European Accessibility Act takes epect in 2025.

title: GDP and the Limits of Macroeconomic Measurement in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: GDP and the Limits of Macroeconomic Measurement in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This article examines how the diffusion of artificial intelligence is widening a long running gap between what GDP records and what economies now produce, and what this implies for the macroeconomic measurement framework on which policy still depends.

Design/methodology/approach: The argument is conceptual. It rests on a synthesis of three established literatures and a reading of recent empirical evidence on AI diffusion through that lens.

Findings: AI enlarges this gap through two channels. The first is the spread of free digital goods that users value highly but rarely pay for, with unrecorded consumer surplus from generative AI now estimated in the tens of billions of dollars annually. The second is the distance between the heavy investment now flowing into AI and the modest productivity the statistics so far record, a lag familiar from earlier general-purpose technologies.

 Originality/value:The article develops an integrated framework that connects three literatures usually examined separately: the welfare critique of GDP, data economics, and the diffusion of general-purpose technologies. Through this framework, artificial intelligence emerges as a contemporary stress test of macroeconomic measurement, revealing a growing divergence between GDP and the value the economy actually produces.

detail.abstract:
Background: Adult family homes (AFHs) and Medicaid-funded home and community-based services (HCBS) face well-documented program-integrity challenges; oversight architectures built for centralized institutions struggle to monitor dispersed, lower-visibility residential networks that remain reliant on reactive post-payment claims audits.

Objective: This study tests whether public administrative records can support a public-data review-priority framework spanning operator concentration, enforcement intensity, and complaint load, assessed before claims-level investigation.

Methods: A 20-indicator review-priority typology, derived from Minnesota's public Medicaid enforcement record, was applied to a three-county Washington AFH pilot (n=3,457 facilities in King, Pierce, and Spokane counties) using state licensing rosters, the Residential Care Services enforcement portal, Census denominators, and shared-contact clustering.

Results: Public data cannot identify billing irregularities, but it supports mapping structural review-priority indicators: 72 multi-license shared-contact clusters covering 164 facilities (4.7% of the pilot universe) and 165 facilities (4.8%) with at least one public enforcement action, with county-level enforcement rates ranging from 3.8% in Spokane to 5.8% in Pierce. The primary contribution is a public-data review-priority layer that specifies, indicator by indicator, what can and cannot be observed before claims access; operator concentration is the most novel public-data signal identified.

Conclusion: Public licensing and enforcement records can reveal where closer administrative review may be warranted; only internal agency claims data can confirm whether a billing anomaly occurred. The study proposes a two-phase model: public-data review prioritization (Phase 1, tested here) followed by claims-informed validation using internal agency data (Phase 2, proposed but not executed), intended to improve review-prioritization efficiency without displacing due process.

title: Who Gains and Who Loses from Wind Power? Employment, Displacement, and Spatial Spillovers in Northeastern Brazil
affiliations: Depart of Economics, University of Sao Paulo, Federal University of Paraiba (UFPB), University of São Paulo (USP) - Department of Economics, Federal University of Paraiba (UFPB) - Economics and Federal University of Paraíba

detail.title: Who Gains and Who Loses from Wind Power? Employment, Displacement, and Spatial Spillovers in Northeastern Brazil
detail.abstract: Wind power deployment is often framed as a source of regional job creation, but its local economic incidence may be sectorally uneven and spatially dispersed. This paper estimates the effects of wind farm expansion on formal labor markets in Northeastern Brazil from 2004 to 2019. Using an annual panel of 1,478 municipalities and a spatial difference-in-differences design, we estimate direct effects on host municipalities and spillover effects on nearby municipalities across industry, commerce and services, and agriculture. The results indicate a pattern of sectoral reallocation rather than broad-based employment growth. Host municipalities experience large short-run gains in industrial employment and establishment counts, while agricultural employment declines, with the strongest evidence in the short run and persistent negative point estimates at longer horizons. Neighboring municipalities also exhibit negative labor market spillovers, especially in industrial wages and wage bills and in short-run agricultural employment and wage bills. Exploratory analyses suggest more negative point estimates in inland municipalities and among low-skilled agricultural workers, although these results are based on smaller effective samples. The findings show that wind farms operate not only as energy-capacity investments, but also as spatially targeted infrastructure shocks with uneven distributive effects across sectors, workers, and municipalities. They also underscore the importance of accounting for spatial spillovers when designing quasi-experimental evaluations of renewable energy infrastructure.

title: Energy Price Volatility and Industrial Competitiveness: A Cross-Regional Analysis of Automotive Gas Oil Dynamics and Manufacturing Sector Performance in Asia and Africa​
affiliations: Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto State University, Sokoto and Xi'an

detail.title: Energy Price Volatility and Industrial Competitiveness: A Cross-Regional Analysis of Automotive Gas Oil Dynamics and Manufacturing Sector Performance in Asia and Africa​
detail.abstract: AbstractThis study examines the impact of Automotive Gas Oil (diesel) prices on manufacturing sector performance in 16 Asian and African economies (1991–2024). Using a Cross‑Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS‑ARDL) framework that accounts for cross‑sectional dependence and slope heterogeneity, we find that a 1% increase in diesel prices reduces manufacturing value added by 0.25% in the pooled sample. However, this average conceals profound heterogeneity. For African oil‑importing countries, the long‑run elasticity is –0.28 (p<0.05) – a significant cost‑push effect. In contrast, Asian economies show no statistically significant effect (energy decoupling), and African oil‑exporting countries also exhibit a null effect because higher global oil prices generate fiscal revenues that offset domestic cost increases. Subgroup CS‑ARDL estimations confirm these opposing forces, resolving a Simpson’s paradox in the pooled African sample. Exchange rate depreciation and regulatory quality improve manufacturing performance in the long run but entail short‑run J‑curve adjustment costs. Inflation is detrimental. Policy implications are clear: African oil‑importers need strategic fuel reserves, targeted subsidies, and grid investment; African oil‑exporters must implement institutional reforms to channel resource rents into productive manufacturing; Asia should sustain its energy diversification trajectory. The findings demonstrate that fossil fuel price shocks affect industrial competitiveness in context‑specific ways, and that resource revenue management is critical for avoiding de‑industrialization in oil‑exporting developing economies.

title: What Is the Optimal Funding Rate? Contract Design for Perpetual Futures

detail.title: What Is the Optimal Funding Rate? Contract Design for Perpetual Futures
detail.abstract: What funding rule should a perpetual futures contract post? This paper makes the rule a design object: tracking intensity, clamp width, and settlement interval chosen against a welfare ledger in which funding rents finance the arbitrage sector. Tracking has an interior optimum in closed form: faster tracking compresses the bubble but taxes the holding clientele, and beyond a fold it kills the rents and strands the market in the desert. The prevailing contract sits at the capacity peak, a volume maximizer's choice, not the planner's. Settlement frequency is neutral absent margin frictions. A finite clamp is optimal once runs exist.

title: Federal Research Funding and STEM Education
affiliations: , World Bank and University of British Columbia, Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Federal Research Funding and STEM Education
detail.abstract: This paper examines how federal science and engineering research funding - although intended to advance research - affects degree production and programs offered in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Using data from 1971-2016, the study implements a triple-difference design that exploits variation across colleges, time, and fields of study. The findings show that federal grants generate 27.4 percent of doctorates and 14.7 percent of undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and mathematics degrees, as well as 6.3 percent of doctoral programs and 3.7 percent of undergraduate programs in STEM annually across 200 U.S. research universities. The impacts are concentrated in biology and engineering, aligning with the priorities of major funders such as the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Science Foundation, and the Department of Defense. These findings suggest that research grants to universities may generate a "double dividend," simultaneously expanding the supply of skilled labor in targeted fields while also advancing scientific discovery.

title: Russian Influence and Belarusian Economic Liberalization

detail.title: Russian Influence and Belarusian Economic Liberalization
detail.abstract: Belarus's deep economic dependence on Russia, spanning energy, trade, and military equipment, has long granted the Kremlin significant leverage over Belarusian internal affairs. This paper argues that proposed privatization of Belarus's state-owned enterprises would dramatically amplify Russian influence by enabling Russian investors, who already account for nearly half of all foreign direct investment in Belarus, to acquire commanding positions in the Belarusian economy. To preserve sovereignty, this paper recommends against privatization, instead proposing reforms to support private sector growth while reducing preferential treatment of state-owned enterprises.

title: Maps on Developing Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Reading
affiliations: and Hakim Sabzevari University

detail.title: Maps on Developing Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Reading
detail.abstract: The study aims to investigate the influence of image-based and text-based concept maps on the reading comprehension abilities of Iranian Intermediate EFL learners. A total of 90 learners participated in the study, consisting of 55 females and 35 males, all between the ages of 18 and 32. Participants were selected from intact classes at three English language schools in Sabzevar, Iran. This research was organized as a quasi-experimental study, in which the participants were segmented into two experimental groups and one control group. The intervention lasted for five weeks, with two sessions each week, each session running for one hour and thirty minutes. The outcomes from the assessments were analyzed using an independent sample ttest and ANOVA test, revealing that the image-based concept map instructional approach improved learners' reading comprehension. In terms of cognitive understanding and creativity, students who utilized image-based concept mapping outperformed their peers in the text-based mapping group. Additionally, the findings indicated that the image-based concept map teaching strategy could assist students in obtaining a more profound understanding of reading materials. Teachers might consider integrating visual mapping techniques to encourage deeper comprehension and facilitate more meaningful learning experiences, which could ultimately lead to better academic performance in language learning contexts.

title: The Hypercomputational Ontology of AI Economic: Embodying the Real World, Human Mind, and the Limits of Turing Machines
affiliations: and Tsinghua University

detail.title: The Hypercomputational Ontology of AI Economic: Embodying the Real World, Human Mind, and the Limits of Turing Machines
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for AI economics integrating computability theory, non-equilibrium thermodynamics, endogenous growth theory, and the philosophy of mind. We resolve the half-century debate between computationalism and anti-computationalism by showing that human brains and physical reality are inherently hypercomputational systems with continuous nonlinear dynamics, capable of solving problems undecidable or intractable for any Turing machine. We introduce the hypercomputational ontological manifold M and dissipative projection operator Pdrop, demonstrating that data is not neutral bits but a topological collapse of continuous hypercomputational dynamics onto discrete symbolic spaces. Modern AI’s success stems not from a breakthrough in Turing computation, but from its ability to compress and approximate hypercomputational solutions encoded in low-entropy data from human minds and physical environments—a process we term extensional alignment. We show that deep reinforcement learning’s strong performance on NP-hard and continuous control problems constitutes a computational outsourcing mechanism: rather than solving problems internally, AI agents delegate computation to the physical environment as an online hypercomputational oracle. We then build a three-tier nested endogenous growth model where growth is driven by AI’s absorption of hypercomputational data, not pure computational power alone. Our model yields three counterintuitive, testable predictions: (1) Pure Turing synthetic data has diminishing marginal value and leads to semiotic collapse via entropy growth in isolated Markov chains; (2) Long-run AI economy growth is bounded by new hypercomputational information from human innovation and physical exploration, not Moore’s Law; (3) Non-algorithmic creative and experimental human labor remains irreplaceable as the ultimate source of economic value. These findings carry profound implications for AI policy, labor economics, and the future of economic growth.

detail.abstract: Scalar Naturalism establishes that the historical dichotomy between capitalism and communism is an artifact of scalar blindness-an epistemological error structurally identical to the wave-particle duality conflict in quantum mechanics prior to formal probabilistic resolution By mapping economic modalities as scale-dependent expressions of multi-level selection (MLS), this treatise provides a unified mathematical and thermodynamic formalization of political economy We define a quasi-functorial mapping between biological and economic categories, tighten the Price equation using discounted Total Factor Productivity (TFP), and mathematically derive how central planning annihilates the evolutionary covariance gradient Using cooperative game theory, Williamsonian transaction cost economics, and the physics of far-from-equilibrium dissipative structures, we demonstrate that macroeconomic efficiency is maximized when macro-level competition is sustained by micro-level cooperative units We define the mathematical boundaries of the firm, the structural compression of agency costs, the resolution of internal capital dynamics, and the mechanism of institutional apoptosis, offering a rigorous formal blueprint for polycentric biomimetic design

title: Credit Lines With(out) Deposits
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) - Fisher College of Business and Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business

detail.title: Credit Lines With(out) Deposits
detail.abstract: Classic theories of commitment financing establish a synergy between making credit lines and taking deposits. We empirically document that private credit lenders are increasingly providing commitment financing to their portfolio companies despite not using deposit financing. The utilization rates and maturities of their credit commitments are comparable to those of banks, and borrowers draw upon them in stressful times. We show that private credit lenders provide this liquidity using a combination of credit lines from banks, uncalled capital commitments, fund advisor support, and fund equity inflows. Although credit lines from banks are ultimately deposit-backed, our findings indicate that private credit lenders are able to substitute, at least in part, alternative funding sources for bank deposit-backed financing.

title: Five Facts About Stablecoins
affiliations: , Circle Internet Financial, Cornell University - Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management and

detail.title: Five Facts About Stablecoins
detail.abstract: We document five facts about payment stablecoins using granular blockchain data from 2020 to 2025. First, stablecoins are functioning as a transaction currency: their onchain transaction volume now exceeds Bitcoin's despite a far smaller outstanding supply, their velocity has risen sharply, and their transaction-size distribution has shifted toward small-value transfers. Second, we develop a Bayesian refinement of the standard visitor-share attribution methodology that uses transaction-timing data to help geolocate individual wallets. This approach shows that stablecoin activity is distributed broadly across the Americas, Europe, and Asia, but that standard methods substantially overstate the cross-regional share of flows. Third, we estimate a structural model of cash management on stablecoin transaction data and find that the typical stablecoin wallet operates on quantitative terms comparable to traditional cash holdings in terms of wallet replenishment opportunities and estimated transaction costs. Fourth, stablecoins are becoming the settlement currency for a rapidly expanding onchain credit market in which lending terms are enforced by rule-based smart contracts rather than by intermediary discretion; balance-sheet accounting disciplined by reserve and currency data indicates that stablecoins' growth reallocates rather than destroys credit. Fifth, stablecoins support programmable, machine-initiated payments: smart contracts participate in roughly a third of stablecoin transactions and over two-thirds of transfer volume on Ethereum, and early agentic-payment protocols such as x402 demonstrate machine-to-machine commerce at sub-cent transaction sizes. Together, these facts suggest that stablecoins are behaving as tokenized money. We discuss implications for traditional financial markets and the design of regulatory frameworks.

detail.abstract: Kenya's devolution of procurement authority to 47 county governments has generated a paradox: a comprehensive legal and institutional architecture for procurement ethics coexists with persistent documented failures of procurement performance. This paper advances a theoretical explanation by integrating institutional theory's three-pillar framework with principal-agent theory's account of information asymmetry and moral hazard. Drawing on primary survey evidence from Lamu County Government (n = 53) and national audit records, the study argues that procurement governance failures are not primarily attributable to the absence of formal rules-the regulatory pillar is well-developed-but to the underdevelopment of normative and cultural-cognitive compliance mechanisms, combined with nested principal-agent structures that attenuate accountability at the staff level. The Lamu case illustrates this concretely: staff exhibit high self-reported ethical adoption, yet the county's audit record documents persistent irregularities-a gap jointly explained as decoupling between formal compliance and actual conduct. The paper develops a three-pillar institutional reform typology, proposes a five-priority research agenda for multi-county comparative scholarship, and derives policy implications for Kenya's national procurement reform architecture under the PPADA 2015 regime.

title: Vector of Needs: Economic Narratives and Market Comovement
affiliations: Independent and Simon Fraser University

detail.title: Vector of Needs: Economic Narratives and Market Comovement

declarations.funderStatement: Bégin wishes to acknowledge the financial support of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and Simon Fraser University.

detail.abstract: Narrative economics argues that stories move asset prices, yet most empirical work flattens complex narratives into simple positive or negative sentiment or broad topics. To address this, we introduce the vector of needs (VoN), a five-dimensional framework that measures the specific human motives a story activates: security, status, control, empathy, and transcendence. We operationalize this framework by applying natural language processing to 4.5 million US news headlines from 2007 to 2022. We then apply the VoN to analyze the cross-sectional structure of market risk. While the VIX measures the level of risk investors expect, the VoN reveals how that risk is distributed across assets. We find that narrative composition significantly predicts future market comovement. Status narratives concentrate comovement, drawing assets together, while transcendence narratives decouple industry returns. Conditional on the VIX and standard predictors, our narrative factors forecast next month's correlation structure out of sample, adding 6.8% incremental R^2 for factor concentration and 6.4% for average pairwise correlation. Ultimately, we demonstrate that different psychological states in the public sphere produce distinctly different shapes of financial risk.

title: Frontier Markets

detail.title: Frontier Markets
detail.abstract: Frontier Market (FM) status serves as a steppingstone for Low-Income Countries (LICs) aspiring to become Emerging Markets (EMs). Since the concept first emerged over three decades ago, FMs have gained substantial investment appeal, particularly after the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. At the same time, the recent series of global shocks starting with the COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the countries’ persistent vulnerabilities. This paper seeks to deepen our understanding of FMs by offering new analysis on the determinants of frontier market status and, using a dynamic country sample, examining the factors that help LICs attain and lose FM status. It finds that building robust macroeconomic fundamentals and ensuring good governance are critical for becoming an FM. In addition, the paper identifies flexible exchange rates, substantial official reserve buffers, and relatively low public debt and deficit levels as key contributors to lessening the sensitivity of FMs’ sovereign spreads to changes in global financial conditions.

title: Pricing Reform Progress
