detail.abstract: Investors reward reform progress. Econometric results suggest that holistic reforms, fiscal spending discipline, and monetary policy credibility are associated with a tightening of Qatar’s external sovereign credit spreads. In particular, investors may view fiscal spending discipline as an integral part of Qatar’s holistic reform and economic diversification. Greater broad-based reform progress also boosts the resilience of sovereign credit spreads to external shocks. The findings support fiscal and monetary policy reforms as part of the broader reform agenda in a holistic manner, as planned under the Third National Development Strategy.

title: Beyond Remittances: A Productivity-Led, AI-Augmented Strategy for Raising Nepal's Long-Term Growth to 5–6 Percent
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Beyond Remittances: A Productivity-Led, AI-Augmented Strategy for Raising Nepal's Long-Term Growth to 5–6 Percent

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, professional, or personal conflicts of interest that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patients, personal data, clinical trials, or animal subjects. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was conducted independently by the author. Computational assistance from AI tools was used for calculations and drafting support, with all analysis and conclusions reviewed and validated by the author.

detail.abstract:
Nepal is about to cross an important threshold - in November 2026, it's officially set to leave its "Least Developed Country" status behind. That sounds like progress, and in some ways it is. But the economy has real problems that don't disappear with a new label.

The biggest one is that Nepal runs largely on money sent home by its citizens working abroad. Remittances keep households afloat and fuel consumer spending, but they don't build an economy. The country produces relatively little, has barely industrialized, and has no strong engine of growth beyond people buying things with money earned elsewhere.

So what would actually change that? This paper tries to answer that question seriously, using an economic model built around Nepal's specific conditions rather than generic development theory. Three paths are laid out and compared: carrying on as things are, making moderate reforms, and pairing those reforms with targeted use of AI.

The findings aren't surprising, but they're worth stating clearly. Remittances can sustain growth in the short run, but getting to a consistent 5–6% annual growth rate requires harder work — better use of capital, stronger institutions, real digital infrastructure, actually developing the hydropower resources Nepal sits on top of, more productive farming, and faster movement of goods at the border.

On AI specifically, the paper stays grounded. It looks at concrete use cases — crop advisory tools, energy demand forecasting, customs automation, Nepali-language technology — and is honest that none of it works without the policy groundwork being laid first. AI isn't a shortcut. Used well, it amplifies reforms that are already happening. Used in isolation, it doesn't do much.

The broader argument is simple: Nepal has a real opportunity to build something more durable than a remittance-dependent economy, but it won't happen on its own.

title: Scaling Representative Deliberation: The Two-Sided Loop — A Governance Design Concept to Balance Legitimacy and Competence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Scaling Representative Deliberation: The Two-Sided Loop — A Governance Design Concept to Balance Legitimacy and Competence
detail.abstract: How can a whole population make high-stakes decisions together efficiently, with low bias, and with enough throughput to be practical? Every institution for collective decision-making is built on a fault line between legitimacy, the sense that a decision is rightfully ours because we shaped it, and competence, the question of whether the decision is any good. Systems force a trade between the two because they ask a single mechanism to deliver both. This paper proposes a standing institution that refuses that bargain. It draws legitimacy from who is in the room-a large, stratified, openly nominated citizen pool filtered only for reasoning quality-and competence from how the room is filtered and tested: random rotating panels, mandatory cost accounting, and three blind independent judging passes whose between-pass agreement functions as a replication test. Drafting is pooled and made competitive on exactly the same terms as judging, so agenda-setting power is dissolved as far as voting power; we call this symmetry the two-sided loop. The aim is not to manufacture perfect statute but to approximate, as closely as today's technology allows, the sovereign ideal that all who are governed should have a say, while minimizing bias, keeping throughput pragmatic, and remaining genuinely implementable. We situate the design against sortition, epistemic and deliberative democracy, multi-body lottocratic proposals, mechanism design, replication, and cryptographic governance. We then give a formal analysis of the replication component, proving an identifiability result: three blind passes are an unbiased detector of panel-level noise but are provably blind to bias carried by the pool itself, with pool-level capture inheriting exactly the same blind spot. The two genuinely novel moves are the symmetric randomized two-sided loop and the use of inter-panel variance as a first-class confidence output; the further contribution is a synthesis that modern encryption, automation, random generation, and digital identity make implementable now rather than only in theory.

title: The Decline of the Jute Industry in India

detail.title: The Decline of the Jute Industry in India
detail.abstract: This paper traces the structural unravelling of India's jute industry from 1921 onward-a decline that was not inevitable, but engineered. Centred on the Hooghly belt of Bengal, the study examines how the Indian Jute Mills Association (IJMA), a British-controlled cartel, worked hand-in-glove with the colonial state to squeeze every last advantage from an industry while shutting out Indian ownership, workers' rights, and long-term investment. Through production records, labour histories, colonial inquiry reports, and Bengali oral sources, the paper maps four cascading crises: the 1921 policy reversal that ended wartime stability; the Great Depression of 1929; the raw material catastrophe created by Partition in 1947; and the slow erosion by synthetic fibres. The argument is simple but uncomfortable: jute's decline was not a market accident. It was the cumulative result of deliberate choices-choices made by people who never bore their consequences.

title: Resilience by Design
affiliations: , , International Monetary Fund (IMF), ,  and Institute of Social and Political Sciences, Universidade de Lisboa

detail.title: Resilience by Design
detail.abstract: The changing global economic landscape is likely to expose the Middle East, North Africa, and Pakistan (MENAP) and Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA) regions to more frequent external shocks, putting a premium on resilient and flexible macroeconomic policy frameworks. By using empirical analysis and model-based scenarios, this paper highlights the important roles of policy frameworks in stabilizing MENAP and CCA economies against adverse global shocks. Two messages stand out from the analysis. First, as countries make progress toward diversifying their exports and deepening domestic financial markets, credible inflation-targeting monetary policy regimes that allow greater exchange rate flexibility could enable faster adjustment to adverse global shocks. Second, adopting strong fiscal rules could help better anchor long-term expectations, reduce risk premiums, and help support countercyclical fiscal responses.

title: Should Oil Economies Worry About Oil Shocks’ Impact on the Banking System? The Case of Oman
affiliations: ,  and International Monetary Fund (IMF) - Policy Development and Review Department

detail.title: Should Oil Economies Worry About Oil Shocks’ Impact on the Banking System? The Case of Oman
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the transmission of oil price shocks to the banking sector in oil-dependent economies, using Oman as a case study. We develop a DSGE model featuring an integrated banking block with endogenous credit rationing and a sovereign wealth fund stabilization rule, calibrated to Omani institutional targets and disciplined by Bayesian methods. Our structural approach disentangles two primary transmission channels: the solvency channel, driven by credit risk and non-performing loans (NPLs), and the liquidity channel, driven by pro-cyclical government deposit withdrawals and sovereign debt issuance. The structural variance decomposition attributes over 54% of non-oil GDP variance and 53% of credit variance to oil price shocks, while bank capital shocks account for less than 0.1%, confirming the quantitative dominance of the liquidity channel. We identify a precautionary liquidity motive—a “liquidity buffer trap”—where banks maintain excess liquidity during booms to hedge against hydrocarbon volatility, structurally suppressing credit to the productive sector. Our counterfactual regime analysis reveals the stabilizing power of credit depth: banking conservatism protects long-term physical capital formation, and the ongoing financialization of the corporate sector— including the rapid growth of Islamic banking and sukuk markets—under Vision 2040 further amplifies this structural resilience. We acknowledge identification challenges inherent in small-sample structural estimation and discuss the sensitivity of results to key modeling assumptions.

title: The Volatility Channel of the Deposit Franchise
affiliations: Prague University of Economics and Business

detail.title: The Volatility Channel of the Deposit Franchise
detail.abstract: Deposit market power creates a path-dependent channel for bank profitability, distinct from the familiar level channel. Because many banks reprice deposits asymmetrically, passing through rate increases more slowly than decreases, funding spreads are convex in the short rate, so expected net interest margins (NIM) depend on the volatility of the rate path, not only its level. We formalize this mechanism in a model with asymmetric deposit repricing and test its predictions using U.S. bank-quarter data from 1984-2025. The effect operates through funding costs rather than asset yields, concentrates in discretionary savings and money-market deposits, and is ordered cross-sectionally by repricing convexity. Deposit franchises therefore contain both static level rents and dynamic volatility exposure.

detail.abstract: Classical technical analysis was codied in an era of human-intermediated order ow, in which chart patterns described the aggregate psychology of the participants who were themselves the market's price-forming mechanism. We argue that a structural change in that mechanism the transition to systematic, information-processing intermediaries that possess the entire technical canon inverts the function of any suciently popularized pattern. The argument rests on three established results of market microstructure: that informed participants prot by exploiting the camouage provided by uninformed order ow (Kyle, 1985); that price formation is the Bayesian updating of a market maker against a ow that mixes informed and uninformed trades (Glosten and Milgrom, 1985); and that large execution requires counterpart that does not exist spontaneously at scale, and must therefore be induced. We formalize a signal inversion result: when a decision rule becomes common knowledge among the uninformed, the location it marks ceases to be a place where the rule's followers are served and becomes a place where they are predictably aggregated precisely the counterpart an informed participant requires. A classical support level, in a mechanism that knows the rule, does not fail by chance; it fails by necessity, because its popularity converts it into a map of the prey. The result is a reexive obsolescence specic to widely diused signals, and it has a sharp methodological corollary: the only robust posture is to localize the structure that induces the trap rather than to predict the direction it resolves toward the latter being, we argue, the single variable in the system without recoverable cause. We delimit the claim honestly: it concerns popularized rules, not all technical information; it localizes, it does not predict; and any operational reading that itself diuses is subject to the very inversion it describes.

title: A Descriptive Atlas of Conditional Exceedance Structure Across a Multi-Asset Universe

detail.title: A Descriptive Atlas of Conditional Exceedance Structure Across a Multi-Asset Universe

publicationDetails.detailsText: An earlier version of this paper is available as a Zenodo preprint at https://zenodo.org/records/20606184

detail.abstract: We present a large-scale descriptive study of conditional tail co-movement across a universe of 161 financial instruments spanning equities, cryptocurrencies, commodities, fixed income, volatility, and foreign exchange, using daily data spanning 1993-2026 for the core equity universe, with some rates series extending to 1960 and crypto series beginning as late as 2024. Our central object is the Conditional Probability of Exceedance (CPE): the empirical frequency with which a target asset's forward logincrement over a horizon breaches a chosen quantile threshold, conditional on a predictor asset's trailing log-increment having breached its own threshold. We compute this quantity exhaustively over a grid of trailing and forward horizons spanning one to three hundred trading days and over a grid of quantile thresholds from the median to the 99th percentile, in both bullish (upper-tail) and bearish (lower-tail) directions, retaining roughly 169,000 pairwise configurations that exceed pre-set support and lift filters. We then extend the analysis to joint conditioning sets of up to ten predictors via a greedy intersection procedure. The study is explicitly descriptive rather than predictive: every threshold is an in-sample quantile and no out-of-sample or forecasting claim is made or implied. Read at the level of asset-class structure rather than individual ranked pairs, the atlas reveals coherent and interpretable regions of strong conditional co-exceedance-within-complex metal linkages, a pronounced volatility-to-equity lower-tail channel, dense intra-crypto coupling, and a recurring crypto-to-commodity association mediated by the post-2024 spot Bitcoin ETFs. We document these structures, characterise their dependence on horizon and threshold, and discuss the important interpretive limits imposed by overlapping observation windows and heterogeneous sample start dates. Alongside CPE, a lift statisticthe ratio of CPE to the unconditional exceedance probability-is computed for each configuration; only signals with lift ≥ 1.5 and a minimum of 100 conditioning observations are retained. An interactive companion dashboard exploring the full CPE atlas is available at https://quantarram.github.io/quantregime-research/notebooks/cpe_dashboard.html.

title: Belonging as Infrastructure: How Campus Environment Design Shapes Sense of Belonging Among Marginalized Students
affiliations: University of Denver and University of Denver

detail.title: Belonging as Infrastructure: How Campus Environment Design Shapes Sense of Belonging Among Marginalized Students
detail.abstract: The campus environment is much more than just the backdrop against which students study; it is a crucial factor in determining whether students feel they belong or are only tolerated. In this paper, it will be argued that while belonging may appear to be a psychological phenomenon that can be engineered institutionally, it is actually something that is either facilitated or denied through space, architecture, symbolism, and politics of design. Based on recent research findings, critical theory, and emerging best practices in higher education planning, the role of campus environment design, ranging from classroom design to wayfinding, gender-inclusive facilities, and culturally symbolic murals, in mediating the experience of belonging among racially marginalized, first-generation, LGBTQIA+, disabled, and religiously diverse students will be analyzed. It will be argued that institutions that see space as neutral are, in fact, making a political decision, and that true inclusion requires a radical reconceptualization of campus design. The paper contributes to the literature on higher education studies, student development theory, and spatial justice.

title: Twelve Voices, One Decision: Evaluating a Persona-Memory FOMC Simulator Across Seventeen Meetings
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Twelve Voices, One Decision: Evaluating a Persona-Memory FOMC Simulator Across Seventeen Meetings
detail.abstract: Central-bank meetings are an unusually clean target for multi-agent LLM simulation. Each meeting yields a discrete decision against public ground truth, the deliberation is conducted by a fixed twelve-member committee, and the supporting documents are released on a published schedule. Existing simulators have been evaluated on a single meeting or on short windows inside one policy regime, so it is not yet clear how persona-and-memory deliberation behaves across a multiyear window that crosses regimes. We instantiated the twelve voting members of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee as persona agents grounded in public material. They deliberated over a release-date-filtered Federal Reserve corpus on a fixed gemini-3-flash-preview backend. For each meeting the system emitted a discrete decision, a draft Statement, draft Minutes, and per-member votes. We scored the outputs against the published policy path along four axes, namely direction, basis-point magnitude, votes, and text fidelity. On the seventeen meetings between March 2024 and March 2026, the simulator labelled 16 of 17 directions correctly, recovered all six cuts, and held magnitude error to 2.2 bp. Statement embedding cosine reached 0.82, and an ensemble LLM-judge averaged 4.07 out of 5. The Minutes were systematically harder, especially in the operative Committee Policy Action paragraph, and the single residual miss was a hedged May 2025 hold. Persona-and-memory deliberation reproduces a substantial share of recent FOMC behaviour and surfaces a clear ceiling at the Minutes level.

title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Thorin Positivity, GGC Factorization and the Riemann Xi Function
detail.abstract: We assemble a single probabilistic framework for the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) organised around one principle: RH is the positivity of a Thorin measure. We show that the reciprocal completed zeta ratio ξ(σ)/ξ(σ + s) is, for σ > 1, the Laplace transform of an infinitely divisible (ID) law; that the associated Thorin density ν σ is unconditionally nonnegative for σ > 1; and that RH is equivalent to the chain U σ ≥ 0 ⇐⇒ ν σ completely monotone ⇐⇒ F σ Stieltjes/Pick ⇐⇒ λ n ≥ 0 (Li), with pointwise positivity ν σ ≥ 0 a necessary condition whose exact strength we determine via Landau's oscillation theorem. We give an explicit-formula representation of the Thorin density and the trigonometric-moment identity λ n = 2 τ >0 (1-cos nθ(τ)). We analyse Kristiansen's signed mixing measure, prove that elementary regroupings cannot repair its sign, and promote the resulting unconditional quasi-infinitely-divisible (QID) quotient factorisation to a central theorem. We then design, in full implementable detail, a numerical protocol to test hyperbolic complete monotonicity (HCM) of the mixing densities, and prove that the slice densities, being truncation-type and discontinuous, can never be HCM, relocating the GGC-upgrade question from the mixing densities (settled negatively) to the component laws. We make concrete progress on the open problems: a Landau-type detection theorem showing pointwise positivity forces every extremal zero onto the line, with the explicit first-negativity bound ν 1/2 (π/2aγ 1) < 0 for an off-line first zero; the equivalence of Gaussian-family Weil positivity with pointwise Thorin positivity; the existence and uniqueness, under RH, of a Krein string with closed-form Weyl function m(s) = (ξ ′ /ξ)(1 2 + √ s)/(2 √ s) and Weyl-matched potential q(x) = 16π 2 e 4x ; a determinantal-pushforward conjecture for the Thorin point process; and, for the GGC questions, two theorems that settle the ends of the truncated-Gamma problem: the centred truncated Gamma is itself a GGC for every truncation level, with explicit Laplace transform, while its logarithm fails infinite divisibility below a positive phase boundary, by a uniformlimit argument; a one-line absolute-monotonicity criterion governs the regime in between. We close with the wider equivalence network (Hermite-Biehler/de Branges, Nyman-Beurling-Báez-Duarte, Weil positivity, the Pólya-Jensen/PF ladder) and a Minimal Positivity Lemma in both original and quotient form.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between teacher benefits and student academic performance across government and private schools/colleges in Ahmedabad city. Using a survey-based descriptive design with a sample of 45 teachers, the research employed univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analyses along with statistical tests including Binomial Test, Chi-Square, One-Sample T-Test, Independent Samples T-Test, and One-Way ANOVA. Findings indicate that while incentives significantly influence teaching style (p = 0.016), no significant difference exists between government and private institution teachers regarding primary motivational challenges. Teachers with more experience tend to earn higher salaries, and permanent staff constitute the majority of experienced respondents. The study highlights that discipline, parental involvement, and syllabus are the most significant factors affecting student academic performance. Perks and incentives are the sole salary-linked motivational factor (p = 0.023). The research contributes empirical evidence to the discourse on educational equity and teacher welfare policy in urban India.

title: How Should a Perpetual Futures Market Liquidate? Auctions, Waterfalls, and Auto-Deleveraging

detail.title: How Should a Perpetual Futures Market Liquidate? Auctions, Waterfalls, and Auto-Deleveraging
detail.abstract: How should a perpetual futures market close a failing position? This paper prices the mechanism space: auto-deleveraging, socialized haircuts, backstop auctions, and forced market sales, each in full equilibrium with the arbitrage sector that anticipates it. No mechanism dominates: auctions lead where capacity is deep, forced sales cascade below a critical depth, and socialization leads for young markets and near the fold. Autodeleveraging is never first; past the small-supply survival region, its events are deaths rather than drawdowns. The optimal waterfall orders mechanisms by social cost with confiscation terminal; switching backstops away from it extends the expected lifetime of the market by 65 percent.

title: The Sweet Cycle

detail.title: The Sweet Cycle
detail.abstract: On a magazine cover in Ginza the author encountered a proposition stated without hedging: that sweetness is justice. The proposition is the occasion of this paper, not its target. What it names, in the idiom of intimate life, is a cycle that appears to harm no one and to benefit everyone who can be seen within it. A firm sells, a person who is indulged feels cared for, a person who indulges feels needed, the bond is strengthened, and the strengthened bond returns as a willingness to buy again. Inside its own boundary the cycle closes upon a surplus of satisfaction, and the satisfaction is real. This paper asks on what grounds, and under what conditions, such a cycle may be judged genuinely good rather than a forged closure that sustains its inner surplus by extraction across its outer edge. The inquiry proceeds by placing several incommensurable frameworks before the same phenomenon, psychoanalysis, neuroscience, the ethics of care, political economy, and feminist theory, and letting each say what it can and cannot say. None is permitted to adjudicate the others. A psychoanalytic foundation, reconstructed here in full from the author's prior work on lack, the objet a, and the cute as a mediation of lack, supplies the structural diagram on which the later analysis is fought. The political economy of amai, in which capital does not merely serve a pre-existing desire but produces and reproduces the desire itself and extracts a surplus from its reproduction, receives the most sustained treatment, because it is there that the difference between a genuine and a forged cycle becomes measurable. The paper does not close on a single verdict. It closes on a plurality of practices, just, ethical, eudaimonic, and co-creative, by which a sweet cycle might be made to keep its value within itself and to return that value to those who make it, with no one reduced to fuel.

title: Do Perpetual Futures Dampen or Amplify Speculative Bubbles?

detail.title: Do Perpetual Futures Dampen or Amplify Speculative Bubbles?
detail.abstract: Perpetual futures are symmetric instruments: longs and shorts post identical margin, and zero net supply pairs every levered position with its opposite. We graft one onto a resale-option bubble market whose single asymmetry is that buying requires storage while shorting requires borrowing. Symmetry delivers a neutrality benchmark; its failure makes the funding rate the published shadow price of the short-side constraint. Leverage and borrow capacity trace a dampening-amplification boundary with an absorbing region. Endogenizing arbitrage capacity yields multiple equilibria, a supply fold, a capacity trap, and an equilibrium-dependent leverage threshold. Under belief neutrality, welfare rises; funding-rule standards dominate leverage caps.

title: When Do Deep Markets Die? Slow Capital, Sudden Runs, and the Lifetime of a Perpetual Futures Market

detail.title: When Do Deep Markets Die? Slow Capital, Sudden Runs, and the Lifetime of a Perpetual Futures Market
detail.abstract: How long does a deep perpetual futures market live? This paper makes arbitrage capacity a state variable: entry is slow, exit after auto-deleveraging is fast, and runs arrive as stress episodes thinned by a global-games threshold. One run kills: confiscation lands capacity below the unstable rest point, so the desert is absorbing and markets die once. The expected lifetime has a closed form under secular supply growth. Approaching the fold, price quality improves while capacity dispersion diverges, so the calm is in prices and the warning is in flows. A state-contingent buffer rule dominates the set-and-forget capitalization that venues use.

title: Driver-Personalized Risk Assessment in Car-Following: Validation of an Optical-Flow-Based Model using SHRP 2 Naturalistic Driving
affiliations: Waseda University, Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, General Motors LLC, Waseda University and Waseda University

detail.title: Driver-Personalized Risk Assessment in Car-Following: Validation of an Optical-Flow-Based Model using SHRP 2 Naturalistic Driving
detail.abstract: Traffic crashes remain a major cause of injury and mortality worldwide, yet the effectiveness of crash-preventive safety systems is often limited by misalignment between system design and an individual driver’s preferences. To address this, we tailored the existing risk feeling formula (RFF) approach to individual drivers’ braking styles. From a 50-driver subset of the Second Strategic Highway Research Program Naturalistic Driving Study dataset, we extracted 1,864 car-following sequences in which accelerator release (”gas-off”) was followed by brake application (”brake-on”). Risk indices were calculated from the drivers’ inverse time headway (1/THW) and inverse time-to-collision (1/TTC) distributions, representing global and optical flow, respectively. For each driver, the driver-specific RFF model (RFFprsn) normalized 1/THW and 1/TTC values by that driver’s own median values at brake-on, as estimated from an independent calibration subset.Brake-on thresholds differed markedly across drivers (median 1/THW: 0.431-0.962 s⁻¹; median 1/TTC: 0.042-0.143 s⁻¹), underscoring the need for driver-personalized risk estimation. In cross-validation, RFFprsn discriminated gas-off from brake-on substantially better than the fixed-weight RFF (area under the curve = 0.939 vs. 0.820), increasing true positives by 15.5% and reducing false positives by 43.4%. These gains under naturalistic conditions were, however, lower than those observed in prior simulator studies. These results support personalized normalization as a practical mechanism for aligning risk estimation with driver-specific behavior under naturalistic conditions, while motivating future context-aware recalibration (accounting for road type, traffic density, weather, and driver state) to address the remaining, and still substantial, within-driver variability.

title: Sovereign Risk and Natural Disaster Shocks
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and

detail.title: Sovereign Risk and Natural Disaster Shocks
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of natural disasters on the domestic sovereign yield curve, shedding light on their distinct transmission channels. Using a sample of 72 developing countries during the period 2000-20, and leveraging a newly compiled dataset on domestic treasury bill and bond yields, the findings from the fixed-effects and the local projection difference in difference estimations point to a disaster premium in the pricing of domestic government securities. While natural disasters significantly steepen the yield curve, their effects are confined to short-term maturity debts. In constrast, a worsening in climate vulnerability shifts upward the entire yield curve. Heightened fiscal stress and monetary policy stance emerge as the main transmission channels. These results underscore the importance of integrating resilience building into debt management and fiscal policy frameworks.

title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, Yale University - Department of Economics, Stanford University and

detail.title: From Trade War to Green Transition: Optimal Electric Vehicle Tariffs with Revenue-Funded Subsidies
detail.abstract: We study the optimal design of trade and industrial policy when governments pursue environmental objectives alongside traditional national welfare. Motivated by the global transition to electric vehicles (EVs) and growing concerns about competitiveness, resilience, and the environment, we develop a framework in which policymakers choose tariffs and domestic production subsidies to maximize national welfare, defined as the sum of consumer surplus, domestic profits, environmental benefits, and tariff revenue net of subsidies. We combine a theoretical model of differentiated-product oligopoly with a structural demand model estimated using vehicle-level data from 13 countries during 2004-2023 that together account for the vast majority of global EV sales. Our central finding is that the optimal policy combines a moderate tariff on imported EVs with a subsidy to domestic EV production financed through tariff revenue. This policy substantially outperforms both outright protectionism and laissez-faire. Relative to current policies, it preserves consumer access to affordable EVs, accelerates fleet electrification, supports domestic producers, and remains budget-neutral. For the United States, the optimal policy more than doubles EV market share, generates over $45 billion in annual welfare gains, and avoids approximately 95 million tons of lifetime CO 2 emissions. A key mechanism underlying these results is the pass-through of tariffs and subsidies to prices, which depends critically on demand curvature, product substitution, and market structure. More broadly, our results suggest that effective industrial policy requires careful attention to market structure and country-specific conditions, balancing consumer, producer, fiscal, and environmental objectives rather than adhering to ideological prescriptions.

title: Does Deep Arbitrage Stabilize or Destabilize Perpetual Futures Markets?

detail.title: Does Deep Arbitrage Stabilize or Destabilize Perpetual Futures Markets?
detail.abstract: A perpetual futures market can be priced efficiently and still run. This paper integrates two findings that pull in opposite directions: (1) deeper arbitrage capacity stabilizes the funding rate and the underlying bubble, and (2) larger positions raise the hazard of autodeleveraging, the rule that confiscates winning positions to close uncollateralized losses. Embedding a global-games run stage in an entry model of arbitrage capacity yields a solvency ceiling: the market limits its own depth. Equilibrium run risk is hump-shaped in lendable supply, and a single elasticity ratio locates where restraining entry raises welfare. A mutualized buffer levy reconciles depth with safety.

detail.abstract: This study examines the socioeconomic impacts of institutional quality and higher education on economic development in Nigeria by analysing how university enrolment, university research output, government education spending, and governance effectiveness influence unemployment, income inequality, and poverty using a time series within a dynamic autoregressive distributed lag framework. The results confirm the existence of stable long run relationships and significant short run dynamics across the models, as evidenced by the statistically significant error correction terms. The findings show that in the long run, none of the explanatory variables significantly reduce unemployment, indicating persistent structural constraints, while in the short run, university research output increases unemployment (β = 0.0003, p < 0.01). For income inequality, long run effects are insignificant, but in the short run, university research output (β =-0.000489, p < 0.01) and governance effectiveness (β =-0.201639, p < 0.01) significantly reduce inequality. In contrast, poverty outcomes reveal stronger long run relationships, where university enrolment (β = 0.663847, p < 0.01) and research output (β = 0.002551, p < 0.01) increase poverty, while government education spending (β =-4.538374, p < 0.01) and governance effectiveness (β =-0.764236, p < 0.05) significantly reduce it, with the interaction between education spending and governance also being significant (β = 0.144382, p < 0.01). Overall, the study concludes that the effectiveness of higher education in improving socioeconomic outcomes in Nigeria depends heavily on governance quality and the efficiency of public expenditure, and recommends strengthened institutional frameworks, improved policy implementation, and enhanced alignment between education and labour market needs to achieve inclusive and sustainable development.

title: The China Imbalance Residual: A Demographic Decomposition

detail.title: The China Imbalance Residual: A Demographic Decomposition
detail.abstract: The Chinese current-account surplus has averaged approximately 2 percent of GDP since 2015, declining from a 2007 peak near 10 percent yet remaining far above what its income level and demographic structure would predict in a global panel. We estimate this gap as the residual against the income-conditional demographic baseline fitted on 140 countries with China held out. The residual averages +5 to +12 percentage points of GDP across four sub-periods of 2000-2024, peaks at +14.3 pp in 2007, and decays at a 16.6-year half-life (bootstrap 95% CI 9.5 to 58.7 years). Country-cluster bootstrap and within-year joint-demographic permutation tests reject the null of zero residual in every period (p < 0.002). The residual is concentrated on the saving side. China's private-saving residual exceeds prediction by +23 to +28 percentage points/GDP across all four sub-periods; the government-saving residual flipped from +3.5 in the 2000s to-4.0 in the 2020s; the gross-investment residual is +12 to +20 pp. Adding household consumption share and gross investment share to the baseline absorbs 70 percent of the residual under a contemporaneous specification and 30 to 50 percent under five-year-lagged regressors that mitigate simultaneous-determination bias. The aging-conditional channel survives lagging: the Z₁ × household-consumption interaction is-0.14 (p < 0.001) contemporaneously and-0.045 (p = 0.021) at five-year lags. A peer-group placebo on Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Korea, Indonesia, India, Singapore, and Japan shows the absorption pattern is shared by Thailand and India but not by the other peers; the residual structure is not generic to developmental-state Asia. Sex-ratio and pension/financial-repression mechanisms produce null Z₁ interactions in crosscountry variation. Projecting the residual decay alongside the United Nations medium-variant demographic projection implies China's current account flips to deficit around 2030 and reaches-2.8 pp of GDP by 2040 (95% CI-4.0 to-0.6), with the deepening demographic baseline rather than the residual driving the reversal.

title: Fuel Pricing Reform in India: A Risk Governance Perspective

detail.title: Fuel Pricing Reform in India: A Risk Governance Perspective

detail.abstract: This paper asks how India should price retail fuel so that oil-price volatility is borne deliberately rather than by whichever party is least able to refuse it. We reinterpret fuel-price controls not as subsidies but as a risk-allocation mechanism, and state a simple accounting identity: the gap between import-parity cost and the regulated price is conserved, so suppressing pass-through relocates it to the oil marketing companies (OMCs), their shareholders, or the budget. Using Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) crude and retail data, we treat the 2026 Iran-war freeze-Delhi petrol held at Rs 94.77 for 562 days-as a natural experiment, and backtest a two-step hedge that buffers transient moves through a stabilization fund while passing large moves to consumers. The freeze swung roughly Rs 100,000 crore between consumers and the OMCs and levied an estimated Rs 28-42 thousand crore on minority shareholders; the hedge bounds the buffer near Rs 16,000 crore on a Rs 45,000 crore seed. We set out the statutory architecture this implies.

detail.abstract:
EU prudential and conduct frameworks increasingly position first-line managers in financial institutions as local owners of risk within their areas of responsibility. Yet this governance architecture does not necessarily provide a clearly articulated mechanism for developing the capacity of those managers to recognise, interpret, and refer emerging legal risk signals before they mature into formal legal, compliance, or supervisory incidents. This article conceptualises that pre-formal weakness as legal erosion: the gradual decline of first-line capacity to identify and escalate legally relevant signals arising in ordinary business operations. 

The article examines whether legal coaching may function as a complementary internal governance mechanism for addressing this weakness. Legal coaching is defined here not as legal advice, compliance monitoring, or a substitute for the legal function, but as a bounded developmental mechanism designed to strengthen Legal Issue Escalation Capacity among firstline managers. Its purpose is to improve recognition, triage, and referral behaviour at the point where legally significant issues first become visible inside operational decision-making. 

Methodologically, the article adopts a doctrinal-conceptual approach. It draws on EU internal governance materials, including Article 74 CRD V, EBA internal governance expectations, conduct regulation, legal professional privilege doctrine, and organisational governance literature on escalation, risk culture, and sensemaking. It does not claim empirical validation of legal coaching as an institutional model. Any frameworks discussed, including signal maps or maturity-assessment tools, are therefore presented as illustrative and heuristic rather than as validated monitoring instruments, performance-management tools, or supervisory templates. 

The article makes three contributions. First, it identifies legal erosion as an under-theorised preformal governance weakness in financial institutions. Second, it distinguishes legal coaching from legal advice, compliance training, and compliance oversight. Third, it maps the legal and institutional constraints that would shape any legitimate deployment of such a mechanism, including confidentiality, privilege, role conflict, professional boundaries, escalation duties, and data protection. The article concludes that legal coaching may be defensible only if designed as a carefully bounded governance protocol that complements, rather than displaces, established legal, compliance, and managerial responsibilities.

detail.title: Common Shocks and Fiscal Divergence: The Evolution of State Liabilities in India

publicationDetails.detailsText: It's a working paper and has not been submitted to any journal yet.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the co-movements and dynamics of state-level liabilities in India from 1994 to 2022 for 21 states. Using a dynamic factor model with time-varying loadings and stochastic volatility, the liabilities-to-GSDP ratio is decomposed into national, liability-specific, and state-specific factors. These factors help to assess how states with different liability levels and economic strength respond to fiscal pressures. The results reveal that common shocks, e.g., the GFC, Covid-19, and Demonetization, play a dominant role in shaping the state liabilities. Over time, the influence of the economically strong and low-liability states has declined. Liability-specific factors, like the states with low and high liabilities, have gained prominence in the post-2014 era. The result is more evident in high GSDP states, indicating growing structural divergence. The empirical results show that states with strong fiscal discipline are characterized by higher own tax revenue and stable law and order. These states mostly rely on their internal debt levels. Besides, they are better insulated from national volatilities. In contrast, states heavily reliant on central transfers and subsidy-driven expenditure remain more exposed and are fiscally vulnerable. These findings highlight the need for a differentiated fiscal approach across India's states, with a policy focus on enhancing internal revenue capacity, rebalancing expenditure priorities, and fostering long-term fiscal autonomy.

title: Antitrust's Controversy with Disruption
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: Antitrust's Controversy with Disruption
detail.abstract:
Most economic progress comes from disruptive firms that offer some new thing, benefiting their customers, workers, and suppliers but often harming rivals who are committed to older technologies or methods.  Antitrust policy has always had an uneasy relationship with disruptive firms, too often exaggerating their harms while underestimating their benefits.  This paper examines four disruptive events in the history of United States competition policy.

First, was the rise of the large technology-driven manufacturing firm in the late nineteenth century that inspired the antitrust movement.  Antitrust policy could have folloowed a policy that was already well developed in state law, using corporate law rules to keep corporations small and their operations restricted within a narrow range.  Instead, in the Sherman Act it adopted a “restraint of trade” standard that emphasized high output, low prices, and innovation rather than small firms.  Contrary to the state law approach, the antitrust approach favored large, vertically integrated firms to the extent that they benefited their consumers, workers, and other suppliers.

A second revolution was in consumer distribution, facilitated by the growth of large, vertically integrated retailers.  Here the antitrust record was far less admirable, giving us the Robinson-Patman Act to protect small firms from larger rivals whose products benefitted consumers greatly but harmed firms dedicated to older distribution methods.  It also produced the Miller-Tydings Act. Until it was repealed, that Act permitted states to authorize resale price maintenance as a way of protecting home-grown businesses from lower cost national rivals.  An additional movement, which the courts were able to beat back, would have imposed ever increasing "death taxes" on chain store owners.

Third was the disastrous litigation in the IBM case in the 1960s and 1970s, which attacked the first great digital revolution in computing by confusing technological advance with predation.  The government finally gave up and dismissed it.

The fourth and final disruption, in internet digital technology, is still under way.  The last portion of this paper considers when antitrust actions against big tech are meritorious and when they are harmful, and warns against repetition of the IBM tragedy.

The history of antitrust law’s several confrontations with competitively disruptive markets offers a great deal of advice: in such markets antitrust policy should watch carefully, be slow to intervene, and particularly cautious about remedies.  Although this advice is probably good in all markets, it is particularly important in markets that are subject to rapid innovation and change.

title: National Investment Pension Model (NIPM ): Transition Financing and Institutional Design for Bulgaria's Pension System

detail.title: National Investment Pension Model (NIPM ): Transition Financing and Institutional Design for Bulgaria's Pension System

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Bulgaria’s pay-as-you-go pension system faces structural collapse. The state budget transfer to the National Social Security Institute has grown from 45% of pension expenditure in 2017 to an estimated 83% in 2026, driven by a worker-to-retiree ratio declining toward 1.1:1 by 2050 and a population loss exceeding 1.5 million since 2005. The replacement rate is projected to fall below 28% by mid-century, with old-age poverty rates potentially reaching 35–40%.

This paper presents the National Investment Pension Model (NIPM) — a comprehensive structural reform replacing the PAYG logic with a strict functional separation. System A provides a universal, unconditional civil protection guarantee at the poverty line (EUR 391/month, 2026), financed entirely from general taxation. System B establishes fully-funded, defined-contribution personal accounts (14.8% contribution rate) managed by an independent board under constitutional protection, with full inheritability and daily transparency.

The transition is financed through a dedicated 5% transition tax on total labour income without ceiling, projected to generate EUR 65–85 billion cumulatively through 2055, with an automatic sunset mechanism tied to the demographic decline of legacy pensioners. Five new modules address identified weaknesses: a liberalized opt-out via personal investment accounts (with mandatory financial literacy certification), a triple-choice package for the transitional generation (ages 50–55), longevity risk management through actuarially fair state annuities, and constitutional entrenchment of personal account property rights.

The net fiscal difference versus the status quo is projected at EUR 230+ billion over 24 years. All projections are nominal and require actuarial verification by the National Social Security Institute.

title: Convergence of Neuroeconomics and Data Science: An Illustration through Neural Network Modelling

detail.title: Convergence of Neuroeconomics and Data Science: An Illustration through Neural Network Modelling
detail.abstract: Economics has inherited ideas from psychology and neuroscience to form a multidisciplinary subject 'Neuroeconomics'. On the other hand, statistics, inspired by neuroscientific research, has embraced computational methods similar to neural network inside the human brain. We are at the center of a historic convergence among these subjects, aiming to understand how brain makes complex economic decisions and which model can better predict economic decisions. This paper explores the multidisciplinary research in economics, psychology, neuroscience and data science, with an attempt to demonstrate the application of neural network models in economic forecasting. The paper explores the latest methods in the field of artificial intelligence that are inspired by neural network models inside human brain. As demonstration, we have applied Long-Short Term Memory Model (LSTM) to forecast KSE-100 Index returns using non-parametric modelling.

title: How do economies with open labour markets work? The role of temporary migration in the European Union
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: How do economies with open labour markets work? The role of temporary migration in the European Union
detail.abstract: This paper studies how temporary migration affects macroeconomic fluctuations and the conduct of stabilisation policies using a two-country DSGE model with search-and-matching frictions and endogenous cross-border labour mobility. The analysis shows that migration responds endogenously to both labour market conditions and exchange rate movements, making it an important channel of cross-country adjustment. Labour mobility alters the transmission of shocks in three main ways. First, it redistributes adjustment to productivity shocks across regions, smoothing output fluctuations in receiving economies while producing more nuanced effects in sending economies. Second, it favorably affects policy trade-offs: migration reduces the output costs of monetary tightening, and it mitigates the crowdingout effects of fiscal expansions. Third, it strengthens cross-country spillovers by transmitting labour market shocks across regions and reshaping their domestic propagation. Overall, temporary migration emerges as a powerful but non-neutral adjustment mechanism that affects both the effectiveness of stabilization policies and the distribution of macroeconomic outcomes across integrated economies.

detail.abstract: We study the drivers of the spread of U.S. municipal green bonds over U.S. Treasury bonds. The spread is estimated using synthetic Treasury bonds priced from the Treasury spot-rate curve and constructed to match green bond-specific cash-flow features. Using 2,912 AAA-rated U.S. municipal green bonds with daily yields from July 2009 to June 2023, we show that spread dynamics are mainly explained by macrofinancial variables and major market or policy shocks, such as the Treasury yield-curve slope, the clean-energy index, gold prices, the Flash Crash, the U.S. credit-rating downgrade, and COVID-19 emergency rate cuts. In contrast, natural disasters have limited explanatory power. Only selected storms matter at national or regional levels, but their economic effects are generally weak. Hence, natural-disaster risk does not appear to be either a systematic or an idiosyncratic source of risk in the market.

title: Cleansing Oil
affiliations: Northwestern University, Judd A. and Marjorie Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Cleansing Oil

declarations.funderStatement: Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia

detail.abstract: I study the dynamics of greenhouse gas emissions following unexpected increases in oil prices from supply disruptions. I find that CO 2-equivalent atmospheric concentrations decrease by 0.10 ppm relative to trend following a 10% increase in crude oil prices. This effect is heterogeneous across gases, reflecting a reshuffling of fossil fuel usage. Natural gas and petroleum products fall sharply across the board, while low-quality coal and bioenergy generation rise. Driven by tighter financial conditions and elevated uncertainty, solar capacity contracts. Hybrid and EV adoption increase markedly, partially substituting for conventional internal combustion engine vehicles.

title: Global Reserve Synchronization and the Evolution of International Financial Integration

detail.title: Global Reserve Synchronization and the Evolution of International Financial Integration
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the global co-movement of international reserves (IR) using an annual panel of 78 countries from 1968 to 2023. Employing a time-varying dynamic factor model with stochastic volatility, the study decomposes reserve fluctuations into global, regional, and country-specific components. The results indicate that a dominant global factor explains a large share of reserve variation, although its importance declines significantly following the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), with regional and country-specific factors becoming increasingly relevant. Consistent with this finding, reserve synchronization weakens after the GFC and declines further during the COVID-19 pandemic, reflecting growing heterogeneity in reserve-management strategies. The study further identifies trade and financial variables as the principal drivers of the global reserve cycle. While rolling correlations reveal a decline in short-run synchronization, Johansen cointegration tests and a Vector Error Correction Model provide evidence of stable long-run relationships between IR and their driving forces. Impulse response analysis confirms that shocks to exports, imports, current account balances, and capital inflows have persistent effects on reserve dynamics. Overall, the findings suggest that major global crises altered the degree of reserve synchronization without fundamentally changing the long-run determinants of reserve accumulation.

detail.abstract: Workers and organizations routinely choose the complexity of tasks that they undertake. We study how cognitive ability and overconfidence shape this choice of task complexity, both theoretically and experimentally. Consistent with our model, we find that more cognitively able individuals choose more complex tasks. Conditional on cognitive ability, we find that more overconfident individuals also choose more complex tasks. About 80% of subjects pick their payoff-maximizing task, and higher cognitive ability predicts more efficient choices of task complexity. But errors are strikingly onesided: nearly all who fail to choose optimally pick tasks that are too complex. Our findings suggest that organizations should pair task menus and incentives for choosing more complex tasks with information and feedback that help workers assess their ability and probability of success. This preserves the benefits of self-selection while reducing costly overreach.

title: (Unobserved) Heterogeneity in the Bank Lending Channel: Accounting for Bank-firm Interactions and Specialization
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - Department of Finance, University of California, Santa Cruz - Department of Economics and Central Bank of Chile

detail.title: (Unobserved) Heterogeneity in the Bank Lending Channel: Accounting for Bank-firm Interactions and Specialization
detail.abstract: The transmission of bank credit supply shocks hinges on unobserved bank-firm interactions, reflecting lending specialization. Using bank-firm credit data, we develop a framework that identifies latent interaction patterns and estimates heterogeneous transmission of credit shocks across unobserved firm types. We document significant heterogeneity in transmission across estimated firm types, revealing hidden dimensions of bank specialization associated with greater credit provision and lower default rates. Accounting for such bank-firm heterogeneity and network structure is essential to understanding the bank lending channel and its real effects. We uncover a novel bank-firm matching channel by which credit shocks are amplified through bank-firm networks.

detail.title: From River to Server: Hydrological Modelling of the Ganga for Sustainable AI Infrastructure!

contentType.other: Original unpublished manuscript submitted for first-time review/publication.

publicationDetails.detailsText: No, the paper has neither appeared nor been accepted for publication in a paper series, journal, or book.

detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital infrastructure has significantly increased the demand for data centres, which require substantial quantities of freshwater for cooling and operational purposes. In a water-stressed country like India, balancing digital development with sustainable water-resource management has become a critical challenge. The River Ganga, one of India’s most important ecological, cultural, and economic lifelines, presents both an opportunity and a responsibility for sustainable infrastructure planning.

This study investigates the hydrological suitability of the Upper Ganga basin for the development of AI data centres by applying the Nash Cascade Model to analyze river-flow dynamics and long-term water availability. Using secondary discharge data obtained from the Central Water Commission of India, the river system is represented as a second-order cascade of linear reservoirs and examined through a state-space formulation involving phase portraits, slope fields, and eigenvalue stability analysis. The results demonstrate that the Nash system converges towards a stable equilibrium, indicating predictable and resilient flow behavior under varying initial conditions. The storage coefficient further provides insight into the basin’s ability to regulate flow fluctuations and maintain hydrological stability.

A multi-criteria suitability assessment identifies Prayagraj as the most favorable location for AI data centre development within the Ganga basin due to its high annual discharge, reliable dry-season flow supported by the Yamuna confluence, strong infrastructure accessibility, and manageable flood risk. The findings demonstrate that mathematically informed hydrological models can provide an effective framework for balancing technological expansion with environmental conservation. The study ultimately proposes a data-driven approach to data centre siting that aligns with sustainable water management and the broader objective of preserving the ecological integrity of the River Ganga.

title: From Compliance to Market Power: Producer Strategy, Structural Fingerprints, and the Limits of Reactive Positioning in Commodity Markets

detail.title: From Compliance to Market Power: Producer Strategy, Structural Fingerprints, and the Limits of Reactive Positioning in Commodity Markets
detail.abstract:
Why do commodity-exporting developing countries accept prices set by buyers, even when their production volumes dominate global supply? Incentive-based accounts attribute this to market access conditions, buyer capability requirements, and regulatory design. This paper proposes a structural explanation grounded in the Market Suffocation Hypothesis (MSH): producers remain price-takers because buyers retain abundant sourcing alternatives, and the structural conditions required to close those alternatives are absent in most commodity-exporting contexts.

The paper extends the MSH to its supply-side analogue and introduces the Producer Market Power Index (PMPI) — a four-component measurement instrument incorporating a buyer concentration modifier from Herfindahl-Hirschman Index calculations and a non-price measure of differentiation depth from WIPO Lex intellectual property data. Six structural fingerprints of successful producer market power are identified inductively from Ethiopian specialty coffee, Colombian palm oil, Vietnamese pangasius, and Costa Rican coffee, and cross-validated against documented failure cases. The paper formalises participation constraints for producer coalitions, drawing on the 2026 UAE exit from OPEC as a live case of coalition fracture under diverging individual time horizons — a dynamic with direct agricultural analogues in smallholder responses to biological asset cycles and climate stress.

A third entry path is identified alongside the compliance sequencing framework: where producers select or pivot to a product for which no low-quality substitute exists, the quality sink is absent by design rather than closed by enforcement. The central implication is that compliance investment and strategic market power are sequentially rational, not mutually exclusive — the infrastructure built for compliance creates the traceability, governance, and buyer relationship assets from which market power can subsequently be developed. The paper establishes a theory-building and diagnostic architecture for identifying when and how producing countries can pursue market power, and proposes an empirical programme for out-of-sample validation.

title: Auditing the Audit Trails: A Cryptographic Framework and a Compliance Survey of 185 Published Machine-Learning Papers in Quantitative Finance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Auditing the Audit Trails: A Cryptographic Framework and a Compliance Survey of 185 Published Machine-Learning Papers in Quantitative Finance
detail.abstract: The U.S. Federal Reserve’s SR 11-7 (April 2011) and the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, effective for high-risk systems on 2 August 2026) require firms deploying machine-learning models in regulated domains to maintain per-prediction audit trails: code state, data state, model state, compute environment, and the prediction itself, recorded with enough integrity protection that an external reviewer can verify any claim ex post. Existing open-source ML tooling (MLflow, Weights & Biases, DVC) targets experiment tracking or artifact versioning; none produces an SR 11-7-shaped audit trail with low-friction integration, vendor-neutral storage, and regulator-export capability out of the box. This paper makes two paired contributions. First, we introduce mr-audit, an open-source Python package that writes one immutable, hash-chained record per ML prediction, capturing git commit, library versions, input hash, model parameters, compute environment, random seed, and prediction value. Records form a linked hash chain via SHA-256; tampering with any record breaks the chain. The package ships with a replay engine, a driftdetection module (Kolmogorov-Smirnov plus Population Stability Index), and a regulator-export bundle. We compare mr-audit head-to-head against five existing tools on nine audit-trail capabilities and on three quantitative benchmarks (throughput, storage overhead, tamper-detection sensitivity). Second, we apply the same compliance rubric to a corpus of 185 published machine-learning papers in quantitative finance posted between 1952 and 2025 (drawn from the 119-paper survey corpus of Khan (2026b) and a 2024–2025 arXivq-fin extension constrained to papers with a discoverable code-repository link). For each paper, an automated pipeline locates the code link, clones the repository, and mechanically scores the six static compliance dimensions: code accessibility, data release, computational environment, random-seed documentation, input-data lineage, and model-state persistence. The static-six analysis followed a pre-specified plan (hypotheses and rubric fixed before the scoring step and deposited at OSF); we are explicit that this is a pre-specified plan, not a timestamp-enforced preregistration, and that the six manual-review dimensions deferred to a follow-up version will be genuinely pre-registered (timestamp-enforced) before any of their scoring begins. On the six automatable dimensions we find: a mean static-rubric score of 1.52 of 6 (full corpus, N = 185); a mean of 3.28 of 6 conditional on the paper carrying a discoverable code link (N = 80); 11 of 185 papers (5.9%) score the full 6 of 6 on the static rubric, all of them within the 80-paper code-link subset (13.8% of it); the temporal slope of compliance is +0.088 score units per year (in the pre-specified range [0.05, 0.20], statistically nonzero); and a 10% rot rate on discovered code URLs (21% if non-GitHub repositories are counted). Three papers (FinRL, FinGPT, Grinsztajn tabular-benchmark) achieve a perfect static score of 6 of 6; they are existence proofs that audit-grade publication is achievable but far from the field’s median. The six manual-review dimensions (bit-identical replay, per-prediction logging, drift monitoring, significance testing, multiple-comparison correction, out-of-sample protocol) require Tier-1 code execution or manual review and are deferred to v2.1 of this paper. The full per-paper scorecard, the scoring pipeline, and an audit-of-audit log are released publicly with the package. The package, the audit pipeline, the corpus, the per-paper scorecard, an audit script that re-derives every numerical claim in this paper from JSON outputs, and a 6,825-record demonstration log on the seven-model volatility-forecasting panel of Khan (2026f) are released at github.com/ayk5511/mr-audit.

title: Which Impact Models Survive Price Diffusivity? Stress-testing the Structural Constraint of Bonart (2026) in Simulation and Public Data

detail.title: Which Impact Models Survive Price Diffusivity? Stress-testing the Structural Constraint of Bonart (2026) in Simulation and Public Data
detail.abstract: Bonart [2026] shows that requiring both realized and counterfactual prices to be diffusive forces the square-root law of market impact for information-neutral traders, and yields a falsifiable diagnostic: de-impacted prices under any valid impact model must themselves be diffusive. The paper names likely violators but does not test them; this paper runs the test. Implemented as a statistical battery and an exact analytic kernel check, the criterion fails every canonical model under realistic autocorrelated order flow, in two opposite directions: permanent linear impact leaves trending residuals, decaying kernels leave mean-reverting ones, and the critical aggregate calibration of the propagator cannot satisfy the individual-level constraint. A minimum-phase factorization yields a violation severity score and a canonical repair, in every case the pure surprise-response model. Empirically, 63 million Binance trades and synthetic metaorders built from public data reproduce the linear-to-square-root crossover on BTC and ETH, with rate scaling consistent with a square root in trade counts (day-cluster bootstrap b = 0.46 [0.43, 0.49] and 0.50 [0.45, 0.57]) and near-zero dependence on volume per execution. On thinner pairs the rate exponent drifts above one-half, and duration scaling deviates from the factorized prediction everywhere; both remain open.

title: Koopman-CMH: A Formal Treatment of Spectral Structure Persistence in Historical Dynamics

detail.title: Koopman-CMH: A Formal Treatment of Spectral Structure Persistence in Historical Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper proves the Koopman-A2 Correspondence (Theorem 1)-the formal result announced as Conjecture 1 of WP-2026-005-and conducts the first pre-registered empirical test of its substantive antecedent. Theorem 1 shows that shared ergodic-class membership implies shared leading Koopman spectrum, conditional on Axioms A2, A3, A4, and a forcing-homogeneity assumption that refines the antecedent stated in WP-2026-005. The empirical test applies a canonical Hankel-DMD estimator to a panel of eight Western European polities across two structurally stationary sub-windows (1820-1913, 1945-2020). The pre-registered binary criterion rejects Question 1 in both sub-windows: no eigenvalue beyond the invariant-measure cluster meets the persistence threshold. A post-hoc power analysis finds effectively zero power at the available effective sample size-the postwar effective sample size (Nₑff = 210) falls below the operator's parameter count-so the verdict constrains detectability, not existence. A credible test requires Nₑff ≈ 1,000. Two methodological results give the paper positive content. The invariant-measure mode is recovered with the directional attenuation Proposition 4.2 predicts, on the one mode whose true value the axiomatic structure fixes a priori. A Juglar-band correspondence recurs across the inter-war break but is not statistically distinguishable from noise (37% match rate in surrogate null panels). The paper recommends canonical Tu et al. (2014) DMD with Gavish-Donoho truncation as the default for macrohistorical panel data.

title: Beyond The Farm Gate: Addressing Labour and Human Right Issues Occurring Downstream in the Textiles and Apparel Value Chain

detail.title: Beyond The Farm Gate: Addressing Labour and Human Right Issues Occurring Downstream in the Textiles and Apparel Value Chain
detail.abstract: Purpose-Our research seeks to understand how actors in the Australian cotton industry can address downstream labour and human rights risks in the textiles and apparel value chain. Design/methodology/approach-Taking the Australian cotton industry as the site of our action research project, we conducted a qualitative thematic analysis of 19 interviews, supplemented by industry engagement and desktop research. Findings-We identify seven opportunities for action by the Australian cotton industry to address downstream labour and human rights risks, which are articulated in the context of a strategic enforcement approach. Originality/value-The research focuses on opportunities for action to address downstream labour and human rights risks, thereby going beyond the traditional interventions by fashion brands and retailers that target upstream actors.

title: The Unified AI Adoption Model
affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University

detail.title: The Unified AI Adoption Model
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) implementation is often treated as a tool-selection problem, yet research on technology uptake, human-AI interaction, organizational change, and AI risk management suggests that outcomes depend on the relationship among people, workflows, governance, and institutional purpose. This article develops the Unified AI Adoption Model, a dual-level approach that integrates the Personal AI Adoption Framework (PAAF) and the Scalable AI Adoption Framework (SAAF). PAAF guides individuals through seven stages-Familiarize, Learn, Evaluate, Experiment, Protect, Ingrain, and Grow-while SAAF guides organizations through Discover, Fund, Plan, Experiment, Guardrail, Scale, and Govern. The article positions AI uptake as a coordinated learning and governance process rather than a onetime deployment. The analysis draws from technology acceptance theory, diffusion of innovations, AI literacy, cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, change management, and current U.S. federal AI guidance. A government-sector scenario involving a state human services agency illustrates how the model can support case-processing assistance while preserving human review, privacy, accessibility, transparency, and public trust. The article concludes with implications for practice and a research agenda for empirically testing AI maturity across individual and organizational levels.

title: Addendum: Operational Maturity in the Global Digital Asset Landscape (June 2026)

detail.title: Addendum: Operational Maturity in the Global Digital Asset Landscape (June 2026)
detail.abstract: This addendum provides a critical update to the 2025 research “Regulated: Cryptos, ICOs, Stablecoins, and AML/CFT in Different Global Financial Centres,” bridging the gap between the regulatory baseline and the maturing enforcement landscape of June 2026. As major jurisdictions transition from policy theory to operational enforcement, this update examines the active impact of the Stablecoins Ordinance (Cap. 656) in Hong Kong, the formalization of the Financial Conduct Authority’s cryptoasset regime in the United Kingdom, and the federal alignment of New York’s regulatory framework under the GENIUS Act. The analysis identifies a global paradigm shift in compliance—moving from “policy design” to “demonstrable execution”—and emphasizes the increasing necessity for real-time reserve auditing, mandatory capital floors, and rigorous governance accountability for institutional market participants.

detail.abstract: The intersection of federal immigration policy and agricultural labor markets has reached a structural impasse. This paper examines the empirical mechanics of H-2A guestworker compensation following the Department of Labor's October 2025 interim final rule, analyzes the elasticity of domestic labor supply in commercial agricultural operations, and identifies the statutory exclusion of year-round livestock and dairy enterprises from the H-2A visa framework. Drawing on primary federal disclosures from the U.S. Department of Labor, USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Federal Register, and independent modeling by the Economic Policy Institute, we deconstruct the multi-layered tensions fracturing the agricultural landscape. Our findings indicate that recent regulatory adjustments will reduce national employer labor expenditures by approximately $1.6 billion annually, relative to an estimated $7.2 billion H-2A wage bill, while domestic labor supply remains structurally inelastic, with only 182 domestic applicants for 415,000 advertised positions in fiscal year 2025. The H-2A program's seasonal architecture creates a critical policy blind spot for livestock operations requiring continuous labor, accelerating capital restructuring toward automated systems. These findings have implications for agricultural policy, labor economics, and the political economy of technology adoption in food production systems.

detail.abstract: Rapid urbanization in Africa has intensified a mobility crisis, with traffic congestion contributing to economic losses, public safety challenges, and environmental degradation. Many adaptive traffic control systems are designed for regulated, lane-based environments and homogeneous traffic patterns, limiting their applicability in heterogeneous urban contexts. This paper examines the Sydney Coordinated Adaptive Traffic System (SCATS) as a reference model to assess its suitability for Sub-Saharan African contexts. While SCATS demonstrates reductions in travel time, stops, fuel consumption, and emissions through real-time signal optimization, its vehicle-centric design and reliance on fixed infrastructure risk worsening existing inequalities when directly deployed. Drawing on these insights, the paper proposes a mobility justice framework to inform an AI-driven traffic control standard for heterogeneous and resource-constrained urban environments. The framework outlines standardization-relevant design principles, including multi-source AI-based detection to replace inductive loops, priority-based algorithms for public and informal transport, and modular, solar-powered infrastructure. By reframing traffic control standardization from vehicle throughput to multimodal equity, this paper contributes a policy-oriented perspective on how adaptive traffic technologies can be responsibly deployed, ethically governed, and integrated into future international standards for sustainable and inclusive urban mobility.

detail.abstract: This article thoroughly analyses international experiences in the legal support of counterintelligence activities, focusing on the approaches of the UKUSA agreement member countries, European Union states and those in Asia. The main aspects of the legal regulation of special services are discussed, including their organisational structure, mechanisms of democratic control, human rights protection and integration into the international legal system. This article also addresses how counterintelligence agencies respond to modern challenges such as cyber threats and transnational crime. Specific recommendations are offered for adapting leading global practices to Ukrainian realities to enhance the effectiveness of counterintelligence activities, ensure national security and comply with international standards.

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence as Monism: Ontological, Organisational, and Methodological Implications
detail.abstract: This paper argues that Artificial Intelligence should be understood as a form of monism: a unified substance that cannot be decomposed into separate elements such as data, algorithms, or technical architectures. Drawing from philosophical traditions of monism, dualism, and holism, the paper contends that AI is not merely a collection of components but a single, indivisible essence reflecting the phenomena it replicates. Treating AI as monism has deep implications across multiple dimensions. Epistemologically, it positions AI as the central interpretive force across technological, organisational, and societal domains, while raising ethical and existential concerns regarding singularity, the homogenisation of innovation, and the concentration of decision-making power. At the organisational level, a monistic approach challenges traditional siloed structures, advocating instead for transversal, problem-centric teams whose mandate derives from the integrity of the problem rather than from departmental hierarchy. In project management, it implies a unified vision and an integrated evaluation of complexity in which no single stakeholder perspective dominates the assessment of outcomes. In data and information management, it calls for architectures that reflect the irreducible unity of the phenomena being modelled. Ultimately, this paper calls for a paradigm shift in how AI is conceptualised, governed, and integrated, suggesting that only by embracing AI as monism can organisations achieve genuine agility and avoid the structural inefficiencies inherent to reductionist approaches.
