detail.title: Traveling Salesman Tardiness
detail.abstract: How fragile is the routing time window of delivery systems against spatial distributional uncertainty? We study the tardiness risk of Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) solutions with respect to a service deadline (target) over the routing time. Using the robust satisficing model, we introduce the TSP tardiness index to quantify the target's fragility under distributional uncertainty in customer locations. Assuming there are m potential customer locations from historical samples on a service region D (of area |D|), we prove that the TSP tardiness index is Θ(n * sqrt(|D|m) / τ) for n realized locations with respect to the routing time target τ, under non-boundary conditions. This result establishes a new scaling law that extends beyond the existing deterministic and probabilistic TSP bounds. We further extend it to a multi-vehicle case and derive simple partition rules for managing delivery systems. Our numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world routing data validate the value of the TSP tardiness index in characterizing and managing the overtime risk of routing systems.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we model fixed-supply decentralized digital networks as a biological population on a finite set. Given that network growth must ultimately be bounded by the total number of addressable human beings and finite amounts of world capital, we hypothesize that digital asset adoption follows a bounded Logistic S-Curve (the Verhulst population growth curve), rather than unlimited exponential growth. We test this hypothesis using a daily multi-asset price series from Sep 2014 to May 2026. We utilize non-linear least squares optimization via the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm, measure model selection using the informationtheoretic Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and use Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) to test for stationarity. Bitcoin (AIC = 81,324.2), Ethereum (AIC = 41,141.5), and Solana (AIC = 18,086.9) all exhibit a clear preference for bounded logistic S-curve models. Their asymptotes approach stable thermodynamic limits ($190, 737 for Bitcoin, $2, 570 for Ethereum), which we confirm using Monte Carlo bootstrap tests. The S&P 500 index, which serves as our mathematical control, does not show a preference for the bounded model, suggesting it grows with unbound exponential compounding. Finally, independent 365-day rolling cumulative return analytics show that Bitcoin's compounding return steadily decays through time. This slope is significantly negative (-6.49e-4 per day, p = 2.61e-67), providing direct, stationary mathematical support for saturated Verhulst adoption dynamics.

detail.title: Intra-ASEAN Bilateral FDI and Demographic Gravity: A Sub-Regional Replication
detail.abstract: Does bilateral FDI within ASEAN follow the demographic gravity gradient-older source countries investing more in younger destinations-consistent with the income-conditional demographic gravity framework (Peters 2026a)? Using the IMF Coordinated Direct Investment Survey (CDIS) for all ten ASEAN economies, 2009-2024 (706 positive bilateral FDI pairs), I find that the unconditional demographic gravity effect is positive but statistically insignificant (dZ₁ = +0.40, p = 0.44). Conditioning on destination income activates the signal: dZ₁ = +2.55 (p < 0.05) with a negative income interaction (dZ₁ × log GDP/cap destination =-0.21, p < 0.05), implying that demographic divergence predicts more FDI toward lower-income ASEAN destinations but is near-zero toward high-income ones. The post-2020 external shock (US tariffs, China export surge) did not amplify the demographic gradient-if anything, it weakened it (dZ₁ × Post-2020 =-0.21, p < 0.05). Singapore dominates intra-ASEAN FDI at 75% of source volume; results persist qualitatively but lose significance when SGP is excluded. The findings partially replicate the income-conditional demographic gravity mechanism for FDI flows at the sub-regional level but qualify the extension: demographic gravity in FDI is income-conditional and was not reinforced by the 2020-2024 external shock.

detail.abstract: Recent empirical work by Wallace et al. (2026) demonstrated that growth mindsets predict interest in growth-oriented organizations primarily when held with high certainty (mindset strength), and that social validation amplifies certainty. The present paper develops an ecological extension of active environmental instruction rather than passive self-selection: fixed-mindset organizational contexts teach a competing epistemology through the cumulative micro-interactions of performance management, attribution norms, and recognition practices. Third, the values-asidentity mechanism proposed by Wallace et al. (2026) is more precisely characterized as deeplevel belief integration-the process by which a mindset becomes organized into the automatic, identity-constitutive schemas that govern interpretation of achievement-relevant experience-and this integration is distinguished from declarative certainty by its resistance to contextual challenge. Five testable hypotheses are derived, each with specific operationalizations and research designs. Implications are developed for the design of mindset interventions, organizational culture change, and the measurement of belief robustness across social contexts.

title: Truly Terrible Ten? Notes on Territorial Supply Constraints
affiliations: Pforzheim University of Applied Sciences and

detail.title: Truly Terrible Ten? Notes on Territorial Supply Constraints
detail.abstract: The European Commission's classification of Territorial Supply Constraints (TSC) as inherently harmful Single Market barriers ("Terrible Ten") relies on a rigid legal binary that overlooks complex vertical market dynamics. Recent economic literature demonstrates that a per se prohibition of TSC risks harming longterm consumer welfare by dismantling vertical restraints that may successfully resolve freerider problems, stimulate non-price competition, or secure product availability in thin markets. Moreover, existing empirical evidence is heavily constrained by data limitations and relies primarily on descriptive price-dispersion tracking, making it inherently incapable of isolating causal effects of 'true' TSC or net consumer welfare effects. Rather than prematurely closing perceived gaps in competition law with rigid ex-ante bans, European competition policy should adopt an effects-based framework (Rule of Reason) capable of differentiating between harmful market foreclosure and welfare-enhancing vertical coordination.

title: Demographic Gravity Within ASEAN: Does China's Export Surge Disproportionately Reach Older Destinations?

detail.title: Demographic Gravity Within ASEAN: Does China's Export Surge Disproportionately Reach Older Destinations?
detail.abstract: China's 2020-2024 export surge, a $1.2 trillion global surplus record achieved despite a 20% decline in US-directed exports, provides a natural experiment for testing whether demographic aging of destination countries predicts higher import absorption. Within ASEAN, where the demographic spectrum runs from Thailand (Z₁ = +0.20, median age ~40) to Laos (Z₁ =-2.29, median age ~24), the China export shock is held approximately constant while destination demographics vary sharply. Using UN Comtrade China export data by HS2 chapter (2010-2024) for all ten ASEAN economies, I find that demographic aging strongly predicts the level of China exports in the cross-section (β = +1.88, p < 0.001, panel with year and chapter fixed effects), consistent with the income-conditional demographic demand-absorption mechanism of Peters (2026a). However, the incremental 2020-2024 shock did not disproportionately accrue to older ASEAN destinations (Z₁×Post =-0.17, se = 0.33, p = 0.60). The surplus deflected primarily to younger, production-chain-integrated economies-Vietnam (+135%) and Cambodia (+261%)-reflecting supply-side assembly hub logic rather than demographic demand absorption. This distinguishes two distinct channels: (1) a demographic demand baseline that aging countries sustain at elevated import levels, and (2) a shock-incidence channel driven by production-chain positioning that is orthogonal to demographic position. The data limitation-four HS2 chapters (29, 84, 87, 88), omitting electronics (HS85)-constrains interpretation.

detail.abstract:
This study presents a quantitative analysis of an intraday mean reversion trading strategy applied to SOL/USDT perpetual futures on the Binance exchange. The strategy utilizes previous-day Volume Profile levels (Value Area High, Value Area Low, Point of Control) as context for trade entries, with current-day Point of Control as the profit target. Trade confirmation is provided by a novel "Tape Speed" indicator measuring volume-weighted price momentum. 
A comprehensive 5-year backtest (1,825 trading days, 525,600 five-minute candles) with realistic Binance Futures transaction costs (0.05% maker entry, 0.05% taker exit, 0.02% slippage per side) reveals that a 0.15% stop-loss configuration is mathematically unviable due to transaction costs consuming 93% of the risk allocation. Stop-loss levels of 1.0% to 2.0% demonstrate statistically significant profitability with Sharpe ratios exceeding 2.0 and profit factors above 2.5.

title: When Legitimacy Becomes a Liability: How Economic Securitization Shapes Global Firms' Socio-Political Strategy

detail.title: When Legitimacy Becomes a Liability: How Economic Securitization Shapes Global Firms' Socio-Political Strategy
detail.abstract: Why do governments increasingly invoke national security to criticize foreign multinational enterprises (MNEs)? Additionally, how do affected MNEs respond? I argue that economic securitization (ES)-the framing of foreign investment as a national security threat-is a salient and extreme political risk that follows a distinct life cycle. It is activated when host country legislators face competitive elections in constituencies exposed to foreign economic competition. Under emergent ES risk exposure, firms substitute away from elite-targeted lobbying toward society engagement to establish broader legitimacy. Once ES risk consolidates, however, high-profile social engagement becomes a liability, as local embeddedness now reads as suspicious foreign influence, so MNEs scale back both political and social channels. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design with an original dataset of 5,484 U.S. legislator-session observations (2005-2024) and 634 foreign MNEs operating in the United States (2013-2024), I find empirical support for these propositions. Twenty-one interviews with senior corporate and policy professionals further reveal how MNEs choose among different strategies in response to different risk levels. Overall, this paper theorizes economic securitization as a novel political risk, showing that the trade-off between corporate political and social strategy follows a stage-dependent life cycle. It offers managerial guidance for global firms operating in increasingly politicized contexts.

detail.abstract:
Inventory buildup is widely read as a warning of weaker profitability to come, yet the evidence is overwhelmingly American and one influential account holds that the signal lives in particular sectors. This thesis tests both claims on new ground, using an international panel of 279 inventory-intensive firms across the United States and thirteen European countries over fiscal years 2014-2026 (3,055 firm-years). It builds a peer-adjusted abnormal-inventory measure (AbnInvPeer) from already-filed statements and tests its predictive content through fixedeffects panel regressions with firm-clustered errors, placebo falsification, and a multiple-testing standard applied to its own results. 
Four hypotheses resolve into three economic channels, because the distress test is a binary recoding of the margin test, not independent evidence. H1 (margin): one standard deviation of the signal predicts a 0.24-percentage-point fall in next-year gross margin (β =-0.0152, p = 0.0135), robust in direction across seventeen specifications, yet marginal under multiple-testing correction, significant in no sub-period alone, and carried by the European, not the American, firms. H2 (cash): the same buildup coincides with same-year operating cash flow weaker by 1.87 margin points per standard deviation, the strongest association in the panel, but concurrent and partly mechanical, and so the weakest early warning. H3 (returns): high-buildup firms underperform peers by 4.7% annually equal-weighted (t =-3.03), a spread that vanishes valueweighted and rests on only eleven annual sorts, an association, not an anomaly. H4 (distress): high-stress firm-years face margin distress at 17.1% versus 12.6% (χ² = 8.04, p = 0.005). 
The sharpest result is a rejection. The sector-concentration claim of an exploratory phase of this study (semiconductors driving the signal at β =-0.179, estimated on six firms) collapses by a factor of nine on fifteen firms and survives none of thirteen specifications, turning the wrong sign in its home market; Fisher's (1997) taxonomy motivates the test and does not survive it. Documenting this self-correction is treated as a contribution.

detail.abstract: Why do organisations systematically reproduce the blind spots they most urgently need to overcome? This article proposes that the answer lies not in information deficits or motivational failures but in the semantic architecture of the communicative fields through which organisations constitute their collective perception. Drawing on Learnable Theory (Magni, Marchetti & Alharbi, 2023, 2024, 2025), the article develops a theoretical integration between the epistemological distinction between declarative and enacted knowing and the linguisticcognitive constructs of the Umbra Cone (Cono d'Ombra) and the Inverse Difference (Differenza Inversa). The article situates these constructs within the theoretical traditions of organisational learning - specifically the literatures on sensemaking, double-loop learning, and the espoused/enacted gap - before arguing that Learnable Theory advances those traditions by providing a precise linguistic mechanism for the production and maintenance of the gap between what organisations say they do and what they actually do. The Umbra Cone is the structural zone of non-pertinence constitutively produced by a dominant frame; the Inverse Difference is the formal mechanism that generates it. Together they explain not merely that enacted knowing exists and resists revision - what the prior literature has established - but why it has the specific architecture it does: why certain domains are constitutively unavailable to deliberate revision while others remain accessible. The article makes the epistemological argument for why standard diagnostic tools, including 360-degree feedback instruments, are structurally incapable of accessing enacted knowing, and directly addresses the counterargument that subordinate observers can and do see leadership contradictions that leaders cannot: the observer is not blind, but the instrument's linguistic architecture forecloses their capacity to express what they perceive. A single theoretical illustration applies all five steps of the Inverse Difference procedure to an archetypal pattern of corporate communication, demonstrating the analytical sequence from frame identification to regeneration. Five theoretical propositions close the article. The central theoretical contribution is a structural account of the mechanism by which organisations learn not to see, and a theoretically grounded procedure for identifying the architecture of that unseeing in the language organisations use to describe themselves.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) refers to systems capable of semi-autonomous planning to achieve pre-defined goals. It is reshaping innovation processes across industries; yet socially impactful industries such as construction, healthcare, and education remain resistant to technological changes. Grounded in disruptive innovation theory (DIT), this study explores how agentic AI challenges and reshapes innovation dynamics in the construction industry: a sector characterised by slow technological adoption, complex institutional constraints, and fragmented project structures. A qualitative approach is employed to conduct semi-structured interviews with 34 construction professionals across seven regions. Together with five categories of archival data, our findings reveal three dimensions: (1) triggers of innovation, comprising institutional pressure, project delivery crises and data fragmentation; (2) resistance to disruption, comprising institutional professional legitimacy and project liability; and (3) institution-enabled innovation, comprising agent governance, risk allocation and knowledge embeddedness. The results show that the construction industry occupies a contested space between sustaining and disruptive innovation trajectories. Heavily regulated, socially impactful, and liability-intensive industries are both reliant and constrained by institutional mediators to shape their pace of technological disruption. This study introduces the concept of institution-enabled innovation as the third pathway beyond existing DIT emphasis on either market competition or technological performance. It contributes by empirically extending DIT application in a sector-specific analysis, while highlighting its societal implications as shaped by institutions. Practical recommendations are offered for construction practitioners and policymakers seeking to navigate advanced AI adoption in highly institutionalised settings.

title: Demographics and Chinese Sovereign Debt: Testing the Macro Channel

detail.title: Demographics and Chinese Sovereign Debt: Testing the Macro Channel
detail.abstract: Benguria, Rojas & Saffie (2026) formalize how yuan revenue exposure and low restructuring costs make dollar-to-yuan debt conversion optimal for developing sovereigns, with demographic aging endogenizing restructuring costs through fiscal deterioration. This note tests whether the demographic-Chinese debt interaction implied by the BRS mechanism is detectable in aggregate current account outcomes across 102 developing and emerging-market economies. It is not: the Z₁ × Chinese public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) debt interaction is statistically zero (β = 0.099, SE = 0.625, p = 0.87) and economically negligible across all specifications. The income-conditional demographic baseline is fully intact (Z₁ = 6.987, SE = 3.282, p < 0.05; Z₁ × log GDP/cap =-0.728, SE = 0.371, p < 0.05; N = 102). The null finding is informative: the BRS mechanism operates through a microeconomic sovereign restructuring channel rather than a macroeconomic savings-investment channel. The aggregate current account is not the right diagnostic for the BRS mechanism.

detail.title: Does iXBRL Reporting of Pay-versus-Performance Affect Say-on-Pay Voting?
detail.abstract: This study examines the economic consequences of the SEC’s mandated inline XBRL (iXBRL) pay-versus-performance (PvP) disclosures. We investigate whether this structured reporting framework alters the information environment surrounding Company-Selected Measures (CSMs) and Compensation Actually Paid (CAP), thereby influencing shareholder voting on executive compensation. We document three primary findings. First, concerning the faithful representation in CSM choices, firms with greater reliance on non-GAAP metrics in executive contracts are significantly more likely to designate a non-GAAP metric as their CSM. Second, regarding compensation relevance, changes in the designated CSM exhibit an incremental and positive association with changes in CAP, after controlling for total shareholder return. Third, as evidence of the shareholder use of PvP disclosure, we find that post-iXBRL mandate shareholder dissent ratios become significantly more sensitive to excess executive compensation. Furthermore, we find that the increased say-on-pay vote sensitivity to excess pay is driven by the iXBRL format of information rather than new information per se. Collectively, our findings provide early evidence on corporate reporting choices under the iXBRL-based PvP disclosure rule and demonstrate that machine-readable data mandates mitigate information processing costs, thereby enhancing the efficacy of shareholder say-on-pay governance.

title: Robust Dynamic Programming for Inventory Control: Joint Supply and Demand Uncertainty
affiliations: , Durham Business School and

detail.title: Robust Dynamic Programming for Inventory Control: Joint Supply and Demand Uncertainty
detail.abstract: We study a multiperiod robust inventory problem with joint demand and supply uncertainty, in which the quantity received is an uncertain fraction of the quantity ordered, and an adversary selects demand and yield after the order is placed. Existing robust inventory methods gain tractability either from static reformulations, which discard the sequential order--adversary interaction and so protect against shocks that cannot co-occur, or from affine decision rules, which lose exactness once yield enters multiplicatively. We instead solve the exact sequential min--max dynamic program. The difficulty is that, unlike additive demand, the order quantity itself determines the decision maker's exposure to the worst-case yield, a decision-dependent uncertainty in which a larger order widens the range of adverse outcomes, so which realization is adverse depends jointly on the order and the inventory state. Preserving this decision-first timing lets us characterize the optimal policy exactly: the optimal order combines multiple linear inflation rules (order-up-to targets scaled by a factor that compensates for yield loss), selected according to the inventory state, and collapses to a single base-stock rule only when yield is deterministic. This characterization yields closed-form short-horizon policies, a fixed-point terminal valuation under which a myopic inflation rule remains optimal over a certified state region at every horizon, and worst-case representation bounds showing that the number of affine pieces can be exponential under yield uncertainty but grows only linearly when yield is deterministic. Exploiting the same geometry, we develop a decomposition algorithm in the spirit of robust dual dynamic programming whose stage subproblems are solved by exact algebraic oracles rather than linear programs. In experiments, the exact robust DP policy achieves lower cost than static and affine-rule robust benchmarks, with the largest gains when demand or supply is extreme.

title: AI–Human Capital Complementarity in Workplace Decision-Making
affiliations: University of Manchester and Faculty of Economics, Chulalongkorn University

detail.title: AI–Human Capital Complementarity in Workplace Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is diffusing rapidly into workplaces, but its benefits are unevenly distributed across workers. Many workers report performance gains from AI use, but a smaller share report that AI assists them with decision-making. The worker- and job-level characteristics that distinguish these two patterns of AI integration remain poorly understood. This paper investigates which worker characteristics are associated with AI-enhanced performance versus AI-assisted decision-making, applying an AI–human capital complementarity framework. It additionally distinguishes the speed and quality dimensions of AI-assisted decision-making, examining whether complementarity patterns differ between the two. Probit models with marginal effects are estimated for 2,134 AI-using workers in the manufacturing and financial services sectors across seven OECD countries (OECD, 2023). Four outcomes are examined: improved performance, AI-assisted decision-making, faster decisions, and better decisions. Logistic regressions are reported as a robustness check. Motivational predictors (AI enthusiasm and being born after 1980) are positively associated with AI-enhanced performance, but human-capital and authority-based predictors (higher education and supervisor or managerial status) become statistically significant only for the decision-making outcomes, consistent with AI–human capital complementarity. Formal AI training predicts both outcomes but more strongly decision-making. The generational effect on performance disappears for decision-making. A gender difference emerges only for decision quality, not decision speed. AI’s benefits in worker decision-making are conditional on human capital and organisational authority. Motivation drives broad performance gains, but decision-level AI integration requires structured human-capital inputs. These findings imply that policies seeking inclusive AI-driven decision-making should prioritise training and educational investment alongside motivational engagement.

detail.abstract:
Amendments to the Fair Work Act now allow workers in Australia a right to disconnect. The implementation of this right precipitated a polarised public debate that was not consistently evidence-based, encompassing the oftencontradictory perspectives of unions, employers, business lobbies and politicians. This study offers a more nuanced and evidence-based understanding of the right to disconnect, its benefits and challenges and the possible impact on Australian employment practices and relations. It provides an international comparative analysis; it explores the literature on
related topics such as work–life balance, occupational stress, management
practices and productivity; and it proposes a model of the consequences of
technology-enabled flexible work. The comparative analysis and literature
review are supplemented with themes identified in Australian media
coverage through a Leximancer analysis. The findings discuss the
advantages and limitations of diverse top-down legislative or self-
regulatory pathways experienced overseas by early adopters. While the
right to disconnect can improve work–life balance, health and well-being
and productivity, its implementation requires careful consideration of
industry-specific contexts, clear policies and cultural shifts in workplaces to
mitigate the risks associated with hyperconnectivity. These insights are
useful for Australia as it enters the implementation phase of the right to dis‐
connect.

title: Performative Day-to-Day Traffic Management via Differentiable Surrogates
affiliations: Rice University and Rice University

detail.title: Performative Day-to-Day Traffic Management via Differentiable Surrogates
detail.abstract: As the traffic authority monitors and manages the transportation network to mitigate today's congestion, the decisions also reshape tomorrow's demand with travelers adapting their route and departure-time preferences from one operating day to the next. This makes day-today traffic management stateful and performative: the deployed policy changes the distribution of network conditions it is later judged on, and the gradient linking a policy change to the future state it creates appears in no logged trajectory because logs record the network only under policies already deployed. We show that repeated risk minimization therefore stalls at a performatively stable, not optimal, point, while optimizing a fitted surrogate without restraint is exploited wherever that surrogate is wrong. We propose a framework that decouples system identification from policy improvement: it calibrates a differentiable closed-loop surrogate from observed data and improves the policy against it only under a local-fidelity certificate and a rollout trust region. Exploiting the dissipative structure of day-today route adjustment, we bound the realized suboptimality of a surrogate-trained policy over a finite horizon, including under a stale or imperfectly calibrated surrogate, and express it as a single per-round error budget that is auditable against the levers the authority operates. On a Braess mechanism probe and on the Sioux Falls network across pricing, metering, and assignment channels, our proposed framework closes 0.70 of the oracle gap, compared with 0.50 for repeated risk minimization and 0.37 for direct surrogate optimization, and sustains a 57-60% improvement over the uncontrolled network under model mismatch, where surrogate optimization collapses to under 8% and a frozen policy degrades. The result is a deployable controller that converts a structural network change into a brief, bounded transient rather than a lasting loss of performance.

title: Forecasting Venezuela's Post-Maduro Recovery: Security, Trade Reliability, and Strategic Redevelopment to 2040
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Forecasting Venezuela's Post-Maduro Recovery: Security, Trade Reliability, and Strategic Redevelopment to 2040

keywords: And Foreign Influence. Using Qualitative Strategic Forecasting
The Study Develops Five Plausible Futures: Strategic Recovery

detail.abstract:
This study forecasts Venezuela’s post-Maduro redevelopment from 2026 to 2040 and evaluates whether the country can reemerge as a reliable trading partner. Rather than treating Venezuela’s reopening as a conventional economic transition, the paper frames it as a security-conditioned redevelopment process shaped by political legitimacy, corruption control, state capacity, organized crime, narcotics trafficking, illicit finance, illegal mining, infrastructure reliability, resource governance, and foreign influence.

Using qualitative strategic forecasting, scenario analysis, national security assessment, and geopolitical risk analysis, the study develops five plausible futures: Strategic Recovery, Managed Instability, Criminalized Resource Economy, Foreign-Influenced Proxy State, and Failed Redevelopment. The central finding is that Venezuela has the material foundation for recovery but not yet the institutional foundation for full trade reliability. Oil, natural gas, gold, bauxite, iron ore, hydroelectric power, agriculture, freshwater, fisheries, and Caribbean access create major commercial potential. However, resource abundance alone will not determine Venezuela’s trajectory. Reliability will depend on whether the post-Maduro state can enforce contracts, secure infrastructure, regulate ports and customs, control corruption, dismantle or contain criminal networks, formalize mining, restore financial credibility, and maintain strategic autonomy among competing foreign powers.

The most likely near-term scenario is Managed Instability, in which oil, gas, mining, electricity, and infrastructure activity expand while corruption, weak courts, narcotics networks, illegal mining, security threats, debt disputes, and geopolitical competition continue to constrain full reliability. Strategic Recovery remains possible if market reopening becomes an institution-building process. Conversely, Venezuela may become more commercially active yet remain strategically unreliable if illicit networks, corrupt officials, or foreign-aligned actors capture the benefits of reopening. The study contributes an integrated forecasting framework for assessing trade reliability in resource-rich transitional states and argues that Venezuela’s future will be determined less by what it owns than by what it can govern.

title: On the Structural Limits of Ranking Under Non-Separable Valuation.

detail.title: On the Structural Limits of Ranking Under Non-Separable Valuation.

detail.abstract: Many selection systems operate under capacity constraints: search engines return finite result sets, platforms recommend limited inventories, and hiring systems filter candidate pools. We formalize a class of selection problems where valuations are non-separable-where the value of an item depends on which other items are selected. Under such complementarities, selection cannot be reduced to ranking without allocative loss. We formulate network-dependent allocation, prove that no single ranking function can simultaneously guarantee optimal allocation for both separable and non-separable valuations, establish a separability sufficiency theorem, and characterize the computational complexity by mapping to the cardinalityconstrained quadratic knapsack problem. We distinguish retrieval from allocation as formally distinct problem classes and show that ranking necessarily compresses the valuation space from 2 n-1 to n dimensions, discarding interaction information. We also show that, when inferential costs are non-trivial, inferential infrastructure can affect inclusion probabilities. Contribution: A characterization of ranking sufficiency: ranking guarantees optimal allocation if and only if valuations are separable.

title: Financial Sustainability and Earnings Integrity: Do Ethical Screens Mitigate Accrual Anomalies?

detail.title: Financial Sustainability and Earnings Integrity: Do Ethical Screens Mitigate Accrual Anomalies?

detail.abstract: This study investigates whether the ethical screening inherent in US Shariah-compliant equities functions as a governance mechanism to mitigate earnings management by examining the persistence of accrual-based anomalies. Using data from 1993 to 2023, we analyze 175 size-accrual portfolios against the CAPM and Fama-French factor models, employing GRS tests and regime-switching frameworks to assess risk-adjusted performance and structural stability. The results reveal a widespread absence of significant alphas, indicating that these screened equities are effectively insulated from manipulative earnings practices. Notably, we document a structural "decoupling" from the broader market, where returns are driven primarily by Size, Value, and Momentum, rendering standard profitability and investment premiums redundant. By empirically positioning Shariah screening as an ex-ante governance filter where debt constraints substitute for external monitoring, this research challenges the universality of the accrual anomaly. For investors, these findings highlight Shariahcompliant funds as a defensive, high-integrity asset class highly suitable for ESG portfolios, best benchmarked using a parsimonious Size-Value-Momentum framework. Ultimately, these ethical investment frameworks foster financial stewardship and a transparent corporate sector, though future research is needed to verify if this structural decoupling persists in emerging Islamic markets and alternative regulatory regimes.

detail.abstract: I introduce a zero-shot large language model classification of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Form NT 10-K and Form NT 10-Q late-filing body narratives and show that the resulting "accounting-issue" class is a strong forward indicator of subsequent same-filer restatement-class disclosure. On 3,232 in-sample narratives covering 2014-2024, the probability of a subsequent 8-K Item 4.02, 10-K/A, or 10-Q/A within ninety trading days is 32.6% for the accounting-issue class against 23.5% for the residual class (two-proportion 𝑧 = 5.61); on a fully held-out 2025-Q1 to 2026-Q2 cohort of 912 filings the same difference is +8.4 percentage points (𝑧 = 2.83). Eighteen of twenty-four cell specifications survive a family-wise correction, including a strong Form NT 10-Q cohort effect (𝑧 = 6.77) and a null Form NT 10-K cohort effect (𝑧 = 0.50) that, to my knowledge, has not been documented before. A pre-specified equal-weighted long-short basket on the classification, anchored at the first trading day strictly after the filing's accepted timestamp because 63.5% of in-sample filings clear the SEC's intake queue after the 16∶00 Eastern Time market close, is back-tested under an explicit per-capital simulation: each month a new long-short basket position is opened at 1/4 of available cash (matching the average four overlapping ninety-day positions), held for ninety trading days, then closed. The fair quantitative benchmark for a long-short strategy of this kind is the Fama-French five-factor plus momentum maximum-Sharpe tangent portfolio at its natural unleveraged scale (sum of absolute weights equal to one), whose annualized volatility is 4.7%. Rescaled to the same 4.7% risk budget, the strategy grows from one dollar in 2014 to $1.33 by end-2024 with an annualized Sharpe ratio of 1.30, against the tangent's $1.55 at an annualized Sharpe of 1.96; the tangent is in-sample optimal and therefore upward-biased by mean-variance optimism. The strategy's monthly per-capital long-short return is regressed on the same six factors, with Newey-West heteroskedasticity-and-autocorrelation-consistent standard errors; the residual annualized alpha is +30.1 percentage points (𝑡 = 2.81, Newey-West HAC), the in-sample 𝑅 2 is 17.5%, and the small-cap-minus-large-cap factor loading is significant (𝛽 SMB = +0.97, 𝑡 = 3.60). The cumulative residual alpha trail-the part of the strategy's per-capital return that is orthogonal to the six common factors, rescaled to the same tangent risk budget-grows to $1.39 at an annualized Sharpe of 1.55, indicating that the factor-adjusted contribution accounts for the bulk of the strategy's risk-adjusted return. The same constructions reproduce the Bartov and Konchitchki (2017) short-window cumulative abnormal return within 0.15 percentage points for Form NT 10-K and 0.05 percentage points for Form NT 10-Q once the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) daily file including delisting returns is used in place of a free-tier equity feed; the free-tier feed by contrast under-recovers the magnitude and reverses the sixty-day post-filing drift sign, which I document as a quantified delisting-return artifact whose implied magnitude is consistent with the empirical literature on delisting returns. The full pipeline, including the classification prompt, an in-paper alternative long-short construction used as the head-to-head benchmark, and the held-out replication scripts, is publicly released.

title: Regime Dynamics in the Indian Yield Curve: A Markov-Regime Switching Analysis of Monetary Policy Cycles

detail.title: Regime Dynamics in the Indian Yield Curve: A Markov-Regime Switching Analysis of Monetary Policy Cycles
detail.abstract: This paper examines regime dynamics in the Indian government bond yield curve using Markov Regime Switching on the term spread, defined as the 10-year G-Sec yield minus the 91day T-bill yield , over the sample period January 2012 to April 2026. Unlike advanced economies where yield curve inversion reliably precedes recession, India's administered short end through the RBI liquidity corridor and structurally suppressed long end through statutory liquidity ratio requirements necessitate a distinct analytical framework. A three-regime model with switching mean and variance is selected based on Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, identifying a tightening regime characterised by compressed spread and low volatility, a neutral easing regime of moderate spread and low volatility, and a crisis regime of wide spread and extreme volatility. Critically, the model independently identified the 2013 taper tantrum, 2020 COVID emergency period, and 2022 Russia-Ukraine shock as distinct crisis episodes purely from term spread volatility dynamics, without any crisis dates provided as inputs. Regime classifications are validated against documented RBI policy decisions, CPI inflation, India VIX, and foreign portfolio investor debt flows. The findings demonstrate that despite institutional distortions, the Indian term spread contains genuine latent regime information about monetary policy cycles that linear models cannot capture, providing a forward-looking complement to the backward-looking transmission analysis of the companion papers in this series.

title: Recursive General Equilibrium and the Endogenous Origins of Business Cycles

detail.title: Recursive General Equilibrium and the Endogenous Origins of Business Cycles
detail.abstract: Classical general equilibrium theory specifies the conditions under which equilibrium may exist, but offers limited insight into the dynamics of its attainment. This paper addresses that gap by developing a recursive dynamic formulation of the Symmetric Model of General Economic Equilibrium, interpreted here as the Autopoietic Model of Economic Reproduction (AMER). The economy is represented as an operationally closed system in which products and resources recursively reproduce one another through decentralized exchange and feedback. The analysis shows that, once realistic time lags in price transmission between interdependent product and resource markets are introduced, the adjustment process does not converge to equilibrium but generates persistent endogenous oscillations. Explicit analytical conditions for the emergence of such dynamics are derived and linked to behavioral parameters, including the speed of price adjustment, demand inertia, and cyclical changes in the propensity to save and the propensity to expand production. These propensities are themselves influenced by optimistic and pessimistic expectations generated by the cycle. The paper further shows that this mechanism is robust across extensions with money, foreign trade, and multi-level production, thereby shifting the focus of general equilibrium analysis from equilibrium states to the recursive dynamics of decentralized coordination.

title: "Is Anything Okay?": The Biblical Roots of Jewish Complaint Humor
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business and City University of New York (CUNY) - Paul H. Chook Department of Information Systems & Statistics

detail.title: "Is Anything Okay?": The Biblical Roots of Jewish Complaint Humor
detail.abstract: The Yiddish word "kvetch," meaning to complain with relentless creativity, describes one of the most durable features of Jewish humor. This paper argues that the comedic tradition of kvetching is not a modern cultural accident but has deep biblical and Talmudic roots. The Israelites of the Exodus complained about water, food, leadership, and the wilderness itself, even as every grievance was met with miraculous provision, and the Talmud records Moses rebuking them as "ingrates, children of ingrates." Adam's first recorded words after the fall were themselves a complaint. Drawing on this textual foundation, the paper distinguishes complaining from blaming, positions the kvetch as blame with plausible deniability, and presents a thematic taxonomy of Jewish complaint humor: complaints against God and fate, Jewish mothers and wives, synagogue life, health and hypochondria, food and restaurants, schnorrers and money, and life under antisemitism and oppressive regimes. Across these categories, the kvetch emerges not as an expression of despair but as a mode of engagement, a form of intimacy with God, community, and history. The paper concludes that Jewish complaint humor functions as a survival mechanism that transforms grievance into connection.

title: Beyond Formality: The Firm-Size Wage Premium in Colombia
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Javeriana and Pontificia Universidad Javeriana

detail.title: Beyond Formality: The Firm-Size Wage Premium in Colombia
detail.abstract: Firm-size wage premia are well documented in advanced economies, but their magnitude and interpretation in middle-income labor markets with large informal sectors remain less settled. This paper documents the firm-size wage premium in Colombia using harmonized microdata from the Gran Encuesta Integrada de Hogares (GEIH) covering 2008 to 2025, excluding 2020. Employment is concentrated in solo work and micro-firms, while real hourly wages rise sharply with firm size. After controlling for gender, age, age squared, education, formality, and sector-year fixed effects, workers in firms with 101 or more employees earn about 43 percent more than otherwise comparable solo workers. The premium is positive throughout the sample period, with no evidence of secular decline. Because the premium survives formality controls, it is not simply a relabeling of the formal-informal wage gap. More specifically, there is a steep size gradient within informal employment, and a narrower large-firm advantage within formal employment relative to intermediate-size firms. Combined with the thin middle of the Colombian firm-size distribution, the premium is consistent with labor-market frictions that may constrain the growth of small businesses and limit worker reallocation toward larger, potentially more productive firms.

title: The Risk Threshold Position Size as Neural-State Management: Why Accumulated Drawdown, Not Per-Trade Risk, Triggers Execution Failure
affiliations: Independent Research

detail.title: The Risk Threshold Position Size as Neural-State Management: Why Accumulated Drawdown, Not Per-Trade Risk, Triggers Execution Failure
detail.abstract: A persistent and poorly explained phenomenon among retail traders is the catastrophic single-session loss the destruction, in one day, of capital that was built gradually over many sessions of competent operation. The standard account attributes it to a failure of discipline or character (overcondence, lack of emotional control). We argue instead that it is a predictable consequence of a measurable, individual neural threshold, crossed not by any single loss but by accumulated drawdown within a sequence of losses that the trading strategy itself treats as normal. We ground the mechanism in established neuroscience: nancial loss is processed by the amygdala, which mediates loss aversion (De Martino et al., 2010); the perception-degrading, decision-compromising eect of monetary loss operates through amygdala and prefrontal networks (Laufer et al., 2012); and acute stress chemically impairs the prefrontal cortex, the seat of deliberative control (Arnsten, 2009). On this basis we advance four contributions. First, that each operator possesses an individual risk threshold : a level of accumulated drawdown above which execution transitions from deliberative (prefrontal) to reactive (amygdala-driven), after which knowledge of method is inaccessible. Second, that risk is non-linear in this respect: under an asymmetric strategy, a sequence of small, individually-acceptable losses (e.g. seven stops at 3%) sums to an accumulated drawdown (21%) that crosses the threshold even though no single loss appears dangerous. Third, that correct position sizing is therefore not a function of per-trade risk or of account survival, but of keeping the worst statistically-normal accumulated drawdown below the individual threshold making sizing a tool of neural-state management. Fourth, we report a validated intervention (gradual scaling, small-lot testing, and pyramiding only on realized prot with stops in prot) and its outcome in a single documented case. We frame the operator's viability as a product of two binary factors knowledge of method and knowledge of one's own threshold where ignorance of either yields zero, and we report an observed prevalence of the destructive pattern in roughly 80% of a 1,000-student population.

detail.abstract: This paper extends the Hicks–Sraffa Supermultiplier (HSSM) by endogenizing the wage elasticity of labor demand as ε_L(h) = ε₀ + φh, where φ > 0 is an automation sensitivity parameter. The modified two-dimensional system yields four results. First, a unique non-trivial steady state exists in which capacity utilization converges to its normal level and the investment share is strictly lower than in the exogenous model. Second, the Jacobian determinant is always positive, ruling out saddle-point instability. Third, the endogenous elasticity strengthens stability quantitatively through the trace channel and dampens Harrodian instability, while leaving the qualitative condition γv < α unchanged. Fourth, at the boundary γv = α the steady state loses stability through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation: the first Lyapunov coefficient is positive, so no stable endogenous cycle emerges and the economy diverges in Harrodian fashion beyond the threshold. A novel algebraic result shows that the bifurcation threshold and the natural frequency at the bifurcation are jointly invariant in the automation parameters (ε₀, φ), so technology policy alone cannot eliminate instability risk. Numerical simulations calibrated to OECD averages confirm all four results. The paper situates its findings within the Sraffian Supermultiplier tradition, the Bhaduri–Marglin debate, and the mainstream task-based automation literature.

title: Debt Servicing, Not Debt Stock, Curbs Inflation in Ghana: A Dual-Model ARDL Test of Fiscal Theory

detail.abstract: This study examines how the composition of public debt and its servicing obligations affect price stability in Ghana between 1980 and 2020. Using a dual‑model approach, the empirical work separates the cash‑flow impact of public debt servicing (PDS) from the maturity‑risk effect of short‑term public debt (SPD). The econometric strategy applies Dickey‑Fuller Generalised Least Squares (DF‑GLS) and Phillips‑Perron unit‑root tests, together with an Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds‑testing procedure to handle variables with mixed integration orders. The bounds test confirms a stable, long‑run cointegrating relationship in both the PDS and SPD specifications. Empirically, the results show that PDS has a statistically significant negative effect on domestic inflation in both the short run (coefficient = −0.81, p < 0.10) and the long run (coefficient = −0.93, p < 0.05). In contrast, SPD is statistically insignificant over both horizons. These findings challenge the usual expectations of the fiscal theory of the price level, suggesting instead that high debt‑servicing costs reduce aggregate demand by crowding out productive public spending. Among the control variables, exchange‑rate depreciation is the main positive driver of price levels, while economic growth acts as a strong dampener. The error‑correction terms (−0.87 and −0.90) indicate a rapid adjustment toward the long‑run equilibrium. The results imply that debt restructuring should be paired with careful demand management, and that stabilising the local currency should take priority over altering debt‑maturity profiles to preserve overall economic stability.

detail.abstract: Paper 8 of the Demand-Side Paradox series. Presents the first practical mechanism of the demand-side architecture: AI-enabled microentrepreneurship. Building a business no longer demands the capital, time, or expertise it did three years ago; the model inference cost behind these tools fell roughly 280-fold between 2022 and 2024, a 95 to 98 percent reduction versus hiring. The result is a solopreneurship boom with no modern precedent, 5.5 million US business applications in 2023 and some 29.8 million solopreneurs generating about $1.7 trillion, roughly 6.8 percent of output. This is a genuine earning path inside the AI economy, but a skewed one: the median solopreneur earns near $50,000 and most stay small. The mechanism is real and necessary, and it is honest about what it cannot do alone.

detail.abstract: Paper 10 of the Demand-Side Paradox series. The capstone. After nine papers of diagnosis, it assembles the answer, which is not a single policy but a system across layers. Ownership routes productivity gains to labor by design through ESOPs, cooperatives, and sovereign wealth funds. The work layer redistributes hours through the four-day week. Tax and incentives, including a robot tax tested by South Korea's natural experiment, realign who captures the gains. Education and corporate responsibility carry the rest. Korinek and Stiglitz show formally why this must be built deliberately: in economies with incomplete markets, the individual decision to automate carries a macroeconomic externality no firm internalizes, so the market overproduces labor-saving innovation and will not self-correct toward a stable demand base. Every structural transition that worked was built. None was found.

title: India’s Pension Design needs BhARaT: Behavioral Assessment of Retirement Risk Tolerance – and Why Age-Based Defaults Fall Short
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, Risktyle,  and

detail.title: India’s Pension Design needs BhARaT: Behavioral Assessment of Retirement Risk Tolerance – and Why Age-Based Defaults Fall Short
detail.abstract: As India-along with many other countries-reforms its pension arrangements by shifting towards Defined Contribution systems, the risk of retirement security falls increasingly on individual citizens. Where financially unsophisticated citizens bear this burden, regulators have a responsibility to ensure that products and advice are commensurate with individual risk preferences, rather than defaulting to naïve, one-size-fits-all products like Life Cycle Funds or Target Date Funds. These approaches-the dominant default pension investment mechanism in the USA (as "safe harbor" under the Pension Protection Act of 2006), mandated across all MPF schemes in Hong Kong since 2017, and now law in Ireland as of January 2026-rest on the assumption that age is the primary driver of risk preferences, and that individuals should mechanically rotate into "safer" assets as they grow older. The PFRDA has recognized this, recommending innovative pension product options in a recent consultation paper-but "investor suitability" and guidance remain a formidable challenge for a country as vast and diverse as India, with nearly 1.5 billion citizens. This paper argues that the age assumption is not only theoretically weak but empirically unsupported-and that default choice architecture built on it risks systematically mis-serving the very citizens it is designed to protect. We apply Kahneman-Tverksy's 1979 seminal paper (KT), and its updated Muralidhar-Berlick Risktyle extension (MB) to 172 Indian respondents, quantifying individual risk preferences decomposable by gains and losses-across Age, Gender, Education, Occupation, Religion, Geography, and Primary Asset Held. Indians are noticeably risk-seeking and geography and religion appear to matter for risk preferences

title: Identifying Preference Heterogeneity with the Staircase Method
affiliations: and University of Warwick - Warwick Business School

detail.title: Identifying Preference Heterogeneity with the Staircase Method
detail.abstract: In preference elicitation, variation in individuals' responses may reflect not only heterogeneity in underlying preferences but also decision noise. We investigate how to disentangle these factors using the staircase method, a widely used elicitation procedure based on dynamically adjusted binary choices. We show that the method contains a previously overlooked design feature: individuals giving different responses are assigned to different subsequent choice sets, thereby generating comparable groups. Exploiting this feature, we develop a simple nonparametric test that identifies the degree to which observed variation reflects preference heterogeneity rather than decision noise. This test requires no extra measures and only a few rounds of choices. We validate it through theoretical and numerical analyses and derive implications for survey design. Applying the test to two publicly available datasets on risky and intertemporal choice, we find that its conclusions are consistent with those obtained from estimating structural models. More broadly, our approach provides a practical tool for model selection and for assessing the impact of measurement error when additional data are limited.

detail.title: Strategic Approaches to Asset Management and Crisis Resilience in Industrial Organizations During Economic Crises
detail.abstract: This paper examines which firm policies help industrial organizations maintain liquidity and protect economic value when adverse macro shocks hit. Framed within standard economic mechanisms-aggregate-demand contractions, cost-push shocks, and financial frictions-the analysis links asset-management choices to three transmission channels: (i) cash-flow timing constraints in production (working-capital and cash-in-advance frictions), (ii) price and wage rigidity affecting markups and employment, and (iii) credit market tightness that amplifies downturns (financial accelerator). Using a comparative case approach across the 2008-2009 recession and the 2020 pandemic shock, the paper evaluates policies that economics predicts should stabilize firms: liquidity reserves interpreted as precautionary savings, access to committed credit as a buffer against external finance premia, operational working-capital adjustments that shorten the cash-conversion cycle, rules-based risk sharing with suppliers and customers, and the option to delay irreversible investment. Outcomes are assessed with sectorlevel indicators-output, employment, inventory-to-sales ratios, and recovery times-alongside firm-disclosed measures when available. The central result is conceptual: policies that relax cashflow constraints and reduce amplification through prices, quantities, and finance are associated with smaller output and employment losses and quicker normalization. The contribution is an economics-grounded playbook that connects firm policies to macro transmission, offering clear testable predictions for industrial sectors during crises.

title: Between Brussels and Beijing: Macao as a “Third Pathway” for Cross-Border Data Flows in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area

detail.title: Between Brussels and Beijing: Macao as a “Third Pathway” for Cross-Border Data Flows in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area
detail.abstract: The Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area is, on paper, a single market; in the law of data it is three. The mainland channels outbound personal information through a security-led architecture of assessments, certifications and standard contracts; Hong Kong has left the cross-border provision of its 1996 ordinance dormant for nearly thirty years; and Macao applies a civil-law statute descended from the European tradition. As the United States and China pull their data spheres apart, this fragmentation has turned from a technical inconvenience into a strategic problem. This paper makes the case for an actor the literature has almost entirely overlooked—Macao—as a workable “third pathway” for compliant cross-border data flows, distinct from the well-trodden mainland–Hong Kong route. I deliberately do not rest that case on the much-invoked prospect of a European Union adequacy decision, which Macao has never sought and is unlikely to obtain soon. The argument turns instead on four assets that already exist or are visibly taking shape: a GDPR-lineage statute; the Mainland–Macao Standard Contract operationalised in September 2024; the Hengqin Guangdong-Macao In-Depth Cooperation Zone, which in practice has begun to function as a regulatory laboratory; and a Sino-Lusophone role to which Brazil’s January 2026 adequacy has lent unexpected legal weight. Reading these developments through regulatory-competition theory, a qualified Brussels Effect, and China’s tradition of zonal policy experimentation, I argue that Macao’s value lies in a double function—an external bridge toward the European and Portuguese-speaking data spaces, and an internal sandbox within “One Country, Two Systems.” The paper meets the obvious objections head-on—an unreformed 2005 statute, a supervisory authority that is not independent, and United States measures that fold Macao into “China”—and turns them into a sequenced reform agenda. Among its proposals is a “certification-first” bridge that would use the Greater Bay Area’s emerging mutual-certification machinery, rather than full adequacy, as the near-term legal vehicle. It closes with concrete implications for compliance officers, regulators and investors.

title: Prices versus Quantities Revisited: What Do Policymakers Need to Know to Set Pigouvian Taxes and Subsidies?
affiliations: Harvard University, Harvard University - Department of Economics, Boston University - Department of Economics and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston - Research Department

detail.title: Prices versus Quantities Revisited: What Do Policymakers Need to Know to Set Pigouvian Taxes and Subsidies?
detail.abstract: What information do policymakers need to design Pigouvian taxes or subsidies? Standard logic suggests that it is sufficient to know the size of the externality and unnecessary to know about quantities. Yet this logic is incorrect if interventions have fixed costs, taxes create deadweight losses, or there are distributional concerns. We present a model in which these considerations can make it more valuable for policymakers to learn about equilibrium quantities. We apply the model to congestion pricing, which has high fixed costs, and to a proposed housing subsidy in Boston that features deadweight losses and distributional concerns.

title: Do Mutual Fund Managers Herd Toward Sustainability?
affiliations: Auckland University of Technology, Auckland University of Technology, Southern Illinois University Edwardsville - Department of Economics & Finance and Auckland University of Technology

detail.title: Do Mutual Fund Managers Herd Toward Sustainability?
detail.abstract: Using Morningstar's fund-level sustainability (ESG) rating data for a large sample of mutual funds domiciled in Australasia, we present strong evidence of herding in mutual funds with high sustainability ratings (high-ESG-rated) relative to unrated or low-ESG-rated funds. Herding in funds with high sustainability ratings is intentional, not driven by fundamental information, and independent of fund age, size, past performance, and investment focus. More importantly, we show that herding in funds with high ESG ratings dampens the correlation between the returns on these funds and their non-sustainable counterparts, thus creating diversification potential via a sustainable investment approach. Finally, fund herding behaviour is associated with lower subsequent fund performance, implying that herding towards sustainability does not necessarily reflect informed trading by fund managers while no effect is found on subsequent fund flows. Our findings provide novel insight into investor behaviour in the growing market for sustainable investments.

title: The Impact of Mathematical Literacy within STEM Education on the Financial Resilience of Youth in Kazakhstan: A Regional Econometric Analysis
affiliations: Nazarbayev Intellectual School of Physics and Mathematics in Aktobe, Nazarbayev Intellectual School of Physics and Mathematics in Aktobe, S Seifullin Kazakh Agrotechnical Research University, S Seifullin Kazakh Agrotechnical Research University and Nazarbayev Intellectual School

detail.title: The Impact of Mathematical Literacy within STEM Education on the Financial Resilience of Youth in Kazakhstan: A Regional Econometric Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the causal relationship between STEM-driven mathematical literacy and youth financial resilience across Kazakhstan's regions from 2018 to 2024. Using an Instrumental Variables approach to address endogeneity issues, we estimate the impact of mathematical competencies on youth indebtedness and debt burden. The empirical findings reveal a highly nuanced dual nature of this relationship. On one hand, a spatial fintech effect is identified: developed STEM infrastructure accelerates digital integration, increasing overdue debt due to aggressive microfinance scoring. On the other hand, cognitive competencies remain a crucial determinant of long-term financial resilience. These insights contribute to optimizing educational policies.

title: Explainable AI for Anti-Money Laundering Detection: A Hybrid Ensemble Approach Validated Under Federal Regulatory Remediation

detail.title: Explainable AI for Anti-Money Laundering Detection: A Hybrid Ensemble Approach Validated Under Federal Regulatory Remediation
detail.abstract: Financial institutions face mounting pressure to modernize anti-money laundering (AML) transaction monitoring while satisfying regulators' growing demand for transparency in automated decision-making. Black-box machine learning models, despite strong detection performance, are difficult to defend to examiners and investigators who must justify Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filings on a case-by-case basis. This paper presents and evaluates a hybrid explainable AI architecture-combining gradient-boosted ensemble models with deep neural networks and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) value attribution-deployed at enterprise scale during an AML platform consolidation at a major U.S. money services business operating under a U.S. Department of Justice and FinCEN Deferred Prosecution Agreement (DPA). The DPA mandated demonstrable, auditable improvement in transaction-monitoring coverage and detection accuracy within a fixed compliance window, a constraint that required not only strong model performance but defensible, interpretable outputs suitable for direct regulatory examination. Implementation results include transaction-monitoring coverage expanding from approximately 30% to 95% of volume, a 60% reduction in false-positive alert rates, and ensemble detection accuracy of approximately 98.5%. This paper discusses the architectural and organizational implications of building AML detection systems for explainability from the outset, including the integration of SHAP attribution into SAR narrative construction, the operational role of investigator feedback in model tuning, and the comparative tradeoffs between custom-built and platform-based AML implementations. The findings offer financial institutions, regulators, and RegTech practitioners a field-validated case study of explainable AI deployed as production compliance infrastructure rather than as a research prototype.

detail.abstract: Chronological age remains the dominant variable in retirement planning, workforce policy, and later-life risk assessment, yet it tells us almost nothing about who is functionally capable and who is not. This study argues that the relevant unit of analysis is not age but adaptability and that adaptability in later life is best understood as two empirically distinguishable and nonredundant dimensions: enacted labour-market agency, reflecting current behavioural engagement; and accumulated adaptive reserve, reflecting the life-course stock of education, income diversity, and socioeconomic resources that buffers future vulnerability.

title: Silent Failure: Validation-Regime Selection as One Source of Deep-Learning Fragility in Volatility Forecasting

detail.title: Silent Failure: Validation-Regime Selection as One Source of Deep-Learning Fragility in Volatility Forecasting

detail.abstract: Deep learning models for volatility forecasting often look strong on aggregate metrics but struggle when volatility is high. One plausible cause has gone largely untested: the volatility of the window used to select the model. When that window is usually calm, tuning on such a window may leave the model poorly scaled for stress. We test this directly with a controlled experiment on S&P 500 realised variance. Two pipelines are identical except for a single factor: whether Optuna selects hyperparameters on a calm window or a slightly stressed one. The training data, the test data, and the search protocol are all held fixed, and temporal leakage is controlled. Any difference between the arms must therefore come from the validation regime alone. For a Temporal Fusion Transformer, calm-window tuning produces a high-volatility QLIKE of 1.10, while stress-window tuning lowers it to 0.44. The difference is significant under a Diebold-Mariano test. The mechanism is one of magnitude rather than tracking. Both arms follow the direction of volatility about equally well, but the calm-validated model forecasts variances that are too small. In the high-volatility regime its mean forecast is only 44% of realised variance, and its standard deviation only 33% of the realised. The stress-validated model reaches 85% and 82% respectively. This scale deficit is costly when volatility is high but nearly free on average, because most test days are calm. That is why aggregate metrics hide it. The effect is robust. It holds for a smaller LSTM, across sub-periods, across shorter training windows, and under per-window re-selection. It also strengthens under a tighter regime definition. These checks rule out the training span and the 2020 shock as explanations. We also document a regime reversal: deep networks lead in calm conditions, while rolling-window GARCH leads in high volatility. That contrast sets a frozen network against a continually refit GARCH, so it reflects how each is used in practice rather than an intrinsic ranking. Stress-aware selection reduces the high-volatility failure but does not remove it, since tail-risk coverage still falls outside formal bounds. The broader contribution is to show that part of deep learning fragility under market stress is a controllable consequence of model-selection, rather than arising solely from architecture or data.

title: More Than Words: Visual Sentiment in Social Media Videos and Stock Returns
affiliations: Xiamen University, Beijing Jiaotong University, School of Economics and Management and School of Economics, Minzu University of China

detail.title: More Than Words: Visual Sentiment in Social Media Videos and Stock Returns
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether sentiment conveyed through videos predicts stock returns. Using a large language model framework, we construct a daily market-level visual sentiment index (SVS) from facial expressions in short videos posted by influencers on Douyin (China's version of TikTok) and compare it with a caption-based textual sentiment measure (STS). We find that SVS predicts future market returns and an initial positive return response is followed by a partial reversal over subsequent trading days, with the predictability concentrated in intraday returns. 𝑆𝑉𝑆 contains predictive information distinct from STS. Textual sentiment attenuates the initial positive return response associated with visual sentiment. Additional tests support a sentiment-based interpretation of SVS: its predictive effects are more pronounced in up markets, retail-oriented portfolios, and active trading environments. Overall, visual sentiment in short videos carries market-relevant information beyond accompanying text and helps explain the timing and dynamics of sentiment-driven price responses.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how the connection of taxation to public benefits can decrease tax payers' perceived tax burden, affecting their labor-leisure decision. We present a model of tax and benefit (mis)-perception, in which payoff maximizing work effort increases when the perceived tax burden decreases. Increasing the salience of benefits funded by taxation and the probability of receiving them decreases this perceived tax burden. We use two real-effort online experiments to test the suppositions of the model. In a flat tax system, we find that information on the accrual of benefits increases perceived tax burden and decreases labor supply. In a progressive tax system, we find that full benefit salience improves motivation to remain in the unemployment insurance system and that effort increases under benefit salience when the unemployment rate is high. As such, behavioral responses to the salience of benefits also requires the expectation of their need.

title: Alcohol Consumption and Intimate Partner Violence: Long-Term Effects of a Temporary Alcohol Ban
affiliations: ,  and Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics of Management, Cornell University

detail.title: Alcohol Consumption and Intimate Partner Violence: Long-Term Effects of a Temporary Alcohol Ban
detail.abstract: We study the effects of temporary restrictions on alcohol availability on alcohol consumption and intimate partner violence. We exploit a policy in Kerala, India, that sharply restricted hard liquor sales in bars in 2014 and was fully reversed in 2017. We estimate difference-in-differences and event-study models exploiting cross-district variation in pre-policy exposure to hard liquor consumption. We find that bar-based alcohol consumption declined sharply following the policy but returned to pre-policy levels within roughly ten months, consistent with consumers substituting toward lower-alcohol fermented drinks, such as beer and wine, sold through permitted outlets. We find no evidence of substitution toward hard alcohol consumption at home during the policy period. Domestic violence declined among higher-exposure, higher-wealth households during the policy period and increased following the policy's repeal, with effects concentrated in less frequent forms of violence. Overall, our findings suggest that temporary alcohol restrictions reduce alcohol consumption and intimate partner violence in the short run, but these gains dissipate once the restrictions are lifted.

title: Budget 2025 And 2026: An Analysis of Key Impacts and Responses within the Hospitality Sector

detail.abstract: This research outlines the key budgetary measures recently introduced by the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the subsequent impact on the Hospitality sector and the wider implications on the Events and Tourism sector from the perspective of leading sector bodies, institutions and sector responses. The paper focuses on four key budgetary measures introduced including Business Rates, Green Levy, National Living Wage and Apprenticeship Funding as outlined in Budget 2025. This forms the basis of this research paper and the key areas of analysis that will focus on the nature of the measures introduced and the response made by leadership teams and business owners. The paper outlines the findings from a mixed methods qualitative and quantitative approach, utilising an opened and closed ended questionnaire to managers, senior leaders and business owners analysing their operational reactions to the budgetary measures in those four areas. Furthermore, triangulation based on the document analysis will be undertaken further understand budget measures, impacts and consequences. The study includes 95 valid participants and this is the first in a two-part research paper with the second research paper post Budget 2026. The primary theoretical lens for this research is an Institutional Theory examining how hospitality organisations respond to regulatory changes based on three isomorphic processes of change: coercive, mimetic, and normative. The purpose of this paper is to conduct ongoing live research of contemporary issues in the hospitality sector where the data and findings can be shared and disseminated amongst faculty staff for module updates, student workshops and as part of a wider research project.

title: Psychological Empowerment as a Mediator in Virtual Teams: A Critical Review of Transformational Leadership and Employee Engagement
affiliations: University of Vocational Technology and University of Colombo

detail.title: Psychological Empowerment as a Mediator in Virtual Teams: A Critical Review of Transformational Leadership and Employee Engagement
detail.abstract: Rapid expansion of remote and virtual work has reshaped how leadership influences employee motivation and engagement. While transformational leadership proven to be associated with higher employee engagement, lesser attention is given towards psychological mechanism through which this relationship operates in a digital environment. This conceptual review proposes psychological empowerment-comprising meaning, competence. Self-determination and impact as the key mediating mechanism linking transformational leadership to employee engagement in virtual teams. Focusing on Job Demands-Resources model, Social Exchange Theory, and Self-Determination Theory, this paper argues that in virtual contexts characterized by autonomy, reduced visibility and increased self-regulation demands, leadership influence is perceived through empowerment rather than direct behavioural mechanisms. The framework further identifies contextual boundary conditions, including communication quality, technostress, team maturity and cultural context. Hence by integrating leadership and motivational perspectives, this paper provides a context-sensitive conceptual model and provides directions for future empirical research in virtual settings

title: DB-KAUNet: An Adaptive Dual Branch Kolmogorov-Arnold UNet for Retinal Vessel Segmentation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) - Institute of High Performance Computing, affiliation not provided to SSRN, South China University of Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: DB-KAUNet: An Adaptive Dual Branch Kolmogorov-Arnold UNet for Retinal Vessel Segmentation
detail.abstract: Accurate segmentation of retinal vessels is crucial for the clinical diagnosis of numerous ophthalmic and systemic diseases. However, traditional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) methods exhibit inherent limitations, struggling to capture long-range dependencies and complex nonlinear relationships. To address the above limitations, an Adaptive Dual Branch Kolmogorov-Arnold UNet (DB-KAUNet) is proposed for retinal vessel segmentation. In DB-KAUNet, we design a Heterogeneous Dual-Branch Encoder (HDBE) that features parallel CNN and Transformer pathways. The HDBE strategically interleaves standard CNN and Transformer blocks with novel KANConv and KAT blocks, enabling the model to form a comprehensive feature representation. To optimize feature processing, we integrate several critical components into the HDBE. First, a Cross-Branch Channel Interaction (CCI) module is embedded to facilitate efficient interaction of channel features between the parallel pathways. Second, an attention-based Spatial Feature Enhancement (SFE) module is employed to enhance spatial features and fuse the outputs from both branches. Building upon the SFE module, an advanced Spatial Feature Enhancement with Geometrically Adaptive Fusion (SFE-GAF) module is subsequently developed. In the SFE-GAF module, adaptive sampling is utilized to focus on true vessel morphology precisely. The adaptive process strengthens salient vascular features while significantly reducing background noise and computational overhead. Extensive experiments on the DRIVE, STARE, and CHASE_DB1 datasets validate that DB-KAUNet achieves leading segmentation performance and demonstrates exceptional robustness.
