detail.abstract:
For more than four decades, research in strategic human resource management (SHRM) has at­tempted to establish systematic relationships between human resource practices and organizational performance. Despite extensive empirical effort, findings remain inconsistent, context dependent, and frequently characterized as a “black box” problem. This paper argues that the persistence of this difficulty reflects a deeper conceptual issue: the mis-specification of the dependent variable. Organizational performance is an emergent system-level outcome influenced by multiple interact­ing organizational subsystems, making it an implausible direct target for HRM theory.

This paper proposes a reframing in which organization capability, rather than performance, becomes the appropriate focal outcome for HRM’s strategic contribution. Organization capability is defined as the evidenced ability of an organization, as designed, to achieve specified outcomes under defined conditions through the integrated functioning of its human and structural elements. By repositioning HRM’s role within capability formation and readiness, the paper offers a clearer theoretical pathway linking human resource systems to organizational outcomes. The argument contributes to ongoing debates regarding the explanatory limits of SHRM research and provides a conceptual foundation for more coherent empirical investigation of HRM’s strategic value.

The paper contributes to debates in strategic human resource management, organization theory, and the resource-based view of the firm by clarifying the role of HR systems in capability formation and organizational effectiveness.

title: Automation Threat and Labor Market Power

detail.title: Automation Threat and Labor Market Power
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of automation threat in firms' labor market power. Employing the production approach, I show that workers in an average German manufacturer receive 79 cents on the marginal euro. Using automation threats proxied by local labor market regions' exposure to industrial robots, instrumented by plausibly exogenous shift-share factors, I find that robot exposure increases employer power over routine workers in East German districts with weaker unions, where spatial frictions are more pronounced. The empirical findings are consistent with the wage bargaining model in which employers retain the "right-to-manage" their workforce composition and unions representing different worker groups bargain separately with the firm.

title: Embedding Biodiversity in Business Strategy: Challenging Control Systems to Achieve Nature Positive Goals
affiliations: Scuola Superiore Sant’Anna, Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies - Institute of Management, Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies - Institute of Management and Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies - Institute of Management

detail.title: Embedding Biodiversity in Business Strategy: Challenging Control Systems to Achieve Nature Positive Goals
detail.abstract: Nature Positive (NP) is a global ambition to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. Despite the growing popularity and adoption of NP-related objectives, the implementation of such commitments is far from effective and difficult to control. This study examines the extent to which management control systems (MCSs) for halting biodiversity loss can facilitate the achievement of NP goals. Drawing on a multi-case study of four Italian organizations operating in the agri-food sector, we observe that MCSs are primarily used to build environmental capabilities and strategy implementation. Moreover, our study shows that organizations resort to collaboration and stakeholder engagement to leverage external technical knowledge, overcome the ambiguity of NP targets, and project control beyond organizational boundaries to influence suppliers' behavior. Based on these insights, we develop a conceptual framework to draw the relationship between MCSs, key capabilities, organizational strategy, and NP commitments. The framework highlights the iterative and relational nature of control in addressing complex ecological goals, extending the understanding of how MCSs operate in contexts of sustainability and biodiversity management.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural and behavioural determinants of gold preference over equity investment in six Asian economies — India, China, Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, and South Korea — over the period 1997 to 2025. Drawing on data from the World Gold Council, the Bank of Korea, the Reserve Bank of India, the International Monetary Fund, and peer-reviewed behavioural finance literature, the paper argues that gold demand in these markets reflects a combination of rational portfolio responses to recurring currency depreciation and institutional distrust, culturally embedded savings traditions, and well-documented behavioural biases including loss aversion and the certainty effect (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979). The paper identifies a consistent empirical pattern: episodes of currency depreciation are followed by measurable surges in household gold demand across all six markets studied. This pattern holds regardless of cultural differences, suggesting that macroeconomic vulnerability — rather than culture alone — is the primary driver of gold preference. However, cultural factors are shown to influence the baseline level and form of gold demand (jewellery versus investment), reinforcing the core preference established through economic experience. The paper also identifies a policy paradox specific to gold-importing economies, particularly India, where household gold demand — individually rational as a hedge — creates aggregate current account pressure and foreign exchange vulnerability. The paper concludes with a limitations section acknowledging the boundaries of the analysis and directions for future research.

detail.abstract:
Public procurement plays a critical role in the implementation of externally financed development projects in Uganda. However, the increasing reliance on development partner financing has created operational challenges arising from the coexistence of Uganda’s Public Procurement and Disposal of Public Assets (PPDA) framework and the procurement rules of international development partners such as the World Bank, African Development Bank, and United Nations agencies. This paper examines the legal, institutional, and operational mechanisms through which Uganda can reconcile development partner procurement requirements with the PPDA framework while maintaining compliance with both domestic law and financing agreements.

The study analyses the legal provisions contained in the PPDA Act, particularly the provisions recognizing the supremacy of international agreements and donor funding conditions where conflicts arise, and assesses the extent to which these provisions facilitate harmonization. The paper identifies key areas of convergence and divergence between the PPDA framework and development partner procurement systems, including eligibility requirements, local content preferences, procurement thresholds, procurement methods, standard bidding documents, complaints mechanisms, review processes, and approval procedures. It further evaluates the implementation challenges associated with managing dual procurement regimes, including legal uncertainty, procurement delays, audit risks, duplication of oversight mechanisms, and capacity constraints within procuring and disposing entities.

The paper finds that Uganda already possesses a sufficient legal foundation for harmonization and does not require fundamental legislative reform. Rather, the principal challenge lies in establishing clear operational mechanisms to manage conflicts between procurement regimes and reduce implementation risks. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a structured hybrid procurement model that retains the PPDA framework as the primary system for planning, accountability, records management, ethics, oversight, and contract management, while allowing project-specific application of development partner rules where legally required. The study recommends the adoption of government-wide harmonization guidelines, standardized project procurement annexes, conflict matrices, enhanced e-GP integration, targeted capacity building, and a unified complaints and review framework.

The paper concludes that effective reconciliation of development partner procurement guidelines with Uganda’s PPDA framework is both legally feasible and institutionally desirable. By adopting a predictable and transparent harmonization approach, Uganda can reduce procurement delays, strengthen accountability, improve project implementation performance, and maximize the developmental impact of externally financed investments while safeguarding national procurement objectives and value for money.

detail.abstract: This paper undertakes a critical literature review of management control systems (MCS) research addressing the question of how organizational control mechanisms conceptualize and respond to biodiversity challenges. Using a structured Scopus-based search, 127 relevant studies were analysed across diverse organizational disciplines. The review finds that research is fragmented, predominantly performance-and reporting-oriented, and highlights organizational practices shaped by legitimacy and impression management logics. While biodiversity is widely acknowledged as a critical concern, most studies treat it in vague or generalized terms, with limited theoretical grounding and a tendency to reproduce neoliberal narratives of ranking, competition, and commodification. We argue that these approaches risk reinforcing the very dynamics that drive biodiversity loss. The paper concludes by advocating for ecologically grounded reorientations of MCS research that moves beyond reporting analysis, towards defining the role of organizational figures and non-financial measurement systems.

title: Life Cycle Management Implementation as Information Processing: The Role of Conscious and Unconscious Reflection
affiliations: Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa, Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies - Institute of Management and Ivey Business School

detail.title: Life Cycle Management Implementation as Information Processing: The Role of Conscious and Unconscious Reflection
detail.abstract: Formally similar sustainability management practices are often implemented in different ways, yielding heterogeneous environmental outcomes. As these practices typically rely on a key diagnostic phase, examining how organizations interpret and engage with the information generated is crucial to understanding variation in their implementation. This paper investigates how companies process environmental information when implementing Life Cycle Management (LCM). We draw on a longitudinal qualitative analysis of eleven Italian companies participating in a project based on Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) assessment, a life-cycle-based computational method. Our findings show that the depth of reflection on life-cycle results shapes distinct LCM implementation trajectories. When reflection remains unconscious, life-cycle information is used instrumentally, leading to a business-case-oriented form of LCM implementation. By contrast, conscious reflection on life-cycle information prompts a critical rethinking of established practices, leading companies to implement LCM according to a holistic life-cycle thinking. The study contributes to sustainability management literature by highlighting information processing as a pivotal mechanism shaping environmental practices implementation pathways.

title: Can Corporate Governance Reforms Reshape Supply-Chain Contracting? Evidence from Gender Quotas
affiliations: Business School, National University of Singapore, Alberta School of Business, University of Alberta and University of Navarra, IESE Business School

detail.title: Can Corporate Governance Reforms Reshape Supply-Chain Contracting? Evidence from Gender Quotas
detail.abstract: We study whether corporate governance reforms reshape contracting in global supply chains. Exploiting staggered board gender diversity (BGD) interventions in 37 customer countries as plausibly exogenous shocks, we examine their effects on the contracting outcomes of U.S. suppliers, which are not subject to comparable national policies. We find that U.S. suppliers with greater female board representation are more likely to obtain new contracts from customers in countries that adopt BGD reforms. These effects are stronger when the interventions are more likely to alter customer board composition and when customers possess greater bargaining power over suppliers, consistent with a customer-driven changes in governance preferences following the reforms. Mechanism tests indicate that the effects are more pronounced when customer firms have weaker pre-intervention ESG profiles, where board changes have greater scope to shift supplier-selection criteria toward board gender diversity, and when customer-supplier country pairs are more institutionally and culturally distant, where governance alignment may be more valuable in mitigating cross-border contracting frictions. Finally, U.S. suppliers more exposed to BGD-intervened customers subsequently increase female board representation, particularly when they have greater access to female director networks, and these increases are followed by improvements in operating performance. Overall, our findings highlight global supply chains as a channel through which governance reforms can have cross-border effects.

detail.abstract: AI-enabled mobility services create value through personalization, but data intensity can undermine consumer openness. This study examines whether stronger customization cues increase acceptance or backfire by reducing perceived service authenticity. Using a 2 × 2 scenario experiment with an AIenabled multimodal urban smart assistant (MUSA) and 1,946 Italian respondents, we test how customization intensity and benefit framing shape authenticity, use/share intention, and data-sharing decisions. Results show that higher customization intensity is associated with lower perceived authenticity, whereas authenticity increases use/share intention. Mediation analyses show that this negative effect operates through authenticity. Within high-customization conditions, utilitarian customization outperforms hedonic or prosocial customization. Collective-purpose cues played a more limited and context-dependent role. Item-level evidence shows highly selective disclosure willingness, with mobility-relevant data more acceptable than intimate or weakly mission-related data. The findings extend privacy-calculus and personalization research by identifying authenticity as a key evaluative mechanism in responses to AI-enabled personalization.

title: Practice-Specific Drivers Shape how Smallholder Tea Farmers Manage Diverse Nature-Related Risks in Northern Vietnam
affiliations: Deakin University

detail.title: Practice-Specific Drivers Shape how Smallholder Tea Farmers Manage Diverse Nature-Related Risks in Northern Vietnam
detail.abstract: Agriculture, and tea production in particular, depends on nature while contributing to its degradation, exposing farming communities to interacting nature-related risks. Sustainable farm management practices (SFMPs) can mitigate these risks, yet uptake in smallholder systems depends on how farmers perceive threats, evaluate options, and intend to act. Drawing on Protection Motivation Theory and the nature-related risk lens of the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD), we examine smallholder tea farmers' intentions to adopt or continue five SFMPs: irrigation, soil mulching, organic fertilizer application, intercropping, and integrated pest management (IPM), across four risk domains: climate variability, pest and disease pressure, water scarcity, and soil degradation. We surveyed 312 smallholder tea farmers in Vietnam to identify practice-specific predictors and compare their contributions across domains. Current adoption was widespread but uneven: organic fertilizer had the highest rate (82.4%), while irrigation, soil mulching, and IPM each exceeded 50%, and intercropping had the lowest (28.8%). Future adoption intention was highest for irrigation (74.0%) and organic fertilizer (70.5%), moderate for IPM (62.2%) and soil mulching (51.9%), and consistently low for intercropping (34.9%), despite its multifunctional role. Adoption efficacy was the most consistent predictor of adoption intention, although practice-specific drivers were evident. Institutional support and climate knowledge were most prominent for water-related practices; education, and self-efficacy in the more knowledge-intensive IPM, whereas risk perception and experience were most prominent for intercropping and soil mulching. This is the first study to link smallholder tea farmers' risk and coping appraisals across multiple nature-related risk domains to practice-specific adoption intentions. We show that while adoption efficacy is a consistent driver, the remaining predictors differ systematically across risk domains and practices. This practice-by-risk-domain framework is transferable to other smallholder and perennial-crop systems, providing a basis for more targeted extension and policy strategies to strengthen the sustainability of smallholder farming systems.

detail.abstract: This paper examines Karachi-Pakistan's largest city, financial capital, and home to over 20 million people-as a case study in what urban governance scholarship terms the "neoliberal city": a mode of urban governance in which economic and institutional elites shape city development in close alliance with private capital, while formal democratic institutions remain fragmented and comparatively weak. Drawing on Pierre's typology of urban governance modes, Stoker's account of networked governance, Blanco's network governance theory, and Saunders' theory of the local state, the paper's original 2017 analysis examined Karachi under the Muttahida Qaumi Movement's (MQM) post-2005 rule, when the party paired "city of the future" boosterism-signal-free corridors, Port Grand's Singapore-style waterfront redevelopment, extensive public-private surveillance infrastructure-with large-scale private capture of urban space, exemplified by the Bahria Town real estate empire and a landmark Supreme Court case in which the civil society organisation Shehri successfully challenged the Pakistan Army's seizure of a public recreational ground for private commercial development. This paper extends that analysis through a subsequent structural rupture: the 2013 Pakistan Rangers security operation that dismantled MQM's decades-long dominance, followed by MQM's 2023 electoral boycott and the Pakistan Peoples Party's (PPP) unexpected capture of the Karachi mayoralty-the first time in the city's history PPP has held that office. The paper's central finding is that Karachi's core governance dysfunction-a fragmented local government structure in which the elected mayor directly controls barely a quarter of the city's geographic area, with functional authority narrower still once fragmented service silos are accounted for, no city-wide master plan, and no constitutional protection for local government-has persisted essentially unchanged across this complete transfer of political power, suggesting that Karachi's "neoliberal city" condition reflects durable institutional and constitutional design choices rather than any single party's specific ideological project.

This paper introduces the TOPLDDF Architecture - Trusted x Open-Interoperable x Permissioned x Legal x Deterministic x Digital Finance - a complete constitutional working process for establishing Sovereign Trust in institutional digital finance. TOPLDDF fills the structural gap that no prior infrastructure, standard, or framework has resolved: the simultaneous constitutional verification of trust (T), legal enforceability (L), open-interoperability (O), permissioned identity (P), deterministic settlement (D), and digital finance grounding (DF) before value moves on institutional digital infrastructure. Without TOPLDDF, trust in institutional digital finance is self-asserted, legal enforceability is assumed, enforcement is manual, and trust signals fragment across jurisdictions. With TOPLDDF, trust is a constitutional fact. Note on Human Supervision: TOPLDDF is a machine-executed constitutional architecture. Human supervision monitors the machine and the institutional framework - not the TOPLDDF process transactions themselves. Where automation is incomplete, human action is required under Conformance Authority mandate: oracle source certification, scoring model certification, and post-enforcement legal review. Human override of threshold-triggered events is constitutionally prohibited. This paper completes a three-paper constitutional architecture that together constitute an independent, standalone, trust-based digital finance execution ecosystem: 2Q-H-C-T-L-I (scoring engine, SSRN 6601100/6739600), AITS v1.0 (constitutional standard, SSRN 6813082), and TOPLDDF (complete working architecture - this paper).

TOPLDDF is an independent, universal architecture. It is not a GL1 application, not a VARA application, not any specific environment's application. It is a constitutional architecture specification that any institutional digital finance infrastructure can host, provided it satisfies the AITS Ten Implementation Conditions. The implementation environment is the constitutional ground - GL1 (MAS Global Layer One) is the ground in which this paper demonstrates TOPLDDF; VARA, BIS Innovation Hub, and any AITS-compliant infrastructure are equally valid grounds. For cross-border institutional settlement, two implementation environments may operate simultaneously under one TOPLDDF constitutional framework - the O (Open-Interoperable) and D (Deterministic) dimensions provide the constitutional bridge across environments. The G-Grade travels with the asset. The circuit breaker fires on both environments. Regulatory notifications reach both jurisdictions.


TOPLDDF has one mandatory component and flexible components. Mandatory: AITS v1.0 (Naser, 2026c; SSRN 6813082) - the constitutional standard governing every design decision. AITS is not a tool. It is the constitutional authority. Without AITS, there is no constitutional standard and trust becomes self-asserted. Flexible: the scoring model (2Q-H-C-T-L-I v1.1, SSRN 6601100/6739600, in this paper; or any AITS-certified model), the operational layer architecture (six-layer GL1-environment reference in this paper; or any environment-appropriate architecture satisfying all AITS Ten Conditions), and the implementation environment (GL1 in this paper; any AITS-compliant infrastructure). The six-step working process is constitutional minimum: Admissibility Screening (all five AITS Pillars) -> Eligibility Scoring (2Q-H-C-T-L-I) -> AITS Trust Verification -> Decision with Full Explanation -> Settlement or Enforcement -> Continuous Monitoring. Additional steps may be added by any implementation. The sequence cannot be reordered.

title: Decentralized Equilibrium Search Under Central Governance Primal-Dual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Inventory Coordination

detail.title: Decentralized Equilibrium Search Under Central Governance Primal-Dual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Large-Scale Inventory Coordination
detail.abstract: We study the problem of coordinating inventory replenishment decisions across thousands of retail stores sharing a common warehouse, under binding capacity constraints and contractual service-level commitments. Classical inventory theory-from the Newsvendor model to multi-echelon base-stock policies-assumes known demand distributions, optimizes each store independently or sequentially, and produces static ordering rules calibrated to historical statistics. These assumptions break down in largescale practice: demand is non-stationary, stores compete for scarce warehouse capacity, and service commitments must be honored dynamically. We propose a primal-dual multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework in which store-level PPO agents optimize local replenishment policies while a central planner enforces system-level constraints through Lagrangian dual variables. The dual variables admit direct economic interpretations as shadow prices: prices warehouse capacity scarcity, and prices the cost of the service-level commitment. Together with a bullwhip penalty coefficient , they constitute a three-lever governance system with provably orthogonal controls over fill rate, capacity feasibility, and order volatility. We validate the framework on 143 weeks of the Walmart public sales panel (store-department pairs). The system achieves an 89.9% demand fill rate under standard conditions. Under a 50% demand surge-a structural non-stationarity that no calibrated static policy can anticipate-PPO achieves 86.5% fill rate while the Newsvendor oracle falls to 39-47% regardless of whether its parameters are correctly recalibrated, a 1.83 performance gap. This result reveals that the adaptability advantage of MARL is structural rather than empirical: state-conditional ordering solves a real-time capacity allocation problem that static ordering rules cannot solve in principle.

detail.abstract: This whitepaper presents a strategic framework for deploying SafeWatch AI (marketed as Safe2Watch), a workplace safety intelligence platform that transforms fragmented environmental, health, and safety (EHS) data into actionable executive dashboards, hazard monitoring views, and compliance readiness indicators. The platform addresses a persistent industry gap: organizations collect rich safety records incidents, near misses, inspections, training logs, and hazard readings but lack a unified analytical layer that leadership can trust without months of integration work. SafeWatch AI introduces a CSV-first ingestion model paired with a modern single-page application (SPA) built on React, TypeScript, and Vite. Eleven structured data categories map directly to operational reality, enabling safety teams to upload spreadsheet exports from existing systems and immediately populate dashboards for risk analytics, OSHA-aligned compliance tracking, and site-level operations views. Unlike legacy EHS suites that require enterprise middleware before any value is visible, SafeWatch AI delivers demonstrable insight within a single browser session. Performance of Decision-Making: Executive dashboards compute KPIs directly from uploaded records, eliminating weeks of slide-deck preparation. Structured Data Ingestion: Eleven validated CSV templates cover core safety events, compliance artifacts, and operational entities (sites, departments, employees, equipment, training, corrective actions). Improved Stability of Reporting: Consistent column schemas and ingest-time validation reduce schema drift and reporting inconsistencies across sites. Extended Analytical Reach: Risk analytics, hazard monitoring, and compliance views share a single inmemory data store, enabling cross-module correlation without duplicate data entry. Optimized Resource Utilization: A lightweight client-side architecture (Vite + React) minimizes infrastructure overhead during pilots and proof-of-concept deployments. These benefits collectively contribute to a higher safety ROI by reducing reporting labor, accelerating hazard response, and enabling evidence-based capital allocation for corrective actions.

title: Exploring Future Circularity Scenarios of Lithium-Ion Batteries in the European Union: A System Dynamics Approach

detail.title: Exploring Future Circularity Scenarios of Lithium-Ion Batteries in the European Union: A System Dynamics Approach
detail.abstract: The European Union's transition toward climate neutrality is accelerating demand for lithium-ion batteries to electrify the automotive and household sectors. This makes the European region susceptible to vulnerabilities in material supply, end-of-life management, and recycling capacity. Despite growing research on battery circularity, existing models typically address single countries or isolated end-of-life pathways, lacking a comprehensive EU-wide, multi-pathway perspective. This study develops a system dynamics model to assess the long-term evolution of the vehicle and stationary battery market, end-of-life flows, and material recovery across all EU-27 countries up to 2050, integrating country-level heterogeneity and cathode chemistry transitions. The analysis quantifies how the interplay of extended use, remanufacturing, repurposing, and recycling shapes future battery demand, material dependency, and self-sufficiency. Results show that electric vehicles will dominate battery demand by 2050. Phase-out policies and high repurposing rates lower stationary demand, but increase reliance on imports for electric vehicle batteries. Collection and recycling capacity must expand substantially to meet regulatory targets, although recycling infrastructure remains concentrated in a few countries. Under coordinated expansion efforts, recovery of critical raw materials such as lithium, nickel, and cobalt could partially meet European self-sufficiency targets. The findings of this study highlight that excessive second-life deployment delays material recovery, whereas balanced integration of remanufacturing and recycling improves circularity and resource resilience. To meet European sustainability objectives, it is essential to implement flexible, chemistry-specific, and regionally integrated strategies. These strategies should connect battery design, collection, and recycling infrastructure to balance circular economy goals with resource security.

detail.abstract: Background: Agricultural Terms of Trade (ToT) used as index of measuring farm-sector welfare, depicting the skewed burden pulled by variations in input costs and related finished goods prices. This study will be exploring whether India's Goods and Services Tax (GST 2.0) reform generated an advantageous scissors effect. Methodology: In this study used a weighted average price index (WPI data, Laspeyres 1871) methodology from the period of January 2025 to February 2026 borrowed from official website of the office of economic adviser, under the ministry of statistics and programme implementation, India. And categorised the study period into three phases as pre-GST 2.0, Transition phase, and post implementation phase respectively. Findings: Study found statistically and economically positive improvements in agricultural ToT Phases, 127.13 from pre-reform, 132.19 during post reform phase disseminating a net gain of 5.1 percentage. Structural decomposition analysis demonstrates that the Index of Price Paid (IPP) remained widely stationary across phases i.e. 153.97 to 153.34, whereas Index of Price Received (IPR) depicted sharply surging i.e. 195.75 to 202.70, resulted that indirect tax cut led to margin on farm inputs while pushing demand side market. Conclusions: These observations in ToT carry significant policy implications for agricultural taxation, input subsidy rationalization, and inclusive rural development in emerging economies. This study contributes to empirical literature on tax incidence in agriculture and offers an understanding of how indirect tax architecture constructs sectoral competitiveness and farmer welfare.

title: The Trust Premium: Institutional Credibility as a Productive Asset in an Era of Global Resource Mobility

detail.title: The Trust Premium: Institutional Credibility as a Productive Asset in an Era of Global Resource Mobility
detail.abstract: This paper argues that institutional trust has become a productive economic asset in its own right, and that its scarcity relative to increasingly mobile capital, talent, and technology represents one of the defining features of twenty-first-century economic competition. As globalization has reduced barriers to the movement of productive resources, the factors traditionally generating durable competitive advantages have become more replicable and less capable of sustaining long-term differentiation. What cannot be easily replicated is institutional credibility: confidence that contracts will be enforced, property rights protected, and regulatory frameworks maintained with sufficient predictability to support long-term investment decisions. Drawing on verifiable data from Argentina, Estonia, and Brazil, and using sovereign bond spreads, World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators, and skilled migration research as observational proxies, the paper develops the concept of the Trust Premium: the economic advantage enjoyed by societies perceived as institutionally credible. The Trust Premium is distinguished from adjacent constructs, including institutional quality, social capital, and country risk premium, by its emphasis on perceived credibility in a context of high resource mobility. The central proposition is that as capital, talent, technology, and information become increasingly mobile, institutional credibility becomes the scarcest productive asset in the global economy. The paper proposes three research propositions for systematic empirical investigation and identifies implications for policymakers, investors, and individuals navigating an era of rising institutional competition.

detail.abstract: The transition towards electrified, software-defined, and increasingly autonomous mobility systems represents more than a technological shift in propulsion systems. It reflects a broader reconfiguration of industrial systems in which competitive advantage increasingly depends upon how capabilities, software architectures, supply chains, capital, and ecosystem relationships are governed across interconnected networks. Beyond its comparative analysis of automotive manufacturers, this study makes a twofold contribution. First, it identifies governance architecture as an emerging determinant of industrial competitiveness under conditions of technological and industrial transformation. Second, it develops a practical governance assessment and decision architecture through which governance structures may be evaluated, monitored, and adapted in response to changing industrial conditions. In doing so, the paper moves beyond descriptive case-study analysis towards an applied governance-science methodology capable of supporting strategic planning, capital allocation, industrial policy evaluation, and long-term competitive positioning. The paper argues that contemporary automotive transformation is best understood as a contest between alternative governance architectures rather than a purely technological race. To examine this transition, the study develops a Governance Architecture Framework (GAF) and Governance Domain Index (GDI) for evaluating how governance authority, capability ownership, dependency structures, capital allocation mechanisms, and value-creation pathways are organised across industrial systems. The framework is structured around four governance domains: Platform Architecture Strategy, Vertical Integration, Legacy Manufacturing Inertia, and Global Market Orientation. The framework is applied through a comparative assessment of multiple OEM governance architectures, including Tesla, BYD, Volkswagen, Rivian–Volkswagen, Ferrari, XPeng, Huawei, BMW Group, SAIC-GM-Wuling, and Chery Automobile. Rather than treating manufacturers solely as firms, the analysis interprets them as alternative governance configurations through which authority, dependency management, coordination mechanisms, and value creation are organised and sustained. The findings identify a growing tension between architectural continuity and architectural adaptation as organisations respond to emerging sources of value creation associated with software platforms, artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, data ecosystems, and advanced manufacturing networks. Whilst some firms pursue competitive advantage through extensive vertical integration, others increasingly compete through platform ecosystems, software-defined architectures, strategic partnerships, and ecosystem-based governance models. The study concludes that long-term industrial competitiveness is determined less by the selection of a single technological pathway and more by the ability to position governance authority, capability ownership, and strategic control around future sources of value creation. By reframing automotive transformation as a problem of industrial systems governance, the paper contributes an integrated governance-science framework for evaluating industrial resilience, adaptability, strategic sovereignty, capital deployment, and long-term competitive positioning under conditions of technological, geopolitical, and industrial uncertainty.

detail.abstract: The global automotive sector is undergoing a structural reconfiguration from mechanically integrated, internally governed (ICE-based) industrial systems toward software-defined, platform-centric architectures, in which competitive advantage is determined less by product differentiation than by the governance of platforms, software, production, and capital. Recent developments, including capital-intensive scaling constraints among new entrants, accelerated vertical integration across Chinese manufacturers, and the emergence of cross-border production and platform-sharing strategies—signal a systemic shift in how industrial performance is generated and sustained. Across these developments, a persistent misalignment is evident: firms are advancing new mobility propositions whilst operating within industrial systems designed for a different technological and economic logic, resulting in increasing exposure to capital inefficiency, operational fragility, and constrained scalability. This paper advances a governance architecture lens for analysing automotive industrial systems at system level. It positions China’s integrated automotive model as a critical empirical reference point within a broader comparative framework, illustrating how system-level coherence can materially alter performance trajectories. This is contrasted with transitional configurations characteristic of incumbent manufacturers adapting legacy ICE-based systems, and with emerging software-defined or platform-decoupled architectures that reconfigure the relationship between design authority, manufacturing, and control. The analysis is structured around three governance configurations. These three configurations are: vertically integrated systems, hybrid or transitional systems, and software-defined platform systems. These configurations are interpreted through the executive abstraction that industrial performance is a function of platform control, production integration, software coherence, and capital allocation. The contribution of the paper is to reframe automotive competition as an outcome of industrial system design and transformation rather than firm-level strategy alone, linking the transition from ICE-based architectures to software-defined systems with shifts in control, capital deployment, and operational integration. The analysis demonstrates that system-level coherence, particularly the alignment of platform control, software integration, production capability, and capital allocation emerges as the primary determinant of scalability, capital efficiency, and strategic resilience across competing automotive models. It provides a decision-oriented framework for senior executives, investors, and strategic advisors to assess capital exposure, platform dependency, and governance risk across evolving automotive systems, including OEMs, suppliers, capital providers, and strategic partners, with particular relevance to Asia-Pacific industrial dynamics and cross-border production strategies.

detail.abstract: TR-03 explores ESG Governance as an industrial systems challenge rather than a reporting exercise. Through a systems engineering perspective, the report examines the relationships between product development, supply-chain governance, lifecycle stewardship, capital allocation, and sustainable value creation within mobility and industrial ecosystems. Illustrative applications are drawn from Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), CATL, and related industrial systems. Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) considerations are increasingly influencing product development, supply-chain management, investment decisions, regulatory compliance, and organisational governance across industrial sectors. Regulatory developments including the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) have accelerated the transition of ESG from a voluntary sustainability initiative towards an increasingly important governance and operational requirement. Despite this shift, many organisations continue to approach ESG primarily as a reporting and compliance exercise, resulting in fragmented environmental, social, and governance activities that remain disconnected from enterprise strategy, product development processes, lifecycle management, and long-term operational performance. This paper argues that ESG challenges are fundamentally systems challenges. Drawing upon principles of Systems Engineering, systems thinking, lifecycle analysis, and industrial governance, the paper proposes that ESG performance is not determined by isolated sustainability initiatives, but by the interactions between governance structures, stakeholder systems, product architectures, supply chains, operational activities, capital allocation decisions, and strategic objectives. Consequently, ESG Governance is reframed as an enterprise architecture challenge requiring organisations to manage complex interdependencies across industrial ecosystems rather than individual organisational functions. To address this challenge, the paper introduces a Systems Engineering Framework for ESG Governance designed specifically for product development and industrial systems. The framework integrates governance, stakeholder management, lifecycle stewardship, supply-chain resilience, and sustainable value creation within a coherent enterprise architecture. Supporting the framework are a series of practical governance instruments, including the Rosemonte ESG Governance V-Model™, ESG Strategic Diagnostic Matrix™, Stakeholder Influence & Pressure Zones™, and ESG Governance Maturity Index™, providing structured mechanisms for evaluating governance capability, stakeholder pressures, lifecycle impacts, strategic risk exposure, and organisational resilience. Illustrative applications are drawn from mobility and industrial ecosystems, including Jaguar Land Rover's evolving partnership architecture, CATL's role within global battery supply chains, and emerging governance challenges surrounding sustainability, capital access, stakeholder expectations, and investment frameworks within advanced technology sectors. These examples demonstrate that ESG increasingly influences product development decisions, partnership architectures, supply-chain structures, lifecycle performance, investment attractiveness, regulatory compliance, and long-term competitive advantage. The contribution of the paper is twofold. First, it extends existing ESG frameworks by introducing a Systems Engineering perspective capable of analysing ESG as an integrated enterprise system operating across product lifecycles, supply chains, stakeholder ecosystems, and governance structures. Second, it provides a practical governance architecture and decision-support framework through which organisations can strengthen lifecycle stewardship, improve supply-chain resilience, reduce environmental impacts, manage strategic risks, and support sustainable value creation within increasingly complex industrial and mobility systems. The central proposition of this paper is that ESG Governance can be managed more effectively when viewed through a systems lens, enabling organisations to move beyond compliance-oriented approaches towards integrated governance architectures capable of strengthening organisational resilience, lifecycle stewardship, supply-chain performance, strategic capital allocation, capital access, and sustainable enterprise value creation across increasingly complex industrial ecosystems.

title: Payment Infrastructure Exposure and Sanctions Spillovers: Cross-Border Credit Contraction Beyond the Target

detail.title: Payment Infrastructure Exposure and Sanctions Spillovers: Cross-Border Credit Contraction Beyond the Target
detail.abstract: Financial sanctions are typically analyzed through their direct effects on target states. This paper argues that they also generate significant spillovers onto third countries through a distinct channel: dependence on sanction-vulnerable financial infrastructure. We introduce the Payment Feasibility Spillover Exposure (PFSE) index, a novel composite measure that captures the extent to which countries depend on Western-centered payment and intermediation networks subject to OFAC and EU enforcement. Using the 2022 Russia SWIFT exclusion as a quasi-natural experiment, we examine how cross-border bank lending evolves around the shock for countries with varying levels of PFSE. A difference-indifferences estimator exploiting crosscountry variation in pre-shock infrastructure dependence shows that countries with higher PFSE experience significantly larger contractions in cross-border credit following the shock (β1 =-0.039***, SE = 0.010). The gap between the most and least exposed countries in our sample implies a predicted post-shock differential of approximately 10.5 percentage points in cross-border credit. Results are robust across 13 specifications. The infrastructure channel has independent predictive power when trade exposure is excluded (PFSE3: β1 =-0.019**, p = 0.015), though full separation from the trade channel requires a larger panel. These findings suggest that the architecture of financial intermediation itself constitutes a meaningful structural dimension of sanctions exposure, with distributional consequences for third-country access to international credit.

detail.title: ​Utility of expanded hands-on training approach to workforce capacity development for vaccines lot release in Africa: experiences of the GHPP VaccRelease project
detail.abstract: Background: Training regulatory staff in Africa as a means of providing technical support for the official lot release (LR) of vaccines is an established approach to sustainably strengthen the regulatory capacity for overseeing the quality, safety and efficacy of vaccines. In this study, we analysed the suitability and effectiveness of a series of expanded hands-on trainings in vaccines LR conducted by the VaccRelease project at the Paul-Ehrlich-Institut (PEI), and herein present the lessons learned.Method: Using a systematized mixed-methods approach, we collected post-training feedback from trained individuals of six trainings conducted on-site at PEI from August 2023 to November 2025 for 16 participants from three partner countries.Results: Employing the expanded hands-on approach to trainings contributed to enhancing the competencies and expertise of trained fellows in a spectrum of vaccines LR disciplines - including quality management system, approach to method transfer and biostatistics, LR process flow, experimental testing and lot summary protocol review - for which trainings were offered. Amongst the several cited strengths of the training, the experience, competence and work ethics of the trainers was most prominent. Moreover, the training’s on-site nature emerged as an invaluable asset that offered a practical understudy template vital for the implementation of training outputs. The most cited area for improvement of the trainings conducted - mainly by the trainees with limited baseline LR expertise - was the limited time for specific hands-on practice. Notwithstanding, that offered in the training proved optimal enough in averting any significant impairment to the achievement of training outputs. Further, the trained fellows showed a clear implementation plan to ultimately improve the performance of the LR function in their respective institutions.Conclusion: Overall, these findings have significant practical implications, and offer evidence-based recommendations for developing similar future hands-on training initiatives.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is beginning to decouple economic productivity growth from traditional labor inputs, creating a gap in existing macroeconomic models used to forecast technological change.


This paper introduces the , a dynamic model designed to estimate the productivity impact of artificial intelligence across sectors based on three core drivers: technology adoption, capability advancement, and sectoral exposure.


The framework incorporates S-curve diffusion dynamics and sector-specific sensitivity to cognitive automation in order to model the uneven economic impact of AI across industries. Call centers are used as a canonical early example of AI-driven productivity transformation.


The MAEF framework provides economists, policymakers, and business leaders with a structured approach for forecasting AI-driven productivity expansion and labor displacement across the global economy.

title: Financial Market Infrastructures Evolution in a Tokenized Economy
affiliations: , International Monetary Fund (IMF), Center for Innovative Finance, University of Basel and International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Financial Market Infrastructures Evolution in a Tokenized Economy
detail.abstract: This paper examines how tokenization and distributed ledger technology may transform Financial Market Infrastructures (FMIs) by enabling smart contracts to perform a growing share of functions traditionally undertaken by central securities depositories, central counterparties, and trade repositories. It argues that while record-keeping, settlement, collateral management, and reporting can increasingly be executed on-chain, key functions requiring legal certainty, governance, accountability, and discretion remain institutional in nature. The analysis assesses which activities across issuance, clearing, settlement, and reporting can migrate to code, where limitations persist, and how risks evolve in tokenized environments. It finds that tokenization is more likely to reconfigure than eliminate FMIs, creating new efficiencies while introducing novel operational and governance risks. The most plausible outcome is a hybrid FMI model in which technology and institutions jointly provide the trust, resilience, and oversight required for financial stability.

title: Assessing the Culture of Health from Employees’ Perspective: A Company-wide Survey in Eni, Italy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and SDA Bocconi

detail.title: Assessing the Culture of Health from Employees’ Perspective: A Company-wide Survey in Eni, Italy
detail.abstract: Background: The concept of a Culture of Health (CoH) highlights the role of social and organisational contexts in enabling individuals to make healthy choices and thrive. In corporate settings, CoH initiatives may generate shared value for both business and society, but few empirical studies have assessed employees’ perceptions directly, especially in European contexts.Objective: To assess employees’ perceptions of Eni’s corporate CoH, focusing on satisfaction, awareness, utilisation, perceived value, unmet needs, and differences across occupational and demographic groups.Methods: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among all Eni employees based in Italy (N = 20,142), yielding 4,878 valid responses (24% response rate). The questionnaire explored awareness, use and satisfaction with corporate health services, perceived relevance, barriers and facilitators, and expectations for improvement.Results: Overall, 72% were satisfied with working at Eni, and 70% with Eni’s health and well-being initiatives. The most valued features were preventive programmes (67%), family coverage (56%), and access to a nationwide network of accredited providers (46%). Awareness and utilisation were higher among executives and managers, women, and employees in large cities, while younger and blue-collar workers reported lower awareness and use. Emerging needs included dental care (59%), cancer prevention (49%), cardiology (38%), and elder-care support (32%).Conclusions: Employees perceived Eni’s health strategy as a valuable complement to the Italian National Health Service, particularly in prevention, specialist access, and family support. Corporate CoH models can support employee well-being and public-private synergies, provided that equity in awareness and uptake is actively addressed.

detail.abstract:
Background: Faith-based organisations (FBO) are key providers of health services in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), particularly in underserved areas. However, evidence on the challenges and resilience of FBO-managed facilities remains limited. This study aims to assess these dimensions to inform health system planning and strengthen government-FBO collaboration.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study of 63 health facilities across 11 SSA countries within the project “Supporting Faith-Based Organizations on the Frontline of Healthcare Service Delivery in Africa”. Data was collected using two tools: the Health Facility Assessment Questionnaire (HFA-FBO) and the Disaster Preparedness Assessment Questionnaire (DPAQ), combining quantitative and qualitative components.

Findings: Facilities faced persistent shortages of specialised staff, limited surgical and emergency capacity, and recurrent stock-outs linked to weak procurement systems. Infrastructure constraints, including unreliable utilities and deteriorating buildings, were particularly pronounced in rural areas. Disaster preparedness was generally low, despite many facilities being located in hazard-prone settings. At the same time, strong community trust, staff commitment, and adaptive practices emerged as key sources of resilience.

Interpretation: FBO facilities remain essential frontline providers but operate under significant structural constraints. Strengthening workforce retention, infrastructure, supply chains, governance, and emergency preparedness is critical to enhance national health system resilience. Greater integration and strategic partnerships between governments and FBOs are needed to ensure equitable and sustainable service delivery.

title: Inattentiveness and the Investment Channel of Monetary Policy
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Inattentiveness and the Investment Channel of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: How does rational inattention interact with financial frictions? I provide new empirical evidence from survey data suggesting that this interaction likely plays a critical role in understanding macroeconomic dynamics. In a simple model, I demonstrate that financially constrained firms tend to be more attentive to economic conditions, consistent with my empirical findings. Embedding this mechanism into a DSGE model, I show that the aggregate investment response to a monetary policy shock depends on this interaction. The model further predicts that credit-constrained firms reduce their investment after an expansionary shock due to tighter borrowing constraints and higher production costs, a prediction I empirically confirm.

title: Credit Expansion in the Caucasus and Central Asia
affiliations: International Monetary Fund - European Department and

detail.title: Credit Expansion in the Caucasus and Central Asia
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes credit developments in the Caucasus and Central Asia (CCA) using several complementary approaches. First, it estimates long-run equilibrium credit levels based on economic fundamentals, providing benchmarks to assess whether observed credit levels are broadly aligned with country characteristics. Second, it applies statistical “gap” measures to identify periods of unusually rapid credit expansion that may signal emerging financial vulnerabilities. Third, it uses the Kalman filter to decompose credit into trend and cyclical elements conditional on macro variables. The results suggest there is scope for further financial deepening in all CCA economies, but the speed of household credit expansion warrants close monitoring. A comparative “horse race” of alternative indicators suggests that no single measure consistently outperforms others across countries, implying that combining various credit gap measures enhances the robustness of risk assessments.

title: VIEX — Visibility Exclusion Index: why search-seeded corpora underestimate algorithmic citation in generative AI engines

detail.title: VIEX — Visibility Exclusion Index: why search-seeded corpora underestimate algorithmic citation in generative AI engines
detail.abstract: This study aims to investigate the selection bias introduced by corpus construction in empirical research on algorithmic citation in generative search engines (Generative Engine Optimization, GEO). GEO research has seeded its corpora from organic search results, a procedure that captures only the intersection of entities visible in search and entities cited by language models. Named-entity recognition was applied to 5,544 responses from three models (Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.6) across two verticals, enterprise management systems and hospitality, comparing the set actually cited to the search-seeded corpus. The search-seeded corpus excluded between 47.5% and 73.2% of the entities cited by the models. Exclusion was not confined to the low-citation tail: in the management vertical, the two most-cited systems, cited in 100% and 99% of category responses, were absent from the corpus. We propose the Visibility Exclusion Index (VIEX) as a measure of bias magnitude and a condition of sampling validity for comparative claims in GEO research. The data indicate that the selection method determines whom the researcher can measure, and that search-seeding systematically underestimates the universe of algorithmic citation.

title: Visibility in Traditional Search and Citability in AI: The Relationship Depends on the Type of Digital Asset

detail.title: Visibility in Traditional Search and Citability in AI: The Relationship Depends on the Type of Digital Asset
detail.abstract: This article aims to examine the relationship between presence in traditional search engines (SERP) and citability in generative artificial intelligence engines (ENDEX) in the hospitality sector. The hypothesis that the two dimensions are equivalent-that is, that appearing on Google would imply appearing in AI engines-is tested empirically across 23 lodging establishments in Campos do Jordao (SP), with an external control in Foz do Iguacu. The results indicate a moderate and statistically significant association between presence in category SERP and higher ENDEX. The relationship, however, is not universal-and the data suggest that the type of digital asset and the nature of the local market are relevant moderating variables. The control (Belmond Hotel das Cataratas, an international reference), absent from the local SERP of Foz, reaches an ENDEX near the sample maximum-evidence that the training corpus of AI engines incorporates sources that transcend local organic ranking.

title: Consumer-Care Pricing in Opaque Marketing Channels
affiliations: , Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr School of Business, Purdue University and ZUEL

detail.title: Consumer-Care Pricing in Opaque Marketing Channels
detail.abstract: Many business-to-business prices are negotiated bilaterally and hidden from rivals. In marketing channels, contract opacity weakens downstream price responses to linear wholesale-price changes because retailers cannot observe rivals' wholesale terms. Anticipating this weaker response, the upstream firm has an incentive to inflate wholesale prices, and retailers' expectations of such opportunism sustain an equilibrium with lower manufacturer profit, retailer profit, and consumer surplus. To examine whether a manufacturer can govern this opacity problem without making wholesale contracts transparent, we develop a model of a manufacturer selling to competing retailers under linear wholesale pricing. Before setting wholesale terms, the manufacturer publicly announces a consumer-oriented pricing rule, modeled as a weight on consumer surplus in its pricing objective. This rule is not assumed to reflect altruism; it is a firm-level pricing policy chosen to maximize manufacturer profit. Under observable contracts, the optimal weight is zero. Under unobservable contracts, however, the manufacturer optimally chooses a positive weight that exactly offsets opacity-induced wholesale-price inflation and restores the observable-contract benchmark. The pricing rule increases manufacturer profit, retailer profit, and consumer surplus relative to the opaque profit-only benchmark. We identify limits: a uniform pricing rule cannot fully correct retailer-specific distortions in asymmetric markets, and the mechanism can be counterproductive under two-part tariffs or downstream decision structures where opacity distorts nonpricing incentives. Extensions show that the mechanism is robust to wary retailer beliefs, broader surplus-sharing objectives, and endogenous consumer-care pricing by retailers. The results position consumer-oriented pricing as a self-enforcing governance device for opaque marketing channels.

title: The Mediating Effect of Trust on Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction in Nigerian e-commerce Platforms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Mediating Effect of Trust on Service Quality and Customer Satisfaction in Nigerian e-commerce Platforms
detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of e-commerce in Nigeria presents a complex interplay between service
quality, customer satisfaction, and the critical role of trust. This study investigates the mediating
effect of trust on the relationship between service quality and customer satisfaction within Nigerian
e-commerce platforms, addressing a significant gap in understanding consumer behavior in emerging
digital markets. Drawing on established theoretical frameworks from service marketing and
consumer psychology, the research conceptualizes trust not merely as a direct antecedent of
satisfaction but as a dynamic mechanism through which service quality perceptions translate into
enduring customer loyalty. The study employs a quantitative research design, utilizing a structured
survey administered to a diverse sample of Nigerian online shoppers across multiple e-commerce
platforms. Data were analyzed using structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized mediation
model, controlling for demographic variables and prior online shopping experience. Findings reveal
that service quality dimensions—including website usability, transaction security, product variety,
and customer support responsiveness—significantly influence customer satisfaction, but this effect is
substantially mediated by the level of trust consumers place in the platform. Trust emerges as a
pivotal conduit: when consumers perceive high service quality, their trust in the platform’s reliability,
integrity, and benevolence is enhanced, which in turn fosters greater satisfaction. Conversely, even
when service quality is objectively high, a deficit in trust can attenuate satisfaction, indicating that
trust functions as a necessary condition for the full realization of service quality benefits. The
mediation effect is particularly pronounced for dimensions involving financial transactions and
personal data privacy, reflecting the heightened risk perceptions in the Nigerian e-commerce context,
where concerns about fraud, product misrepresentation, and delivery reliability are prevalent. The
study further finds that the mediating role of trust varies across different consumer segments, with
younger, more digitally literate users exhibiting a stronger trust-mediated pathway from service
quality to satisfaction compared to older, less experienced users. This suggests that trust-building
mechanisms may need to be tailored to specific demographic and experiential profiles. The research
contributes to theoretical understanding by extending the service quality-satisfaction framework to
incorporate trust as a central mediating variable in a non-Western, emerging market context. It
challenges the assumption of a direct linear relationship, demonstrating that trust is not simply an
outcome but a transformative process that shapes how service quality is interpreted and valued.
Practical implications for Nigerian e-commerce managers are substantial: investments in service
quality improvements must be complemented by deliberate trust-building strategies, such as
transparent return policies, secure payment gateways, verified seller systems, and responsive
customer complaint resolution. Without such trust-enhancing measures, even superior service quality
may fail to generate the expected levels of customer satisfaction and retention. The study also
highlights the need for regulatory frameworks that enforce minimum trust standards across the
industry. Future research should explore longitudinal designs to capture the dynamic evolution of
trust over repeated transactions and examine cultural and institutional factors that moderate the trust-
satisfaction linkage in other emerging economies. Ultimately, this research underscores that in the
Nigerian e-commerce landscape, trust is not a peripheral concern but a foundational mediator that
determines the efficacy of service quality in driving customer satisfaction.

title: When Treatment Misses Need: Marketing and the Misallocation of Opioid Care

detail.title: When Treatment Misses Need: Marketing and the Misallocation of Opioid Care

detail.abstract: There is growing recognition that marketing can create social benefits for consumers as well as economic benefits for firms and communities; and while it can expand access to health promoting products, it can also reinforce market inequalities if misaligned with public need. We study this tension against the backdrop of the US opioid crisis during a time in which medications for opioid use disorder (OUD) were widely available. We link opioid shipments, overdose mortality, media and trade promotion, and healthcare access measures from multiple stakeholders to examine whether marketing mix variables direct OUD treatment toward areas with greater need. We find substantial geographic mismatch, with local retail pharmacies and hospitals/clinics remaining active suppliers for pain opioids. And while treatment supply is positively associated with retail pharmacies and hospital clinics, media and trade promotions only have the same positive effect in counties with high lagged opioid demand. We find that promotions are misaligned in counties with high overdose death burdens and its role in supporting public health treatment is nuanced. The more robust providers of treatment products are distribution through retail outlets and healthcare access at the local level. We include potential implications for a range of stakeholders.

title: Dark Brand: Measuring AI-Assembled Brand Image Accuracy Across Chinese AI Platforms
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dark Brand: Measuring AI-Assembled Brand Image Accuracy Across Chinese AI Platforms
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of dark brand, defined as the brand image that AI systems automatically assemble from publicly available internet content and deliver to consumers without brand-owner participation or review, and presents the first large-scale empirical measurement of its accuracy. We define the dark brand, ground it in brand equity theory (Aaker 1991; Keller 1993) and consideration set research (Wright & Barbour 1977), and develop a three-party cognitive split model describing the structural divergence among brand selfperception, consumer perception, and AI-mediated presentation. To move beyond conceptual analysis, we introduce the Information Unit (IU) method, a systematic evaluation framework that decomposes brand knowledge into atomic, independently verifiable facts, and apply it to measure brand information accuracy across three major Chinese AI platforms (Baidu ERNIE 5.1, Tencent Hunyuan 3 Preview, Zhipu GLM 5.1). Our study covers 233 brands across 19 industries, encompassing 11,958 question-answer evaluations. Results reveal substantial cross-platform variation: mean accuracy ranges from 57.2% to 82.3% across platforms, with 41% of brands scoring below 60 on a standardized composite index. Accuracy varies systematically by information type, with descriptive content showing the lowest accuracy (38.8%-53.1%) and geographic information the highest (83.4%-86.8%). We find that brand prominence strongly predicts AI accuracy, that cross-platform consistency is unreliable (11 brands exhibit a spread exceeding 50 points between their highest-and lowest-scoring platforms), and that the dimensions most critical to purchase decisions exhibit the greatest AI deviation. We propose an accuracy-first principle and a visibility-accuracy quadrant framework for interpreting these findings and discuss implications for brand management in the AI media era.

title: ASQ: Query Sensitivity Analysis — Citability in generative AI engines as a function of prompt design

detail.title: ASQ: Query Sensitivity Analysis — Citability in generative AI engines as a function of prompt design
detail.abstract: This study aims to formalize and expand the concept of Query Sensitivity Analysis (QSA): the empirical finding that an entity's citability in generative AI engines is not a stable attribute of its content, but a function of three independent variables: the entity, the engine, and the query formulation. Experiment 1 (108 responses, accommodation sector, Foz do Iguacu) compared structured natural language (E1) vs. exact keyword (E2). Experiment 2 (5,544 responses, 82 entities across hospitality and ERP) compared branded, categorical, and problem queries across three engines. Results confirm QSA at multi-vertical scale and reveal that sensitivity is a property of the engine x vertical pair: Gemini inverts the profile, being the most robust in hospitality (delta 0.368) and among the most sensitive in ERP (delta 0.828), while GPT is most severe in ERP (delta 0.874). The branded vs. discovery distinction is the determining axis; query subtype (categorical vs. problem) produces a marginal effect (0.014 and 0.023 respectively). A key finding: no entity is Invisible in branded queries: branded citation rates range from 0.968 to 1.000 across all engines and verticals, establishing branded as a necessary but insufficient condition for discovery citability. The specific model versions used were: Google Gemini 2.5 Flash, Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, and OpenAI GPT-4o, all accessed via official APIs on May 22, 2026, with default parameters, without prompt engineering or fine-tuning.

title: Generative AI Exposure and Within-Occupation Wage Dispersion
affiliations: and

detail.title: Generative AI Exposure and Within-Occupation Wage Dispersion
detail.abstract: The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) raises important questions about how new technologies reshape wage structures inside occupations. While prior research has examined technology-driven changes in employment and wage inequality across occupations or worker groups, less is known about whether GenAI exposure is associated with changes in wage dispersion within occupations. Drawing on task-based theories of technological change, we develop a framework of vertical task-rung intensity to explain why GenAI's wagedispersion implications may vary across occupations. We argue that GenAI exposure is more likely to widen within-occupation wage dispersion when occupations combine salient lowerrung codifiable tasks with upper-rung judgment-intensive tasks, creating greater scope for asymmetric task leverage. We test this argument using an occupation-year panel that combines O*NET task measures with BLS/OEWS wage percentiles from 2018 to 2024. Using a difference-indifferences design comparing 2018-2019 with 2023-2024, we find that higher GenAI exposure predicts larger increases in within-occupation wage dispersion, especially in occupations with high vertical task-rung intensity. Supplementary Pew survey evidence supports this mechanism by showing that workplace AI-chatbot use is concentrated in codifiable information-processing tasks, while judgment-intensive decisions continue to require human validation and oversight. A supplementary Ford case analysis using WRDS Revelio role-year data provides additional role-level evidence consistent with these patterns. The study contributes to task-based theories of technological change by shifting attention from between-occupation labor-market effects to wage-distribution changes within occupations.

title: Methodology to Increasing Sales on Delivery Apps for Restaurants
affiliations: Maxima Consulting

detail.title: Methodology to Increasing Sales on Delivery Apps for Restaurants
detail.abstract: This paper presents a methodological framework for designing promotional strategies for independent restaurants operating on third-party food delivery platforms such as Uber Eats, DoorDash, Grubhub, DiDi, and Rappi. The framework is based on four diagnostic phases: product profitability and operational feasibility, schedule and average ticket analysis, customer segmentation, and promotion type selection. It then proposes four execution mechanisms: product discounts, free shipping, free product or bundle-based promotions, and tiered spend-based promotions. The objective is to support restaurant operators in making data-informed promotional decisions that improve profitability, average order value, customer acquisition, and retention while accounting for the high commission structure of delivery platforms. The paper contributes a practical decision-making model for small and independent food businesses in Mexico and the United States.

title: The Bond-Bit Ratio: A Thermodynamic Lower Bound on the Energetic Cost of Information Relative to Matter

detail.title: The Bond-Bit Ratio: A Thermodynamic Lower Bound on the Energetic Cost of Information Relative to Matter

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is founder and CEO of EnviroAI, a company developing environmental monitoring and intelligence technology. The thermodynamic argument presented here is independent of that commercial work and reflects the author's personal research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A single ratio underlies a large class of claims about the energetics of computation, the long-run economics of automation, and the physics of environmental stewardship: the ratio between the minimum energy required to handle one bit of information and the minimum energy required to break one chemical bond. This paper derives that ratio from first principles and fixes its conventions.

At a planetary surface temperature of 300 K, the Landauer bound on irreversible bit handling is approximately 2.87 x 10^-21 J, while the dissociation energy of a single carbon-hydrogen bond is approximately 6.86 x 10^-19 J. Their quotient is approximately 240. This is a floor: a lower bound fixed on one side by the second law of thermodynamics and on the other by the energetics of chemical bonding, and therefore not improvable by any future advance in computing hardware.

We show the ratio is invariant in order of magnitude across the choice of reference bond (200 to 300x), distinguish it carefully from the much larger operational gap observed in deployed systems (10^8 to 10^12), and address the two strongest objections to the comparison: that the two processes are not commensurable, and that the comparison ignores the embodied energy of computing infrastructure.

We then state, as clearly delimited implications rather than proven results, what follows for computation, economics, and environmental stewardship if the asymmetry holds and continues to widen. The conservative claim is narrow and, we argue, unassailable: information is, as a matter of physical law, at least two orders of magnitude cheaper than force, and the gap can only grow.

title: When Platforms Summarize Reviews: Generative AI and Evaluative Signal Translation

detail.title: When Platforms Summarize Reviews: Generative AI and Evaluative Signal Translation
detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly use generative AI to summarize customer reviews, converting dispersed user-generated evaluations into compact, platform-facing representations. This paper examines AI-generated review summaries as evaluative infrastructure through two linked dimensions: representational transformation and operational consequence. Using a 78day panel of 1,188 Amazon products across five categories, Study 1 investigates how AI summaries transform visible review signals into summary-level evaluative representations. The results reveal asymmetric signal translation: AI summaries compress favorable review information and represent evaluative risk less through strict negativity than through mixed or cautionary warning signals. Study 2 examines the potential operational consequence of these representations through a counterfactual ranking simulation. The simulation shows that incorporating AI-summary signals into ranking logic can substantially reallocate Top-20 product visibility, with effects depending on whether platforms operationalize summary valence, strict negativity, or warning-sensitive risk. The findings indicate that AI-generated summaries are not only information-reduction tools; they transform user-generated evaluations into platform-generated evaluative representations that can shape visibility outcomes when operationalized in allocation logic.
